articles.title: EXPLAINER: What is the role of Cardinal Tagle as Dean of the College of Cardinals?
articles.summary: Tagle"s election marks a historic milestone for the Catholic Church in Asia and the Philippines. But what does the Dean of the College of Cardinals do, and why is the position important?

blocks.text: Published October 10, 2026 12:53am
VATICAN CITY —Filipino Cardinal Luis Antonio Gokim Tagle has been elected Dean of the College of Cardinals, becoming the first Asian cardinal to hold the position.
Pope Leo XIV approved the election on October 8, 2026, following the acceptance of the resignation of Italian Cardinal Giovanni Battista Re. The Vatican announced the development on October 9, 2026.
Tagle’s election marks a historic milestone for the Catholic Church in Asia and the Philippines. But what does the Dean of the College of Cardinals do, and why is the position important?
What is the College of Cardinals?

The College of Cardinals is composed of senior Church leaders who advise the Pope and, when the papacy becomes vacant, elect his successor in a conclave. Only cardinals who meet the requirements under Church law may vote in the papal election.
What is the role of the Dean?
The Dean serves as the head of the College of Cardinals in a coordinating and representative capacity. The position is often described as primus inter pares, meaning “first among equals.”
Although the Dean does not govern the Church in place of the Pope, the role becomes particularly important when a Pope dies or resigns, and the Church prepares for a new pontificate.
What happens when a Pope dies?
Under the Vatican’s apostolic constitution Universi Dominici Gregis, the Dean has several key responsibilities during a papal vacancy, known as sede vacante.

The Dean must notify and summon the cardinals to meetings called General Congregations, where they discuss the Church’s needs and prepare for the conclave. The Dean also plays a central role in coordinating the process leading to the election of the next Pope.
If eligible to participate as a cardinal elector, the Dean presides over the conclave. If the elected Pope is not already a bishop, the Dean is responsible for ordaining him a bishop.
Meanwhile, the Cardinal Camerlengo has separate responsibilities concerning the administration and safeguarding of the Holy See’s temporal goods and rights during the vacancy.
Why is Cardinal Tagle's election historic?

Cardinal Tagle is the first Asian cardinal to serve as Dean of the College of Cardinals. His election is a significant development for the Catholic Church in Asia and the Philippines, a predominantly Catholic country with a large Filipino community overseas.
His new position places a Filipino Church leader in a key coordinating role within one of the Catholic Church’s most important institutions.
However, becoming Dean does not automatically make Cardinal Tagle the next Pope. The Pope is elected by eligible cardinal electors in a conclave, and the Dean does not choose the successor alone.
What happens next?

Cardinal Tagle will assume the title of the Suburbicarian Church of Ostia while retaining his existing title of Albano. He will also continue his work as Pro-Prefect of the Section for First Evangelization and New Particular Churches within the Vatican’s Dicastery for Evangelization.

His election is both a historic milestone for Filipino Catholics and an important responsibility in coordinating the College of Cardinals, particularly during a future transition of papal leadership.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: This rare David Bowie self-portrait is going up for auction
articles.summary: Turn and face the strange: ch-ch-changes could be coming to your living room wall. A rare signed David Bowie self-portrait is up for auction and it's even got his handprints — though it'll cost you a…

image.caption: This self portrait, made by David Bowie in 1996, is going to the market for the first time as part of Sotheby’s Modern British and Irish Art Day Auction on Oct. 15. (Courtesy Sotheby's)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Turn and face the strange: ch-ch-changes could be coming to your living room wall. A rare signed David Bowie self-portrait is up for auction and it's even got his handprints — though it'll cost you a pretty penny.
The handprinted 1996 piece is estimated to go for about $60K to $100K

Turn and face the strange: Ch-ch-changes could be coming to your living room wall. A rare signed David Bowie self-portrait is going up for auction and it's even got his handprints — though it'll cost you a pretty penny.
The piece, made by the singer in 1996, is going to the market for the first time as part of Sotheby’s Modern British and Irish Art Day Auction on Oct. 15.
It's estimated to sell for between £35,000 to £55,000 (roughly $66,000 Cdn to $104,000 Cdn).
Bowie originally gifted the painting to his St Ives gallerist. Now, after three decades of being in a private collection, the work is on public view in London ahead of its upcoming auction.
It's part of a series of eight large-scale portraits he made in the mid-1990s, this one being the most expressive of the group.

"This self-portrait captures David Bowie at his most creative and self-reflective. His direct gaze and handprints pressed onto the composition create an unusually personal connection to the artist," wrote Sotheby's senior specialist Jen Hardie in a press release.

"Bold and richly coloured, it demonstrates the strength of Bowie's painting practice in the 1990s and offers a rare opportunity to encounter him not as a musician or cultural icon, but as an artist in his own right."
In case it doesn't end up on your living room wall, have a look at it here.
This self portrait, made by David Bowie in 1996 is going to the market for the first time as part of Sotheby’s Modern British and Irish Art Day Auction on Oct. 15. (Courtesy Sotheby's)

In the painting, which was done on paper, the musician, actor and performer stares directly at the viewer, emphasizing his famously uneven sized pupils — one was larger than the other, creating the impression of differently coloured irises.
And of course, the handprints Bowie pressed himself on either side of the painting's lower third are an especially intimate touch.
So if you’ve ever wanted a literally hands-on piece of Starman history, now’s your chance.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Griffin Jaeger is a reporter and producer with CBC's entertainment unit. He also formerly hosted and produced content for The National’s digital platforms. You can reach him at griffin.jaeger@cbc.ca

articles.title: Ed Davey faces growing revolt against leadership as senior Lib Dem MP quits
articles.summary:
Treasury spokesperson Charlie Maynard reportedly resigned in attempt to unseat leader as party slips in polls

Ed Davey is facing a growing revolt against his leadership of the Liberal…

blocks.text: Ed Davey is facing a growing revolt against his leadership of the Liberal Democrats, following the resignation of a senior frontbench figure on Friday.

Charlie Maynard, the Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson, has handed in his resignation in an attempt to unseat Davey after months of frustration that the party is failing to cut through with voters, the Guardian understands.

Daisy Cooper, the party’s deputy leader, immediately backed Davey, saying he enjoyed the support of the “vast majority of MPs”, who wanted him to lead them into the next election and were “furious at this distraction”.

“We Liberal Democrats are the last line of defence against a Reform UK government, and Ed is determined to lead a strong and united party into the next general election whenever it comes,” Cooper said in a statement.
“As Ed said at conference, we are in the fight of our lives against the right who want to turn our country into their version of Trump’s America.”
Maynard’s resignation, first reported by the Financial Times, came four days after Alison Bennett, the Lib Dem care and carers spokesperson, stood down from the frontbench.

Davey has led the party since 2019, first as acting leader and then officially from August 2020. At the 2024 general election he steered the party to its most successful result in more than 100 years. The party now has 71 MPs, and is the third biggest party in the House of Commons. But the party has slipped to fourth or fifth in national opinion polls behind the Greens and Reform UK, and frustration has mounted over a failure to attract voters in a disparate political landscape.

At the party’s conference in Brighton in September, Davey played down criticism from a Liberal Democrat council leader who questioned whether he was the right person to lead the party. Julian Brazil, the leader of Devon county council, said the party was “sleepwalking into irrelevance” and “lacking ambition”.

Davey unveiled a plan for a £17bn income tax cut in a speech aimed at shoring up the party’s support among former Conservative voters, which he said would be paid for entirely by increased growth, created through rejoining the EU’s single market and customs union.

But his resistance to Labour’s proposals to change the pension triple lock to help pay for a national care service, announced in Andy Burnham’s Labour Party conference speech, was met with opposition by senior and backbench Lib Dems, with one saying his defence of the current policy “gaslights an entire generation into believing it’s for our benefit”.

articles.title: ‘Medieval’ and ‘rather disturbing’: US plan to livestream execution elicits global condemnation
articles.summary: Pentagon said execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, would be broadcast live

blocks.text: The US is facing worldwide condemnation over a “barbaric” plan to execute a disabled man by firing squad and livestream it to the public, with critics comparing the Trump administration to dictatorships in Iran and Afghanistan.
The Pentagon confirmed on Thursday that the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at a military base at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009, would be livestreamed on 3 December.

The United Nations’ office of the high commissioner for human rights warned on Friday that broadcasting the killing would amount to a public execution and “breach the absolute prohibition of torture”.

The plan also drew opprobrium from politicians, religious leaders and human rights advocates in the US and abroad. Hillary Clinton, the former US secretary of state, wrote on social media: “A barbaric idea, beneath our dignity as a country. Push back on this.”

Yassamin Ansari, the first Iranian American Democrat elected to the US Congress, posted: “In Trump’s America, we’re doing public executions now. WTF. This is what happens under brutal dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan. It’s all part of Trump’s authoritarian takeover of the United States.”

Britain, which abolished the death penalty in the 1960s, moved to distance itself from the execution. Bridget Phillipson, the UK’s equalities minister and Labour party chair, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that she found the concept “rather disturbing”.
Phillipson stressed that the decision was a matter for the US government, adding: “They are a close ally. Does that mean that we support everything the US government does? No.”
Under US military law, a president must approve an execution by firing squad. Trump did so on the recommendation of his defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, according to the Pentagon.

Hegseth gleefully confirmed the livestream plan after previously saying that the execution would be public. Speaking to the conservative broadcaster Real America’s Voice, he said people should be able to watch because they need to understand that there were “serious consequences” for such crimes.
Asked whether Hasan had made any final requests, Hegseth replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”

Now 56, Hasan was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013 after being convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. Twelve of those killed and 30 of the wounded were soldiers.

The former army psychiatrist opened fire with a handgun at a medical facility at Fort Hood on 5 November 2009 as soldiers waited for medical checks before deployment. He was shot by a police officer during his arrest and left partly paralysed, and now uses a wheelchair.

The execution is expected to be the first by firing squad carried out by the US military since 1945, when army private Eddie Slovik was executed for desertion during the second world war. The last US military execution of any kind took place in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged.

Hasan’s case comes amid renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the US following the botched lethal injection of Tennessee death-row prisoner Christa Pike last week. Her lawyers said she awoke in hospital “angry and confused” and remained seriously ill and shackled to her hospital bed.
Media have sought to televise US executions ⁠in the past, but have been blocked by the courts. No other country is known to televise or livestream legal executions, experts said.
Indeed, public executions have largely disappeared around the world. Amnesty International recorded at least 17 in 2025, including 11 in Iran and six in Taliban-run Afghanistan.

In the US, executions have been conducted privately for about nine decades. The hanging of Rainey Bethea in Kentucky in 1936, witnessed by thousands, is generally regarded as the country’s last public execution, although another hanging took place in Missouri the following year.

Experts said there was no known precedent for livestreaming a legal execution. The execution of the Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh in 2001 was made available to victims’ relatives through closed-circuit television, but was not broadcast publicly.

The proposed live stream has prompted criticism from religious leaders. Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, said it was a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered”.
after newsletter promotion

Politicians from both sides of the aisle also spoke out. Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House of Representatives armed services committee, said the plan was “disturbing and makes a mockery of our legal system”. The Democratic senator Chris Murphy described public executions as “medieval”.

The Republican senator Thom Tillis said Hasan should face the death penalty but that broadcasting his execution was “beyond disgusting”, arguing that public executions were associated with oppressive regimes.
Others warned that the spectacle would be counterproductive and act as a recruiting sergeant for US enemies seeking fresh propaganda.

Ned Price, a former deputy to the US representative to the United Nations, posted on X: “You can take it from those of us who’ve spent years working on terrorism: the surest way to spawn more radicalized zealots is to glorify violence, embrace a cult of death, and create a martyr for the cause.

“Or take it from [al-Qaida] and ISIS, whose tactics offer the closest modern-day approximation of Hegseth’s proposal. Either way, it’s hard to conjure a more vivid example of his trademark performative bravado, which routinely damages America’s image and, in this case, so ghoulishly leaves us more vulnerable.”

Some experts have raised questions about whether the live stream could be challenged in court. Eugene Fidell, a military law specialist at Yale Law School, said Hasan could seek legal action to block the public display of his death.

Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at the University of California, Berkeley, said the announcement raised serious questions about the dignity of the condemned prisoner and the government’s motivation for staging such an unusual spectacle.
“This is a president who’s about spectacle and that’s, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver,” she told the Associated Press.

Justin Mazzola, deputy director of research at Amnesty International USA, said: “Livestreaming the taking of a life by firing squad would only compound the cruelty of the death penalty and perpetuate the cycle of violence that the authorities purportedly seek to end.

“This announcement adds to the display of cruelty that we have just witnessed in the senseless pursuit of the execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee. The US death penalty is irredeemably broken. It is high time that the US authorities, at all levels, use their power to show human rights leadership and end this ultimate cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment once and for all.”

Other experts argued that public access could increase transparency around capital punishment. Deborah Denno, a death penalty specialist at Fordham University, told the AP that a live stream could make the process more transparent at a time when the botched execution in Tennessee had renewed questions about how the state puts prisoners to death.
It remains unclear whether Hasan will seek to challenge his execution in civilian court, a move that could significantly delay the proceedings.

articles.title: Does Polanski have to go? Greens at the crossroads after Holborn and St Pancras
articles.summary:
Pressure is building on the party leader after byelection defeat, a damaging row over Zionism and polls that show him less popular than Nigel Farage

When Zack Polanski addressed his…

blocks.text: When Zack Polanski addressed his campaigners flush with victory after the Gorton and Denton byelection in February, he declared: “Labour’s electoral stranglehold is over.” The election of Hannah Spencer as the new Green MP for the Greater Manchester seat was a seismic victory, he continued: “I said we were here to replace Labour and this is what replacing looks like.”

But in the wake of Polanski’s defeat in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection on Thursday, and a calamitous row over the party’s stance on Zionism, the debate around what, or who, could be replaced has shifted to Polanski himself.

On Friday the leader of the Green party in England and Wales was defiant after losing to Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali, who took 45% of the vote, to Polanski’s 33%. Asked what was going wrong in his party, which has fallen from highs of 21% in some polls after the victory in Gorton and Denton to around 10-11%, Polanski, responded: “If things are going wrong by the fact that we just tripled our vote share and had our second best byelection result in Green party history, you know what? I’ll take that.” While emphasising that Green members would ultimately decide who they wanted as leader, he said: “Of course I can carry on.”.

That the last few months have been difficult for the Greens – and Polanski in particular – is beyond doubt. Polanski himself is, according to new polling from More in Common, now less popular with voters than Nigel Farage, and is the least popular major UK party leader, falling by four points to a -28 net approval.

His standing, bruised by a series of controversies over a failure to pay council tax and the sharing of a post criticising police, has been further damaged by a controversial motion that was adopted at the Green party conference in Brighton last weekend, equating Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, with racism. Polanski’s decision to abstain from the debate and the vote to instead campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, was condemned by his detractors, but also, more significantly, criticised by senior figures in his own party.

The former Green leader Caroline Lucas told BBC Newsnight on Thursday that Polanski “should have been there and he should have voted”. Asked if he should stand down, she said: “I think let’s just see what happens in the coming days and weeks. Obviously he has been completely taken up with this byelection.” Following his defeat she appeared to temper her position, saying Polanski had “transformed the party” and she hoped he would now “help resolve huge issues we face and transform our internal structures”.

On Friday, pressure mounted, as the leader of the Jewish Greens, Vivien Lichtenstein, called for Polanski to step down, saying it was a “big mistake” for him not to have spoken and voted for amendments stating that any future structure of a Palestinian state should be decided by Palestinians, rather than impose a one-state system.

But there was bullishness among the Polanski faithful, with Greens Organise, the leftwing faction that backed his leadership bid, saying he should stay on. A statement from the group said that “not all growth and success is linear, there will be ups and downs; the real test for a political organisation is how we deal with failure”. It added: “We have reshaped the British political landscape. The Green party can still become the ecosocialist party we need. Zack is still the leader who can get us there.”

Green party supporters pointed out that the party achieved a 13-point swing from Labour in Holborn and St Pancras, traditionally a safe Labour seat. The Camden councillor Hamza Chowdhury – who was overlooked as the candidate in the constituency in favour of Polanski – went as far as saying the result was “a huge win for the Green party and the wider movement”.

Polanski cheerleaders point out that since he was elected leader in September 2025, the party has quadrupled its membership to more than 230,000. As well as the winning of its first ever seat in the north of England, he presided over the Greens’ best-ever performance in May’s local and mayoral elections, including gaining their first-ever directly elected mayoralty, in Hackney, east London.

Nonetheless, the result in north London exposed the dual challenge Polanski now faced, said Luke Tryl, the director of More in Common. At the same time as the replacement of Keir Starmer with Andy Burnham had brought disillusioned progressives back to Labour, Polanski had become a more polarising figure.
after newsletter promotion

A series of missteps, starting when he shared a social media post critical of police after the Golders Green stabbings, had damaged his popularity with the wider UK public, added Tryl. “It was just one of those moments which gave soft Green supporters pause for thought. Similarly, many people don’t vote directly on something like the Zionism is racism motion, but it adds to that sense of ‘oh, I thought these were nice guys who were focused on the environment’.”

The result in north London was a “good one” for Labour, he added, despite the drop in its majority. While governing parties usually get hit hard in byelections, the drop in Holborn was below the average for defending a seat at byelections in any postwar parliament, he noted.

But Labour hopes of the death of the Green party were likely to have been exaggerated. “I think writing off the Greens is premature,” he said. “Burnham has managed, for now, to unite the left, but a lot of big decisions, including on North Sea oil drilling and, more importantly, the budget, are coming down the line.”

As for Polanski, the path towards rebuilding the popularity that saw him win the support of young voters desperate for hope and change would lie in a return to his original economic messaging around “rip-off Britain” and generational fairness, rather than divisive internal battles, said James Baggaley from UCL’s Policy Lab. “The question for the Greens and Polanski now is: do they want to reassure voters on questions of antisemitism and also get back to what they were actually winning on, which was the economy?”

articles.title: Man named Hitler Mussolini elected mayor in Peru
articles.summary: The left-wing candidate won a narrow victory in a remote district in the Peruvian Andes, exit polls show.

blocks.text: A man named Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores has secured a narrow victory in Peru's local elections, exit polls show.
The candidate for the centre-left Ahora Nación party was elected mayor of Queropalca, a remote district in the Peruvian Andes.
Some 229 residents voted for the 45-year-old, putting him ahead of the second-place candidate from right-wing Renovación Popular Perú by just 25 votes.
Despite being elected to represent fewer than 1,000 people, his forenames being those of two notorious fascist dictators has drawn outsized international attention to the small corner of the country.
Data from Peru's elections office showed a little over 700 people had participated in the election, with Simeon securing around 34% of the vote.
He was born in the district in the central department of Huánuco, some 360km (224 miles) from the capital, Lima, according to his candidate profile.

That he shares his name with Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini - "two of the most well-known figures of 20th-Century European totalitarian regimes" - has made his candidacy a "striking event", local outlet Peru21 reported.
Despite the curiosity generated by his name, local media noted that Hitler Guesclin Alba Sánchez had been elected mayor of Yúngar in 2018.
He reportedly beat rival candidate Lenin Vladimir Rodríguez Valverde after campaigning on the slogan "I'm the good Hitler".

A politician named Adolf Hitler Uunona attracted similar attention in 2020 after winning local elections in Namibia - a former German colony where Adolf and other Germanic first names are not uncommon.

articles.title: Watch: 'I am Jane Doe' protests across US call for end to sexual violence
articles.summary: Protests against sexual violence took place across more than 40 US states on 8 October.

blocks.text: Protests were held across the US on 8 October, calling for an end to sexual violence, following allegations of sexual assault involving members of a fraternity at Cornell University.
Survivors, students and advocates rallied and protested in communities and on college campuses across more than 40 states.

This comes after a lawsuit was filed against by “Jane Doe”, who alleges she was given drugs and alcohol before being sexually assaulted by several members of Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity while incapacitated in October 2024. She has accused Cornell University of failing to adequately investigate and discipline those involved.
Following the filing of the civil lawsuit, prosecutors reopened the case. New York Governor Kathy Hochul appointed the state’s attorney general as special prosecutor.

articles.title: Ombudsman inspects vacated office of Jinggoy Estrada
articles.summary: Representatives from the Office of the Ombudsman inspected the office vacated by Senator Jinggoy Estrada, according to a GMA News report, quoting Senate Secretary Renato Bantug.

blocks.text: Published October 10, 2026 12:18am
Representatives from the Office of the Ombudsman inspected the office vacated by Senator Jinggoy Estrada, according to a GMA News report, quoting Senate Secretary Renato Bantug.
“I was informed of the Ombudsman inspection yesterday and of the GSIS ocular the other day," Bantug said.
He added that he did not receive a request from the Commission on Audit for an inspection, but the Commission asked the Senate to clarify the chamber's policies on such matters.
On Monday, the office was seen bare and stripped of furniture, sockets, and tiles.
Senator Vicente Sotto III was supposed to take over the room after replacing Estrada as Senate President Pro Tempore.
The room was missing most of its floor tiles, and there was no furniture such as tables and chairs.
Also noticeable were exposed and hanging electrical wires and the removal of wall sockets throughout the office.
The office’s comfort room was also stripped of tiles from the ceiling, walls, and floor, while the shower and toilet bowl had been removed as well.
In response, Estrada's staff said dismantling fixtures and other materials from a Senate office previously occupied by a senator is an established and accepted practice.
"It must also be emphasized that similar instances of dismantling fixtures and materials from a vacated senator's office have occurred in the recent past," Estrada's office said.

"This is neither new nor unusual — it is an established and accepted practice within the institution, and singling out this particular transition for scrutiny is both unfair and misleading," it added.
In June, Estrada was detained at the Quezon City jail after the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division ordered his arrest on non-bailable charges of plunder.
Since then, he has been unable to attend Senate hearings due to his ongoing detention. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: ‘The real deal’: Sagal Abdi-Wali’s journey from child refugee to Labour MP in former PM’s seat
articles.summary:
Decades of volunteering combined with years of active local party politics, propels Abdi-Wali to victory over Green leader Zack Polanski

For Sagal Abdi-Wali, the new MP for Holborn and St…

blocks.text: For Sagal Abdi-Wali, the new MP for Holborn and St Pancras, being elected to replace Keir Starmer in the north London constituency is “deeply personal”, she said in her acceptance speech.

The 43-year-old has lived in the area since the 1990s when, as a seven-year-old, she fled war-torn Somalia with her mother and four brothers, eventually settling in Gospel Oak in Camden, which largely falls within the constituency. Her journey from refugee to member of parliament was one which she hoped would inspire “people who look like me”, she said. “This is Camden and this is Britain.”

If she represents many in the diverse and youthful neighbourhood, however, Abdi-Wali is also very much a Labour party insider. Decades of volunteering in the community dovetailed with many years of active local party politics, even before she was elected to the borough council in 2022. She became the Labour cabinet member responsible for housing two years later, and in May was elected the first Black female leader of Camden council. She also chaired the local constituency party for four years.

blocks.caption: Zack Polanski, second left, applauds Sagal Abdi-Wali, as she is announced winner in the byelection. Photograph: James Veysey/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Those deep party and community roots help explain how Abdi-Wali was selected from a long list of more than 100 to fight the seat for Labour after Starmer’s resignation last month, say friends – and were also key in seeing off the challenge from the Green party leader, Zack Polanski.

“She genuinely is deeply rooted in so many different parts of the constituency,” says a close friend who was involved in her campaign. “I suppose all MPs like to think they are, but with Sagal it is the real deal.

“There’s a real community connection there, [and] I think the Green party and Zack Polanski underestimated how energetic and big the Labour campaign was going be. I don’t think they knew that those very deep roots in the constituency existed.
“That’s the thing about a byelection, you only have four weeks. So if those roots are already there, you’ve got a huge, huge head start.”

Tulip Siddiq, the Labour MP for neighbouring Hampstead and Highgate, agrees: “Her love of Camden is so obvious, and people really value that. She’s very caring, very local, and she genuinely seems to have a passion for politics and public service.”
After “lots of flat candidates” in the past, Siddiq says, “people like a bit of passion.”

It was walking past increasing numbers of homeless people in King’s Cross in the austerity years of the 2010s that encouraged Abdi-Wali to become more active in party politics, perhaps unsurprisingly given her own background. “It was only when I was old enough to look back and think about it in a philosophical way,” she has said, that she noticed “my mum was always looking after us and made our lives nice, serene … whether we were in a refugee camp or temporary housing.”

blocks.caption: Sagal Abdi-Wali with Lucy Powell, the deputy leader of the Labour party, poses for a selfie with supporters. Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty

blocks.text: Homelessness and housing would be one of her priorities as an MP, she said in her acceptance speech on Friday morning, as would calling for Thames Water to be brought into public ownership and working to increase access to jobs and apprenticeships for young people – all causes that chime with Andy Burnham, too.

Abdi-Wali has long been involved in community groups working with young people, including being a governor of several schools and founding football clubs where she still plays regularly and is “pretty aggressive on the pitch”, according to her close friend. (She is also an “ardent” Spurs fan, the friend says, “which may count against her in the [Arsenal-dominated] constituency”.)

Housing is one issue where she has faced some criticism; Abdi-Wali was the cabinet member in charge of the borough’s housing when in November 2024 the housing ombudsman published a damning report calling the council’s service rude, defensive and inadequate. Friends point out that she had been in the post for only six months and defend her record in the period she was in charge of the brief.
Abdi-Wali also shrugged off a tweet when she was selected by Reform’s Zia Yusuf , which Labour representatives swiftly called “clearly racist” and was condemned even by other senior Reform figures.

“I rang her and said: ‘Are you OK?’” says Sidiq. “I wanted to reassure her that we were there for her. But she said: “‘No, I feel very resilient about it. It’s made me even more determined to get on and do it.’”

articles.title: UK coastguard agency chief faces calls to resign over use of unverified data to back up pay plan
articles.summary:
Regulator says poll cited by Virginia McVea in move to strip rescue officers of pay did not sufficiently back up her claim

The head of the UK coastguard agency is facing calls to resign…

blocks.text: The head of the UK coastguard agency is facing calls to resign after she was found to have used unverified data to back up her controversial plan to strip rescue officers of their pay.

Virginia McVea, the chief executive of the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA), claimed more than 90% of coastguard rescue officers supported the proposal, citing an official survey. Now, after an Office for Statistics Regulation (OSR) investigation, the agency has admitted its poll did not sufficiently back up the claim.

Nicola Savage, a national officer for the GMB union, which represents coastguard rescue officers (CROs), said: “If Ms Mcvea is unable to produce the reports she refers to, we would consider this as a deliberate attempt to mislead. If this is the case, she should resign – as hundreds of coastguards have already asked her to do.”
Joe Robertson, one of several MPs who has campaigned on CROs’ behalf, accused McVea of misleading MPs and coastguards during three separate meetings at which he said she cited the figure.

He called on her to “do the right thing and apologise for misleading MPs, CROs and the public”, adding: “Please also give a written account of how you came to repeat this false line over and over again and why you still have not published the surveys which you promised to MPs in our meeting on 24 June.”

The MCA’s plan to strip coastguards of their pay was a reaction to a major court defeat. A judge affirmed that, while CROs volunteer for service, they are classed as workers with the right to minimum wage and holiday pay because they are paid for their time, among other factors. Rather than respect this status, the MCA tried to stop remunerating CROs in an attempt to reclassify them as volunteers.

This led to heavy criticism from MPs, CROs and coastal communities, with the GMB union saying nearly 600 CROs backed its vote of no confidence in McVea. Seeking to defend the plan, McVea cited the 90% figure, but MPs told the Guardian in July they felt misled by her.

In his letter to McVea this week, the OSR’s director general, Ed Humpherson, told her: “Neither of the surveys [cited] asked CROs directly about their support for the proposed volunteer model, so do not provide evidence relating to the reported claims. [The] MCA has been unable to provide any further evidence to underpin the reported claims.”
Leaked results of an MCA survey, revealed by the Guardian in July, showed CROs had actually been asked how volunteer and worker models would affect their availability.
after newsletter promotion

The results suggested the MCA had included people who said they would become less able to respond to calls if they were volunteers, as well as those who replied “other”, among those in support of the volunteer model. The agency said at the time that “survey findings were considered alongside a range of operational, legal and practical factors”. But it refused to say how.

The plan was ultimately scrapped by the maritime minister, Keir Mather, as he responded to near-universal criticism. CROs are still waiting to find out what system will be adopted, but it is understood the option of not paying coastguards is no longer on the table.
The MCA has been approached for comment.

articles.title: US imposes sanctions on International Criminal Court
articles.summary: The US says the measures are aimed at restricting the tribunal's resources and ability to operate.

blocks.text: The Trump administration has imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), saying it wants to restrict the tribunal's resources and ability to operate.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.
The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.
The announcement comes just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

US President Donald Trump has reacted sourly to the Norwegian prize's choice of winner this year and last, after having expressed a desire to receive it himself. He criticised Pillay for being part of a panel that accused Israel, as well as Hamas, of war crimes during the 7 October conflict.
The US says the ICC has no jurisdiction over it as it never ratified the statute founding it - but the international court has investigated US actions elsewhere.
Rubio said Trump would not allow the ICC to prosecute Americans, adding: "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC."
The US sanctions will stop US companies from providing goods or services to the ICC, such as banking or software.

Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing the sanctions in the hope that the ICC and its member countries would address US concerns. He said the measures had been structured to allow other countries to negotiate a possible solution.
He also called on US allies that were ICC signatories to "rein in" the institution.

articles.title: ‘Abolish ICE’: Mamdani, AOC and other Democrats urge action after New York shooting
articles.summary:
US immigration officer shot man in car where five-year-old child was sitting in the Bronx, sparking fierce protests

Leading New York Democrats expressed anger and demanded curbs on…

blocks.text: Leading New York Democrats expressed anger and demanded curbs on Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) violence after a federal officer shot a man driving a car in which his five-year-old son was sitting, sparking fierce protests.

At least seven shots were reportedly fired and the man was hit in the neck late on Thursday afternoon as children were coming home from school in the busy Marble Hill neighborhood of the south Bronx in New York City.
Federal authorities on Friday morning identified Oscar Belgal as the man shot, saying he was undocumented, from the Dominican Republic and had a felony record.

Marcos Charles, a senior ‌ICE official, said Belgal refused ​to exit his car when approached by ‌federal officers who were trying to arrest him, and then accelerated, ‌struck two ICE vehicles and drove towards other officers. An ICE agent then shot Belgal.
But Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a New York congresswoman, and Zohran Mamdani, the city’s mayor – all of whom are Democrats – led strong condemnation of ICE’s conduct.
Darializa Avila Chevalier, the Democratic New York candidate, rushed to the protests and was knocked over in the chaos as local police and demonstrators clashed.

blocks.caption: Darializa Avila Chevalier at a protest after an ICE officer shot a man in New York, on Thursday. Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPA

blocks.text: The wounded man was conscious and hospitalized, authorities said.

Mamdani called the incident “unconscionable” and said on Thursday night that ICE, part of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), had “whisked him away” from the New York-Presbyterian Allen hospital in upper Manhattan.

A similar incident occurred in Texas last month after a man was shot by an ICE officer in Austin and despite a bullet lodged in his back was taken by the federal authorities from a local hospital to ICE detention about 140 miles away.
Ocasio-Cortez and Mamdani demanded ICE be abolished.
Both Hochul and Mamdani spoke to Donald Trump and Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, by phone on Thursday night.

“I have been on ​the phone with President Trump and Secretary Mullin negotiating ‌the release of the man ICE agents ‌shot. Those negotiations were unsuccessful,” Mamdani told a press conference. He demanded from the Trump ‌administration that ICE stop its enforcement actions in New York City. “ICE is rotten to its core,” he said.
ICE has been stepping up arrests all year despite withdrawing massed militarized ranks from Minneapolis in January and adopting a more covert approach to enforcement.

Both Hochul and Mamdani demanded that ICE cease enforcement operations in New York and the governor said she expressed outrage to the Trump administration on behalf of all New Yorkers. Hochul added that the incident could easily have ended in tragedy.
“No child should ever have to experience the terror of gunfire,” she said. The child was being looked after by his family on Friday.
The streets where the shooting and protests took place were calm on Friday morning but many residents remained shocked and angry.

“Here’s an innocent child that was caught in the crossfire,” said Calvin Hayden, a south Bronx native. “That child could have been killed.” Hayden heard about the shooting the night before and said he was immediately disturbed. He came to Marble Hill to see the aftermath.
“I don’t believe ICE has any reason or right to be in New York City,” he said, adding he thought New York was already equipped on its own to handle immigration disputes without ICE presence.
“There’s a lot of individuals who are not committing crimes and they just want to make a better life for themselves,” he said.
Some drivers on 225th Street yelled anti-ICE sentiments as they drove past the scene.

blocks.caption: A vehicle with a bullet hole and a shattered window at the scene of the shooting. Photograph: David Dee Delgado/Reuters

blocks.text: Mullin said on Friday morning that the ICE officers involved in the shooting did not know there was a child in the vehicle and defended the agency’s actions. He said that Hochul had asked the DHS for a pause on enforcement in New York.
“No, we are not putting a pause on enforcement,” he said.

Mullin criticized New York’s “sanctuary” policies, ​which restrict how much city agencies and police cooperate with immigration authorities, for allowing Belgal to be free instead of turning him over to federal agents, adding that New York was refusing to honor federal requests to turn over criminal immigrants.

Belgal, 28, has prior convictions, was serving five years of probation for felony grand larceny and was also arrested on drug charges in 2025, a case that is still pending, according to the New York police department.

“What happened today was an outrage,” Mamdani said late on Thursday, adding: “When ICE agents opened fire, a five-year-old child – a five-year-old child! – was in the back seat of that car. Thank God that child is physically unharmed.”

Witnesses told local media they heard the child yelling at the officers after the shooting. At least 20 people have been shot by federal immigration agents under the second Trump administration, as well as a rise in deaths in detention.

“ICE is a rogue, lawless and paramilitary surveillance agency. It does not belong in New York City and it should not exist in the United States of America. Abolish ICE,” Ocasio-Cortez said in a statement.
The representative also condemned the retail company Target for allowing federal enforcement teams to use its parking lots as staging areas from which to launch arrest operations.

One witness told the City Reporter, a local news outlet, that she saw a man bleeding on the ground in front of a car and observed an agent holding a small child. Videos also showed bullet holes in the windshield of an SUV, NY1 reported.
Protesters held signs saying:“Jail all killer ICE agents” and “Leave our neighbors alone.”
Hands Off NYC and the New York Immigration Coalition, two local groups, held an emergency press conference to decry ICE’s ongoing presence in the neighborhood.

blocks.caption: Demonstrators protest near the scene of the shooting. Photograph: David Dee Delgado/Reuters

blocks.text: “ICE, get the fuck out of our neighborhood,” shouted Vanessa Gibson, Bronx borough president. “I’m angry that we have to be here … We are a working-class community. We don’t deserve this type of treatment from the White House.” She encouraged the crowd to get involved in opposing ICE, saying: “There are more of us than there are of them. I want this to be a moment that we turn into a movement.”
Protesters gathered at the hospital where Belgal was taken. The police set up barricades and protesters quickly clashed with officers in a chaotic scene.
Demonstrators banged drums and shouted: “Shut it down,” and “ICE out!” as cars driving by honked in support.

Standing outside the hospital, Murad Awawdeh, the president of the New York Immigration Coalition, said he wanted to see an independent investigation into the shooting led by New York officials. He also called on the DHS to release footage of the shooting and for the officer who fired the shots to face prosecution.
“The pain that you’re witnessing is people who are witnessing their neighbors, their family members, their friends being ripped away,” he said.

ICE has arrested more than 19,500 people in New York and nearly 18,000 in New Jersey during the second Trump administration, mostly Latin American immigrant men without criminal histories, Gothamist reported earlier this week using government data, adding that those totals were more than double the number of such arrests in the last 18 months of the Biden administration.
Lex McMenamin and Joanna Walters contributed reporting

articles.title: Trump administration hits International Criminal Court with sweeping sanctions
articles.summary: The Trump administration imposed sweeping new sanctions Friday on the International Criminal Court, which it says is politicized and attempting to illegally prosecute Americans and Israelis. The…

image.caption: The International Criminal Court (ICC) is seen on Dec. 9, 2025, in The Hague, Netherlands. (Peter Dejong/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

The Trump administration imposed sweeping new sanctions Friday on the International Criminal Court, which it says is politicized and attempting to illegally prosecute Americans and Israelis. The court denounced the U.S. move as "an assault on the rule of law" aiming to prevent its work.
ICC denounces the move as an 'assault on the rule of law'

The Trump administration has imposed sweeping new sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal that the United States believes has become politicized and attempted to unfairly and illegally prosecute Americans and Israelis on war crimes charges.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the sanctions on Friday, after the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to South African prosecutor Navi Pillay, a former judge at the ICC and other international courts.
U.S. President Donald Trump has coveted that prize for himself. The move, however, long predated the Nobel Prize announcement.

"We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate against us," Rubio said in a video address posted to social media. "The United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC."
Why the ICC is in the fight of its life with Trump

The sanctions block any assets that the ICC as an institution might have in U.S. jurisdictions and set a six-month timeline for U.S. companies and individuals that have business with the court to wind that business down.

Rubio said both Republicans and Democrats have deep reservations about the court, which was established to prosecute war crimes and crimes against humanity that might not otherwise be handled by the parties involved.

items: Netanyahu is flying freely over Canada as his international arrest warrant remains in place
The Trump administration sanctioned ICC judges. A Canadian judge is fighting back

blocks.text: But he said that only Trump was willing to move against the court.

"Both parties agree on this, but only President Trump has the resolve to take the action needed to end this threat once and for all," Rubio said. "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC."
ICC denounces 'assault on rule of law'

The ICC denounced the step as an attack on the rule of law and the foundations of international order, themes that Rubio had appeared to embrace only two days ago in a speech in front of the Acropolis in Athens.

"It is an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do," the court said in a statement. "It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law."
U.S. sanctions Canadian judge on International Criminal Court

ICC President Tomoko Akane, a citizen of U.S. ally Japan, said the court would "continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes."
She also appealed to other ICC members for support. "This is not just about defending a single institution, but about safeguarding the international order grounded upon the rule of law."
Rubio had said that the U.S. expects its allies to join in the actions against the ICC. Those include many NATO members in Europe and Japan.
"If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, piece by piece, until Americans are threatened no longer," he said.
Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen, posting on X, called the sanctions announcement "a deeply regrettable step. We stand firm in defence of the court."
He said the six-month window before the sanctions take effect "creates scope for dialogue."
As host state of the court, the Netherlands is a strong defender of the ICC.
