articles.title: Macron and Steinmeier struggle to revive Franco-German ties
articles.summary: Presidents Frank-Walter Steinmeier and Emmanuel Macron are about to step down from their offices. Their meeting in France made it clear how urgently the Franco-German partnership needs new momentum.

image.caption: Presidents Steinmeier (l) and Macron and their wives met in Paris for a farewellImage: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The German delegation passed through Paris without being hindered by the student strikes taking place on the streets of Paris. The motorcades moved through the French capital without disruption. Around the Arc de Triomphe and the Champs-Elysees, however, traffic was at a standstill for hours. Due to the high-profile visit, the streets were cordoned off over a wide area.

Emmanuel Macron had decided on a special gesture to send off Frank-Walter Steinmeier, his German guest: The military honors took place under the Arc de Triomphe. And so, early in the morning, the German national anthem rang out in the heart of Paris — amid sunshine and bitter cold.

It was a generous gesture of friendship and symbolism, yet it seemed to be from a bygone era. In both countries, populists on the political fringes are gaining support. In Germany, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) ranks first in nationwide polls. In France, Emmanuel Macron could soon be succeeded by either Jean-Luc Melenchon of the far left or Marine Le Pen of the far right.

Added to this is an economic crisis that threatens prosperity. Unresolved issues of social justice are driving younger generations into the streets. At the same time, social media is increasingly becoming a tool of disinformation and "accelerating doubts about democracy," Macron said in Paris.

While the AfD may soon form its first state government in Saxony-Anhalt, President Steinmeier remained confident. He insisted that Germany would continue to "play a leading role in Europe" in the future and that Germans would remain good Europeans. But he did not say where he drew this certainty from. Questions from journalists were not permitted at the joint press conference at the Elysee Palace.
A future, but no plan

Political scientist Jacob Ross isn't surprised by this. Both Macron and Steinmeier lack a "genuine agenda for Germany, France, and Europe." Both represent political systems that "seek to respond to 21st-century crises with 20th-century solutions," said the expert on German-French relations at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP).

Even though Steinmeier and Macron have different political styles, Ross sees parallels — especially where their policies have failed. One example of this is strategic foreign policy issues, such as dealing with Russia. "For a long time, they pursued a policy based on integrating Russia into Europe, and then both were overwhelmed by the events of 2022 and had to adjust their course," said Ross. Since then, both have merely reacted to current affairs, according to the political scientist.
Little support for Macron's ideas
Emmanuel Macron has made some bold moves for Europe, but without support from Berlin, says Ross. Germany's political leadership has long reacted with caution to proposals from Paris.

A joint initiative that both countries recently promoted to the European Commission is aimed at combating unfair competition. Countries that gain an advantage through unfair practices should face strict European measures.

Macron joined German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in speaking out in favor of this. Although China was not explicitly named, the initiative is seen to be primarily aimed at that country. Beijing uses enormous subsidies to support its companies, whose products flood the European market, while European firms continue to face barriers when trying to access the Chinese market.
How Europe's defense sector is trying to gear up

Germany and France have also long sought greater cooperation in the defense sector. Yet major joint defense projects are making little progress. When the planned joint fighter jet, the FCAS, fell through in June, officials emphasized ongoing cooperation on the future MGCS main battle tank. And yet differences on this became apparent during the state visit.

As German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius arrived in Paris, French Chief of the General Staff Fabien Mandon stated during a hearing in the French National Assembly that Germany had decided to withdraw from the tank project. A day later, Mandon clarified that he had expressed himself ambiguously. But some observers believe that such misunderstandings are a sign of dissatisfaction on both sides — below the political level — regarding cooperation with the other partner.

It is this political level that often ends up having to set the record straight in such cases. This time was no exception: Pistorius firmly refuted the claim that the project was on the verge of being scrapped. "The MGCS project is not over; it is not dead; it has not been terminated by anyone — quite the contrary. It is a core project of Franco-German cooperation on land systems," said the German defense minister.

The focus is primarily on digital information processing in combat, as well as unmanned and automated systems. Germany and France would continue their cooperation, Pistorius insisted, and MGCS is an important future project for both countries and their armed forces.

blocks.caption: The French and German Presidents took part in a ceremony in the heart of ParisImage: Abdul Saboor/REUTERS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The future of defense and space

On Friday, the presidents of France and Germany visited several facilities near Bordeaux that are closely linked to space exploration and nuclear deterrence. These include ArianeGroup, a Franco-German company that, among other things, manufactures the nuclear-capable M51 missiles for French nuclear submarines. The itinerary also included visits to startups that are looking far into the future.

It was unofficially reported during the visit that this focus of the trip was a personal priority for Macron. The French president has long spoken of a European dimension to France's nuclear deterrent. Considering announcements from the US saying it would reduce its commitment to Europe, his views are gaining increasing traction.

As early as 2020, Macron proposed a strategic dialogue on the role of French nuclear weapons in European security. Several countries, including Germany, have since expressed interest. Now, further steps are being considered. The focus is on what Macron once called "forward deterrence," such as joint military exercises and visits to strategically important locations. A permanent deployment of French nuclear weapons in other countries remains off the table. Furthermore, according to French nuclear doctrine, France always retains sole decision-making authority over the use of its nuclear weapons.

Steinmeier's two-day state visit to France ended on Friday afternoon. So far, there has been little sign of new momentum in Franco-German relations. This makes it all the more urgent for the successors to the two presidents to develop a shared vision for the future of the relationship between the two countries starting next year.

Macron and Steinmeier will step down from their posts almost simultaneously in 2027 after ten years in office. The state visit to France thus also served as a final joint meeting, marked by some ceremonial farewells.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: US imposes sanctions on international criminal court
articles.summary:
Trump administration says US ‘doesn’t need’ ICC after accusing court of unfairly targeting Americans for war crime charges

The United States imposed sanctions on the

blocks.text: The United States imposed sanctions on the international criminal court (ICC), its latest escalation against an entity the Trump administration has accused of politicization and unfairly targeting Americans for war crime charges.
The ICC accused Donald Trump’s officials of attempting to “obstruct the course of justice” after “an assault” on the international legal order.
Just hours after a former ICC judge was awarded the Nobel Peace prize, Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, announced in a video that the US would move to impose financial sanctions.

“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us. Because our message is clear: the United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC,” Rubio said in a video posted on X. “We don’t need that court and we don’t want it.”

In a statement, the court warned that “history will judge this moment” and urged other members to ensure it can continue the function. “It is an ⁠attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the Court from doing what ⁠it was created to do. It is an assault ​on the rule ‌of law and ‌on the very foundations of the international legal order,” ‌the ICC said in a statement.

The Trump administration has repeatedly condemned the ICC for issuing arrest warrants for Israeli officials, including Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. It also opened an investigation into the actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, although the case has been closed. “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC,” Rubio said.
The ICC was established in 2002 as an international tribunal to hold countries accountable for war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity.

articles.title: Darth Vader's lightsaber is up for auction
articles.summary: A Darth Vader lightsaber used in the climactic duel in Cloud City, where the villain tells Luke Skywalker "I am your father," is among the highlights of the Ultimate Star Wars Auction to be held by…

image.caption: A costumed Darth Vader character poses at the Hasbro and Amazon Star Wars interactive experience at the Empire State Building in New York in this 2024 file photo. (Evan Agostini/Invision/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

A Darth Vader lightsaber used in the climactic duel in Cloud City, where the villain tells Luke Skywalker "I am your father," is among the highlights of the Ultimate Star Wars Auction to be held by Heritage Auctions on Nov. 12.
Movie prop up for grabs was used in the iconic 'I am your father' duel

In July, a lightsaber with Luke Skywalker's severed hand from The Empire Strikes Back sold for $3.75 million US at auction — the highest price ever fetched for a prop used in a Star Wars film, according to the auction house.
Now, someone can buy the saber that did the severing.

A Darth Vader lightsaber used in the climactic duel in Cloud City, where he tells Skywalker "I am your father," is among the highlights of the Ultimate Star Wars Auction to be held by Heritage Auctions on Nov. 12.

The Vader saber, also used in Return of the Jedi, is expected to fetch at least $1 million US. It is one of more than two dozen lightsaber props that will be up for sale at the auction that spans Star Wars Episodes I through IX, as well as other films and TV shows from the galaxy George Lucas created.

A costumed Darth Vader character poses at the Hasbro and Amazon Star Wars interactive experience at the Empire State Building in New York in this 2024 file photo. (Evan Agostini/Invision/The Associated Press)

Other pieces include the duelling lightsabers forcefully wielded by Ewan McGregor's Obi-Wan Kenobi and Hayden Christensen's Anakin Skywalker in Revenge of the Sith that are expected to go for at least $10,000 US apiece.
An EE-3 carbine blaster wielded by Boba Fett throughout The Empire Strikes Back is estimated to bring in more than $100,000 US.

Also included are a Yoda puppet hand used by Frank Oz in the character's original appearance in The Empire Strikes Back, C-3PO actor Anthony Daniels' signed, personal third-draft screenplay for the original 1977 Star Wars and a TIE Fighter pilot helmet from Rogue One: A Star Wars Story.

articles.title: China agrees to ‘halve’ hybrid car exports to EU in landmark deal
articles.summary:
Brussels says Beijing’s shipments could fall by more than half over four years, cutting millions of vehicles amid fears for European jobs

The EU said it has reached a landmark deal with…

blocks.text: The EU said it has reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.

Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the deal was the first of its kind and the result of “intense” negotiations with China since June to curb a trade deficit of €1.18bn (£1bn) a day, which has caused mounting tensions between the two economic powers.

The deal “opens the prospect of cutting China’s export [of hybrids] by more than a half”, Šefčovič said, adding that this would translate into a reduction in exports of plug-in and battery-powered hybrid cars by “several millions” over the next four years, said Šefčovič said Šefčovič at a press conference in Beijing on Friday.

“It is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tension,” he said, a reference to the usual investigations that must take place before safeguards under WTO trading rules are put in place.

China has been flooding Europe with cars, including hybrids and pure battery electric vehicles (BEVs), threatening European manufacturers. Hybrids combine an internal combustion engine with a small battery. They are sold by carmakers as a transitional step towards BEVs.

Šefčovič said the Chinese had recognised the political pressure building in every member state in Europe with “literally thousands of job losses” at risk because of the flood of cheap imports from China across many sectors including chemicals and textiles.
He said EU leaders were “clearly expecting very fast action” from the European Commission and the Chinese recognised that.
“I am glad to say that the Chinese partners appreciated this very strong political argument, and therefore, we can proceed through the negotiated solution,” he said.
“This ‌is far from the end. It’s a crucial first step, but only a first step,” Šefčovič told ‌reporters in Beijing where he had travelled to hold ​talks with his Chinese counterpart.

Earlier this week senior EU officials said they were heading to Beijing to seek what they called a “proof of concept” or pilot scheme with one sector which they hoped could then be expanded to other areas under pressure from Chinese competition.
Šefčovič said he put “so much emphasis” on the negotiations because it was “very difficult to stop” a trade war once it was declared.
As part of a 16-point agreement, Beijing and Brussels will continue negotiating on cars, export restrictions on rare earths and access to China for more food and drink from the EU.
after newsletter promotion

China said both sides would adhere to “procedures concerning company price undertakings” for hybrid cars suggesting one method of curbing sales would be to set higher minimum price tags for Chinese cars sold in Europe.
The EU commissioner will brief EU diplomats in Brussels on Sunday ahead of a leaders’ summit on Thursday.
A statement from the Chinese ministry of commerce said China is “willing … to continue facilitating the approval of export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU”.

It added that both sides had “reaffirmed their commitment … to properly handle differences within the framework of WTO rules, and to continuing to stabilise and balance bilateral trade and economic relations”.
While China and the EU acknowledged “differences” between them it appears that China has accepted the EU’s request to create a new model for trade balances starting with a pilot on hybrid cars.

articles.title: Author or artificial intelligence? Literature in crisis
articles.summary: AI is a hot topic at this year's Frankfurt Book Fair. An international literary scandal raises questions about machine-generated texts.

image.caption: The pavilion of the Guest of Honor, the Czech Republic, at the 2026 Frankfurt Book FairImage: Hannes P. Albert/AFP

blocks.text: It's the hot-button topic at the Frankfurt Book Fair: How profoundly will artificial intelligence transform the book industry, and how can this transformation be regulated?

Given the warnings about the technology's long-term risks to humanity as a whole, such debates might seem rather narrow in scope. In reality, however, they concern very concrete issues — copyright protection, the power of major tech corporations and the future of creative work. Many of those involved agree that the political measures taken don't go far enough.
This year, however, another aspect has entered the debate: Can we actually recognize when a text has been written with the help of artificial intelligence, and how can it be proven?

These are the questions being asked in the current literary scandal surrounding Haitian-Canadian author Thélyson Orélien. His debut novel, "C'était ça ou mourir," (It Was Either That or Die) was published in Canada in the spring and then in France in late summer.

blocks.caption: The controversy around Thélyson Orélien's book has sparked a larger debate on AI and authorshipImage: Joel Saget/AFP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The migration story was universally acclaimed, with translation rights sold in more than 20 languages. The book even made the longlist for the prestigious Prix Goncourt.

Then, suddenly, allegations emerged that the book had been written almost entirely using AI. Orélien, until then a rising literary star, suddenly found himself branded a fraud, despite denying all the allegations. His nomination for the Prix Goncourt was withdrawn.
So, who should we believe now — the author or the AI that claims to have identified AI-generated writing?
When the origins of texts become uncertain
"We will have to learn to live with doubt," says Hannes Bajohr, a professor of German literature at the University of California, Berkeley.

blocks.caption: Hannes Bajohr, professor for German Studies at the University of California, BerkeleyImage: Jen Siska

blocks.text: He has spent years examining how AI is changing both writing and reading. His prediction: If the origins of texts can no longer be reliably established, we will have to evaluate them differently. What matters will be their quality alone, rather than whether AI was used in the writing process.
Nina George, a best-selling author and honorary president of the European Writers' Council, is unwilling to accept this.
At the Frankfurt Book Fair, she was awarded the Friedrich Perthes Prize in recognition of her commitment to issues including AI and copyright.

blocks.caption: A leading advocate for European authors' rights and copyright reform: Author Nina GeorgeImage: Sabine Kieselbach/DW

blocks.text: George has addressed the European Parliament and the German Bundestag, and speaks and writes tirelessly about the dangers of AI models. It is perverse, she says, that an author should suddenly have to prove that their writing is human. The focus of her campaigning remains the large corporations' self-serving mentality and the protection of copyright.
Can anyone become an author with AI?
But what if an author sees AI not as an enemy, but as a tool that makes writing easier?
American author and artist Luke Stoffel deliberately used AI in his memoir, "How To Win One Million Dollars" and "Shit Glitter," and was open about doing so.
"I'm dyslexic," he says in a video interview. "I've always written and made up stories, but I never dared to take them any further."

blocks.caption: Luke Stoffel openly talks about his use of AI in writing booksImage: Privat

blocks.text: It was only with the help of AI, he says, that he was able to fulfill his dream. The technology drew his attention to weaknesses in his writing and suggested a marketing strategy that actually worked.
Then, in May 2026, he received an award from the Independent Book Publishers Association (IBPA) for the book.

For South African author Coral Hart, AI is actually the foundation of her business model. Publishing under various pseudonyms, she releases more than 200 different novels every year, spanning romance, thrillers and mystery, all independently published.

She sees herself as an ideas person, as well as an editor and publisher. Although none of her books has yet become a bestseller, the business is profitable. According to Hart, each of her books reaches more than 5,000 people.
Many publishers already working with AI

New York-based author Luke Stoffel considers the entire debate hypocritical. Many publishers have been working with AI tools for some time. He's certain that "right now, a million-copy bestseller is being printed that was created with the help of AI. The author won't admit it, and then there'll be a scandal."
It is entirely possible that the scandal surrounding Thélyson Orélien is precisely that story. But we may never know for sure.
For now, the battle against the tech giants continues. Even the companies themselves are increasingly concerned about losing control.

At the very start of the fair, the German Publishers and Booksellers Association issued an appeal to policymakers in Berlin and Brussels, calling for stricter regulation of artificial intelligence, more urgently than ever before. More than 150 publishers have already signed it.
But for now, it remains just an appeal. And the question of what authors themselves should be permitted to do with AI will undoubtedly continue to fuel debate in the future.
Reading 2.0: How AI is changing our books
This article was originally written in German.

Senate screenshot
The amount includes undeclared cash, properties, and income of the Vice President, her spouse Mans Carpio, and their companies

MANILA, Philippines – A financial forensic analyst called as a witness by the prosecution told the impeachment court on Friday, October 9, that Vice President Sara Duterte’s undeclared wealth tops P800 million.

Alexander Cabrera, a certified public accountant and a lawyer who is chairman emeritus of PwC Philippines, said that based on his review of voluminous financial records of the Vice President and her husband, Mans Carpio, the couple has around P817 million in undisclosed assets and income from 2022 to 2025.

The amount covers their undisclosed personal cash based on discrepancies between their audited financial statements and declarations in the Vice President’s Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN), undeclared other personal and real properties, and undeclared income of their companies Cale88, Metro Chow, and Gencorp based on the mismatch between income tax returns and bank inflows.
Cabrera explained that Carpio’s financial records were included in the analysis because they have “absolute community of property” as a married couple.
“We used a conservative method. There’s no duplication in count,” Cabrera added.
The forensic report he produced also flags other behaviors in Duterte’s financial records, which he found suspicious, such as:

items: single, large credit card purchases, such as P205,007.29 for Ginza Inakaya and P111,109.24 for Don Quijote in Japan;
17 insurance policies not declared by the Vice President in her SALN;
and a variation of check kiting (Cabrera calls it “nagtitinikling ang pera“), where funds move in and out of an account through manager’s checks so the amounts won’t be included in year-end reports

blocks.text: Cabrera will be cross-examined by the defense on Monday, October 12.
He is already the last witness of the prosecution panel, which has decided to drop the bribery case against the Vice President. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Judge orders U.S. government to return Arizona man deported to Equatorial Guinea
articles.summary: A U.S. judge has ordered the Trump administration to facilitate the release and return of an Egyptian man who was deported to Equatorial Guinea this year and has since ‌been jailed there.

blocks.text: World·New
A U.S. judge has ordered the Trump administration to facilitate the release and return of an Egyptian man who was deported to Equatorial Guinea this year and has since ‌been jailed there.
Trump-appointed judge's order concerns Ahmed Soliman, a gay man from Arizona
How Trump turned ICE into a mass deportation machine
Ahmed Soliman is one of hundreds of migrants sent from the U.S. to African countries under so-called third-country deportation deals that the U.S. government has ​used to accelerate removals.

Last month, ⁠Soliman said he had ‌faced rough treatment by Equatorial Guinean police officers. Video obtained by Reuters showed police pulling firearms on a group of migrants including Soliman at the Hotel Bamy in Malabo, where migrants were being held.
After Reuters published its story, Soliman was taken into custody and ⁠has been held incommunicado at a police station that has also been used to detain human rights activists.

items: U.S. Supreme Court says Trump can continue deportations to 3rd countries — for now
ICE shooting of New York man in car with 5-year-old sparks protests, anger from mayor

blocks.text: In a ruling seen by ‌Reuters on Thursday, U.S. judge John C. Hinderaker said the Department of Homeland Security must facilitate Soliman's release from custody and his return to the U.S. That includes arranging any travel ​documentation he would need to return, the judge appointed by President Donald Trump said in his order.
The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to ⁠a request for comment. Equatorial Guinea has also not responded to ⁠requests for comment about Soliman's case.

DHS said after the hotel incident that it wasn't responsible for the treatment of individuals outside of the U.S. The department has said in court filings it received assurances from Equatorial Guinea that deportees would be safe there.
Democrats condemn payments to Equatorial Guinea
Soliman, 31, wrote in a declaration ⁠to ⁠an immigration judge ​last year that he feared being killed in Egypt because he is ​gay.
According to court documents and published reports in Arizona, where he resided, Soliman came to the U.S. at the age of four with his family on a religious visa.

An incident between police in Equatorial Guinea and individuals is shown on Sept. 5 at the Hotel Bamy in Malabo, Equatorial Guinea, in a video obtained by Reuters and verified with archival imagery of the hotel. The men being confronted by police were migrants deported from the U.S. (Reuters)

He jeopardized his legal status as a lawful permanent resident in 2021 when he drove a vehicle while under the influence of fentanyl. He was sentenced to over two years in prison for charges including aggravated assault, a charge brought if someone suffers injuries as a result of the accident.

In 2024, DHS began removal proceedings for Soliman, but late last year did not appeal a court ruling that a hearing should be held on whether his fears of persecution were credible. He was deported in April before either that hearing or his challenge to his Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention were heard.

Human Rights Watch said in a report that between January 2025 and August 2026, 536 people had been deported to African countries "that are neither their country of citizenship nor habitual residence."

Reuters has documented ⁠40 of those cases in which migrants granted U.S. legal protection after being persecuted for their LGBTQ status were deported to third countries in Africa that either criminalize same-sex relations or have been described by the State Department as ⁠hostile to LGBTQ ‌people.

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, in a letter last year to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, condemned what she called a "stark departure" in U.S. foreign policy, referring to a $7.5-million payment to Equatorial Guinea from the State Department's account for migration and refugee assistance.

"This highly unusual payment — to one of the most corrupt governments in the world — raises serious concerns over the responsible, transparent use of American taxpayer dollars," the New Hampshire Democrat wrote.
Supreme Court to weigh in on 3rd-country practice
U.S. governments under both parties have long tried to adhere to the principle of not sending persons to countries where they are at risk of cruel and inhumane treatment, including torture.

The second Trump administration is carrying out expansive plans for the deportation of individuals not authorized to be in the country. Democrats and human rights and immigration activists have highlighted cases in which they say due process has not been afforded to deportees, and others in which lawful residents or even U.S. citizens have been targeted in immigration enforcement operations.

items: U.S. deporting thousands of Mexican migrants to Central American countries
Liberia to begin accepting up to 1,200 deportees from the U.S.

blocks.text: More than 25,000 migrant overall have been deported to 29 countries not of their origin since last year, human rights activists have said. UN human rights experts commissioned by its Geneva-based Human Rights Council late last month called on the U.S. to stop the third-country practice.

"These migrants are being transferred to countries or territories with which they have no ties, which can be a traumatizing and isolating experience that compounds harms already suffered which triggered their fleeing to the U.S. in the first place," they said in a statement. Those most at risk, they added, were those who could be targeted due to gender, sexual orientation, gender identity or human rights advocacy.

U.S. Supreme Court justices will hear arguments in December over the Trump administration's policy of deporting migrants to nations other than their own. The court on Sept. 29 let the administration continue the policy for the time being, putting on hold a federal judge's ruling that removing migrants to third countries is unlawful.
With files fro CBC News

articles.title: US imposes sanctions aiming to 'dismantle' International Criminal Court
articles.summary: The US has announced new sanctions on the International Criminal Court. It's the latest in a series of steps by the Donald Trump administration as it seeks to "dismantle" the intergovernmental…

image.caption: The US has had the ICC on its radar more or less throughout the second Trump termImage: John Thys/AFP

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump's administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize.

This comes as the US has in recent months made no bones about pursuing what Secretary of State Marco Rubio has called a "sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court."
The United States and Israel had both strongly opposed the court's arrest warrants for top Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Since 2020 and the back end of Trump's first term, the US had also opposed investigations into military actions in Afghanistan that "deprioritize" alleged US wrongdoings, focusing on the Taliban, but can nevertheless include them.
What did the State Department say about the ICC sanctions?
"President Trump will never allow the International Court to prosecute Americans," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement.

"That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate," he said.
The ICC said the US sanctions aimed to obstruct an "independent" international court supported by more than half of the UN's members.

"The court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes," said ICC President Tomoko Akane.
What is the ICC?
The International Criminal Court is an intergovernmental organization and international tribunal based in the Dutch city of The Hague.

It's the only permanent international court with the theoretical jurisdiction to prosecute individuals for international crimes like genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and illegal aggression.
The ICC was set up in 2002 and is underpinned by the Rome Statute treaty.
More than half the countries in the world, 125 in total, are full parties to the Rome Statute, having signed and ratified it.
Several of the world's most significant powers — not least China, India, Russia, the US and Israel — do not recognize the court's jurisdiction.
There is, however, a grey area in that the court accepts challenges from ratified members against individuals from countries that do not recognize the court.

That is why high-profile arrest warrants against Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, and Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, have been issued in recent years — following respective complaints from Ukrainians and Palestinians.
What were the prior signs of Trump administration pressure on the ICC?
The US has been increasingly critical of the ICC during Trump's second term.

Rubio has often led the charge, for instance, writing an opinion article for the Wall Street Journal in mid-July this year saying, "America never agreed to a world tribunal that can override our own courts and the Constitution."

He argued it was possible for US "soldiers, police officers, Border Patrol agents and elected leaders" to be "dragged before an international court" and tried by judges "from random countries across the globe."

Just over a week later, on July 25, Venezuela's new administration — transformed after the US abduction of Nicolas Maduro in January — announced that it planned to withdraw from the Rome Statute and the ICC.

In response, the US State Department welcomed "the new Venezuelan government's partnership on American-led efforts to dismantle the corrupt and worthless ICC," calling on "all members of the ICC to withdraw from the Rome Statute."

A few days later, the military junta in Chad announced that it was withdrawing from the ICC. It said it had done so after a US request, with Washington urging other African countries to follow in the Russian-backed junta's footsteps.
The recent sexual misconduct scandal surrounding the ICC's chief prosecutor Karim Khan, who was dismissed in July, provided more ammunition the US could aim at the court.
In August, the US imposed sanctions on the ICC's president, Japanese judge Tomoko Akane, and Abdoulaye Seye, a Senegalese trial lawyer at the court.
Sanctions launch was first anticipated during UN General Assembly
These signs had been accompanied in recent months by speculation that, before long, the US would sanction the ICC as an organization, not just members of it.

Last month, reports circulated widely that President Donald Trump might announce the sanctions during his speech at the UN headquarters in New York, with off-the-record sources in the US and the court's seat in the Netherlands saying they were preparing for the measures.
Trump ultimately leveled sharp criticism at the ICC in his address on September 22, calling it an "evil" organization, but at the time made no announcement of new sanctions.

articles.title: The Alberta question: How separatists took hold of the province’s governing party
articles.byline: Grant LaFleche, Mark Kelley, Rachel Ward

image.caption: Separatist leader Jeff Rath, left, has increasingly come in conflict with Premier Danielle Smith over the question of Alberta's sovereignty. (Tim Kindrachuk/CBC)

blocks.text: The Edmonton stage should have been a safe space for Danielle Smith. A place where an Alberta premier could revel in partisan applause.
Instead, it was the scene of a political mugging.
Smith sat on the stage, dressed in a crisp white suit, alongside her cabinet at the United Conservative Party’s 2025 annual general meeting to take questions from the party faithful.
One man, dressed in a blue blazer and baseball cap, stepped up to the microphone and launched into a familiar refrain of western grievance with the federal government.
But he wasn’t there to ask Smith a question. He was there to send a message.
"My question for the room is how many of all of us favour a free and independent Alberta?" shouted Jeff Rath, constitutional lawyer, UCP member and the bulldog of the Alberta independence movement.
The crowd rose in an ovation. Smith, appearing unfazed, shot back with a political maxim Albertans would soon hear repeatedly.
"Well, I support an independent Alberta within a united Canada."
At past AGMs, Smith’s proclamations were received by cheers. But on this day, the audience booed her.

Smith offered her united Canada pitch twice more during the AGM, touting her successes in addressing Alberta’s concerns with Liberal Prime Minister Mark Carney. Why give up now, she said, when victory was at hand?
As before, she was booed. Both times.

Jeff Rath, seen on the big screen, whips up the crowd at the UCP annual general meeting in Edmonton in November 2025 with a call to action for independence. Premier Danielle Smith, seated in white, was booed when she pushed back. (CBC)
The jeering of a premier at an AGM wasn’t normal. Something had changed within the UCP. It was now home to a movement, activated during the COVID-19 pandemic, bent on breaking up Canada.

"There was a cohort of the population who were living in alternative reality in COVID and they just got active," said former Alberta premier Jason Kenney, whose 2022 resignation came, in part, at the hands of that movement.
Separatism cheered, premier booed at UCP convention

A fifth estate investigation found that Smith leaned on this movement during her rise to the premiership. While polling consistently shows independence is out of step with the vast majority of Albertans, the premier nonetheless called a separation referendum for Oct. 19.
Albertans are divided. So is the UCP. And some of the separatists Smith once welcomed into her "big tent" party are now trying to remove her from office.

Through interviews, reviews of government documents and separatist video archives, the fifth estate has identified four critical steps the independence movement took to push Alberta into a referendum that could change the fate of a nation.
Step 1: The takeover

In the spring of 2021, a slender man with slicked-back hair and a thin voice travelled from one Alberta town to another like an itinerant preacher, speaking to whoever would listen. But old- time religion wasn't Dennis Modry’s mission.
He was an evangelist for an independent republic of Alberta.
In the 1980s, Modry was a surgeon hailed for performing the first heart-lung transplant in Western Canada.

But his medical career crashed in 2013, after Alberta Health Services suspended his surgical privileges over performance issues. He unsuccessfully fought the suspension in court and in 2017, he failed to renew his licence. By the time of the COVID-19 pandemic, Modry’s medical career was over.
By 2021, he had embraced Alberta independence as his new calling. In speeches, Modry laid out a path to create a new country through a referendum.
Modry wasn't calling for the formation of a separatist political party. Past attempts in Alberta were electoral failures.
His path to a referendum was through the UCP itself, by transforming it into a government with an "independence focus."

Dennis Modry speaks at a separatist rally in Edmonton in October 2025, urging Albertans to vote to leave Canada. It was one of his last public events after a judge found in March 2025 that he misappropriated $1.3 million from his aunt and uncle. (CBC)

"When Jason Kenney and the UCP were elected, they had 120,000 members," Modry told an audience in Medicine Hat in 2021. "We want to grow that membership to four or five or six or seven hundred thousand people." A group that large, even in a province of nearly three million voters, could shape an election, he said.
If they were successful, Modry was fond of saying, 2023 could be the last provincial election in Alberta’s history.

Modry joined lawyer Jeff Rath and sporting goods store owner Mitch Sylvestre in creating the Alberta Prosperity Project, an organization dedicated to promoting separation. The trio also joined the UCP.
Even with separatists joining the UCP, there was little chance the party would call a referendum so long as Kenney, the premier and party’s founding leader, remained in office.
Kenney would have to go.
Step 2: The takedown

From the start, Jason Kenney wanted to keep separatists out of the UCP. He thought they were more of a nuisance than a clear and present threat, he told the fifth estate, but nonetheless tried to erect a firewall to keep them out.

"I wanted to send a message to them that this is not your party. You want to play in politics? Good for you. It's a democracy. You get to do that in your separatist parties. This is not one of them," Kenney said.

So when the 2017 merger of the Progressive Conservative Party and its rival, the Wildrose Party, created the UCP, Kenney wrote a loyalty-to-Canada clause into the unification agreement, expecting it to be part of the UCP’s foundational principles.
But when the party held its first AGM in 2018, the committee deciding on what principles members would vote on didn't include the loyalty clause on the ballot.
The door that Kenney wanted to slam shut was left open.

Three years later, the COVID-19 pandemic pushed Kenney’s leadership into a crisis. Some Albertans, including those who would join the 2022 Ottawa convoy and border blockade at Coutts, Alta., were enraged by Kenney’s pandemic restrictions. Even some of his own MLAs rebelled, and Kenney was forced into a leadership review.
Modry saw something else in Kenney's political woes.
Opportunity.

"The options are, Kenney is replaced or he's not replaced," Modry said in a November 2021 speech in Brooks, Alta. "Could that party move with a new leader or with Jason to an independence-focused future?"
The sequel to the convoy movement
Kenney told the fifth estate that in the fight for his political life, he didn’t recognize where the threat was coming from.
"I will admit, I and my team were late to notice what was going on," he said.
In May 2022, Kenney received only 51 per cent support from UCP members. He resigned immediately. After the dust settled, Kenney saw what happened.
"Two-thirds of the people voting in that review vote … were brand new," Kenney said. "They came in on COVID anger, anti-vax sentiment. A lot of them were separatists.
"Separatism is the sequel to the convoy movement."
With Kenney gone, and the UCP ranks filling with separatists, a referendum seemed more realistic than ever. What the separatists needed was a new and sympathetic UCP leader.
That person turned out to be a political exile hosting a talk radio show in Calgary.
Step 3: Elect a leader

Danielle Smith had been the leader of the opposition Wildrose Party until 2014, when she crossed the floor to join the governing Progressive Conservatives. But when the 2015 election came, Smith failed to secure the PC nomination in her own riding.
So Smith made her living on the radio.
Eight years later, Kenney’s demise offered the chance for a political resurrection. When she set her eyes on the UCP leadership, Smith extended an olive branch the former premier never would have.

"I knew how important it was to address the issues of autonomy, and I talked to Dr. Modry as one of my first steps," Smith said during a UCP leadership debate hosted by the separatist Alberta Prosperity Project. "I take your movement very, very seriously … because you have the power to be the 'or else.'"
Danielle Smith won the UCP leadership in 2022 in part because she courted the support of the party’s newest membership base: Alberta separatists. (CBC)

During the leadership campaign, the UCP membership rolls exploded. At the time of Kenney’s resignation there were about 60,000 voting party members. On the night of the leadership vote, there were nearly 124,000.
Smith, who declined an interview request from the fifth estate, was the only one out of seven leadership candidates who did not serve in the Kenney government.
The outsider won after six rounds of voting, returning to political prominence with only 54 per cent support. But she led the UCP to a majority government in the 2023 election.

She did not campaign on separation. But after the election, Smith continued to accept separatists in the party. In the spring of 2025, for example, she attended the annual UCP fundraiser held by the Bonnyville-Cold Lake-St. Paul constituency association. Seated on either side of her at the head table were two prominent separatists: the association’s president Mitch Sylvestre and Dennis Modry.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith sits with two of Alberta’s key separatist leaders at UCP fundraising event dinner in 2025. On the right is Dennis Modry and on the left Mitch Sylvestre, who is also a UCP constituency association president. (Bonnyville Cold Lake St Paul UCP Association/Facebook)
The referendum was only one step away.
Step 4: Hold the referendum
In 2025, Modry, Sylvestre and Rath were busy marshalling their forces for a petition campaign to force a referendum.
But there were hurdles. Separatism was unpopular among Alberta voters. And the law required at least 294,000 signatures on a petition for it to qualify for a referendum.

In July 2025, Danielle Smith’s government changed the rules, slashing the number of required signatures to 177,000, and boosting the number of days to get them from 90 to 120. On the same day the law changed, Sylvestre filed a separatist petition with Elections Alberta, asking a direct remain-in-Canada-or-leave question.
Then Elections Alberta got in the way. An independence question came with constitutional implications, so the petition was sent to the courts for review.

This turned out to be a temporary setback. Smith’s government changed the law again in December 2025, stripping Elections Alberta of its powers to refer a petition to the courts. As before, Sylvestre filed papers the day the law was changed. This time his petition, labelled StayFree Alberta, was approved.
The petition ultimately cleared the reduced threshold with 222,600 verified signatures.

Mitch Sylvestre, separatist leader and a UCP constituency association president, delivers the StayFree Alberta petitions to Election Alberta in May 2026 alongside Jeff Rath, standing to his right. A First Nations court challenge tossed the petitions into legal limbo. (Alice Burgat/Radio-Canada)
The fight wasn't over. A group of First Nations chiefs went to court, arguing the Alberta government failed its constitutional duty to consult them on an issue that could impact their treaty rights.
On May 13, 2026, the courts agreed, and stopped the StayFree Alberta question from becoming a referendum.

Smith could have used the ruling as an off-ramp, said Orlagh O’Kelly, a lawyer representing the chief of the Sturgeon Lake Cree. Instead, on May 21, Smith announced her own question, designed to evade a court challenge.
On Oct. 19, Albertans would be given two choices: remain in Canada or start the process of having a binding referendum to stay or leave.
"When Danielle Smith was actually elected in 2023, she didn't run on any of this," said O’Kelly. "Jason Kenney got taken out by that arm of the party and she knows that."
Smith said she was "fiercely loyal" to Canada and would vote for Option 1 — to remain in Canada. She also reassured separatists she empathized with their feelings.
But some UCP separatists reacted to a question about a referendum with outrage. For Rath, Smith was a turncoat. To get the referendum they wanted, they needed an extra step.

"We just need to get rid of her sooner rather than later and proceed to have a special general meeting of the party to vote on her leadership the same way we did with Jason Kenney," Rath told the fifth estate.
Step 5: The removal
As referendum day got closer, Smith repeatedly said her position, and that of her government, is a vote to stay.
Her party is a different story. A spring poll by Angus Reid found some 64 per cent of party members were separatists. Meanwhile, more than 70 per cent of Albertans reject the idea.
Two weeks after Smith’s referendum announcement, UCP party president Rob Smith — no relation to the premier — said the quiet part out loud on CBC’s The Calgary Eyeopener radio show.

Many of the UCP members are pro-independence, Rob Smith said, including "a large number of the leaders across Alberta that pushed" to make the referendum happen. If the premier had not called the referendum, he said party unity would be in jeopardy.
Separatists turn on Smith
For Rath, Smith is the cause of the party’s ills and "a complete impediment to independence."
"As long as Premier Smith is premier of Alberta, Alberta will never be free," Rath said at a separatist rally on the steps of the provincial legislature in August.
Rath believes separatists already have the influence to take Smith out, claiming they sold upward of 8,000 memberships in 2025 to put separatists on the UCP board of directors.

He has been pushing UCP constituency associations to call for a special leadership review, which can only happen if at least 22 of 87 associations call for it. As of this writing, only two have done so.

But as he plots to overthrow Smith, Rath is grappling with his own legal troubles. He is being sued by two First Nations groups that allege he misappropriated millions of dollars from trust funds his law firm oversaw. Rath has said allegations he misappropriated funds from the trust are false.
Jeff Rath speaks at a pro-separation rally outside the Alberta legislature in Edmonton on Aug. 29, and urged the crowd to push out Danielle Smith as UCP leader and premier. (Bob Grieve/CBC)

Divisions are showing within Smith’s caucus. On Sept. 29, Red Deer MLA Jason Stephan publicly split with the premier’s position and announced he voted for Option 2 — that Alberta should hold a binding referendum on whether to leave Canada — via a mail-in ballot.
At the same time, Smith’s popularity with Albertans has reached its lowest point since the 2023 election. But she has held her course.
During an online conference on Sept. 19, a month out from referendum day, Smith fought back tears while running through a list of grievances often heard at separatist rallies.
"Some begin to ask the painful question: Does this country actually want us?" she asked before returning to the same united Canada mantra that earned her boos in 2025.

A week later, the premier was beaming beside Prime Minister Carney at a press conference in the oil hub of Fort McMurray to announce that the federal government was fast-tracking a West Coast oil pipeline. This was proof, Smith said, that Canada was working for Alberta.

Then on Oct. 7, at a press conference at CFB Edmonton, Smith struck a defiant tone when a CBC reporter asked if she had encouraged the behaviour of separatist leaders, her one-time political allies, by calling the Oct. 19 referendum.
"Well, there is no greater critic of me than the same separatist leaders that you are talking about, because I have been making it very clear that my position is to vote to remain."

articles.title: Saudi coalition vows 'firm' response after airport attack kills 3
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia and its allied forces in Yemen vowed a "firm response" to Houthi attacks that target civilians. The kingdom's authorities said three Saudi nationals were killed in Thursday's attack on…

image.caption: Smoke and flames rise from the main international airport in Riyadh on October 8, in this screengrab obtained from a social media video.Image: Social Media/REUTERS

blocks.text: The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen launched strikes that destroyed targets used by the Houthis, a coalition spokesperson said Friday.
Major General Turki al-Maliki said three rocket launch platforms were destroyed, adding that Houthi attacks on civilians would be met with a "firm response."

The Saudi-Houthi conflict has intensified in recent weeks, with Saudi Arabian authorities having said Friday that Houthi attacks on Riyadh's main international airport on Thursday killed three Saudi citizens and injured several people of "different nationalities."

The King Khalid International Airport was targeted twice on Thursday, the kingdom's civil aviation authority said.The first attack aimed at airport facilities and the second targeted an aircraft that belonged to the Saudia airline.
Houthi attacks on Riyadh raise the stakes of reignited conflict
Hundreds of flights were canceled because of Thursday's attacks, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware.
The Indian Embassy later said Air India had suspended operations through to Saturday, while the Lufthansa Group said its airlines would suspend flights to Riyadh through to October 16.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) on Friday recommended airlines not to operate in additional portions of Saudi Airspace in an updated bulletin.
The EASA said recent attacks had demonstrated the ability and the intent of the Houthis to strike targets deeper inside Saudi territory, including the capital.
On Thursday, the Iran-backed Houthis warned employees at Saudi oil facilities that oil installations remain a target.
Why can't the Saudis defeat the Houthis?
The Saudi-Houthi conflict: What to know

The Houthis have fought a Saudi-led coalition since 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war to reinstate the internationally backed government in Sanaa. Houthi rebels took control of the capital in 2014.
But ever since, the Saudi-led coalition has found it hard to turn the tide of the war that quieted under a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022.
In the last weeks, the Houthis stormed down Yemen's coast, capturing a wide swath of territory that has given them greater control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

A Saudi-led coalition has pressed a counteroffensive against the Houthis fighters and recaptured several areas along the strait, Yemeni officials have said. But the fighting appears to be far from over.
Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis?

articles.title: Navi Pillay, former UN human rights chief, wins Nobel Peace Prize
articles.summary: Pillay is recognised for her "efforts to promote peace and international law", the Norwegian Nobel Committee says.

blocks.text: Pillay's work had been "instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted", said the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, Jørgen Watne Frydnes.
"Navi Pillay's commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career," he said.

"At a time of existential challenges - including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time - international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity."
Frydnes said the committee had not been able to notify Pillay that she had won in advance, "so my message to her would be 'if you see a Norwegian number calling, please pick up'".
Shortly afterwards, Pillay reacted to the news by saying "it must be a joke", and thanked those who had gathered to applaud her.

"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked. Last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, gave her medal to the US president in January as "recognition for his unique commitment with our freedom".
Navanethem "Navi" Pillay grew up in South Africa during apartheid as a bus driver's daughter in a poor Indian section of Durban.
She went on to become the first woman to establish a law practice in Natal Province in 1967, and later the first non-white woman to be appointed to the country's high court.
Pillay served as a judge on the UN-backed International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda - focused on the 1994 genocide in which 800,000 people were killed - including four years as its president.

From 2021-25, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory - a fact-finding body established by the UN Human Rights Council to investigate alleged violations of international law.

The commission concluded that Israel had committed genocidal acts in Gaza and that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant, had "incited the commission of genocide" in their speeches and statements.

The three-member expert panel did not speak officially for the UN and had no legal authority. Israel rejected its findings and accused the three members of the commission of serving as "Hamas proxies".

The panel had previously concluded that Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups committed war crimes and other grave violations of international law on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and another 251 taken hostage. The same report also accused Israel of war crimes.
Reacting to Pillay's award on Friday, Israel's Foreign Ministry said it represented a "grotesque weaponisation of an award to legitimise anti-Israel hatred and prejudice".
It said in a statement: "Her role in the relentless, politically motivated demonisation of Israel and promotion of the genoLIE speaks volumes."
Frydnes said the Nobel organisation was not taking a position on whether the Israeli offensive in Gaza amounted to genocide.
Pillay is currently a judge on the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in the case where Myanmar stands accused by The Gambia of genocide against the Rohingya people.
Myanmar has denied deliberately trying to destroy the minority Muslim population, with a government representative telling the court in January that the allegation was "unsubstantiated".

UN human rights chief Volker Turk said Pillay's recognition was "a reaffirmation that human rights, the rule of law and justice, and accountability are fundamental to everything, to peace, to security, and prosperity".

South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa said she had been a "pioneering defence attorney for anti-apartheid activists" who had worked to "uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally".
Amnesty International Secretary-General Agnès Callamard said she was with Pillay when she learned she had won - and called her an "inspired choice" for the award.
"At a time when both international law and justice are under attack, when too many states attempt to hollow them out, her Nobel Peace Prize could not come at a better time," she said.

articles.title: New spate of stabbings, overdoses and fires at Australian immigration detention centres run by ICE-linked US prison firm
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Federal government under scrutiny as documents reveal serious security lapses at Melbourne and Villawood immigration detention centres

  • Get our

blocks.text: A new spate of stabbings, overdoses and drug use in Australia’s immigration detention centres has put the Australian government in likely breach of laws designed to protect staff and detainees, internal documents show.

Earlier this year, Guardian Australia revealed catastrophic security failings across Australia’s onshore immigration network since Management and Training Corporation – a US private prison company used by Donald Trump to hold ICE detainees – won the $2.3bn detention contract in late 2024.

The federal government has repeatedly attempted to take a stick to MTC and its local subsidiary Secure Journeys to improve its performance, including through financial penalties and a fiery meeting last year between the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, and the company’s global president.

But new documents seen by the Guardian show serious security lapses have continued since, including through a spate of eight fire-related incidents at Villawood immigration detention centre and violence and drug use at Melbourne immigration detention centre (MIDC). Those failings have again put the department itself in the crosshairs of Comcare, the federal work safety regulator.

The documents reveal a string of incidents at MIDC involving violence, aggression, illicit substances and improvised weaponry since August. That includes a violent altercation on 18 August between two groups that led to six detainees being hospitalised for “slashing and stabbing injuries made using improvised weapons”.
On 10 September, a detainee was found overdosed in his room, requiring staff to administer Naloxone, a drug that reverses opioid overdose effects.

The incidents at MIDC prompted Comcare to warn the government that it was failing to control the rising number of “incidents of this type at MIDC and across the broader immigration detention network”. That failure meant it was likely to be in breach of the law, the document said.

“I have formed the reasonable belief that the department is contravening section 19 of the WHS Act by failing to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of workers and other persons,” Comcare said in its notice. “In particular, the risks associated with violence, aggression, and the presence of illicit substances and improvised weaponry are not being adequately managed.

“While the department has advised that a range of actions have been undertaken to address these risks, it has not sufficiently demonstrated that the control measures currently in place are effective in eliminating or minimising the risks, so far as is reasonably practicable.”
Comcare said the information available indicates these hazards pose an ongoing risk of serious harm to workers and others in the centres.
A separate Comcare document revealed that a series of eight fire-related incidents had taken place at Villawood immigration detention centre between February and May.

blocks.caption: Fire damage to a room at Villawood

blocks.text: That’s despite prior warnings to government to intervene after previous fires lit inside Villawood exposed serious gaps in MTC’s preparedness. That includes one fire on 23 September 2025, when MTC staff rushed into a detainee’s room to save him from a fire without proper safety equipment, causing two workers to be hospitalised.

The regulator found the department had not conducted its own systematic review of “all fire and smoke control measures falling within its influence or control”, a likely breach of work health and safety regulations.
after newsletter promotion

“The occurrence of multiple notifiable fire incidents over a period of approximately four months, particularly after previous regulatory intervention concerning substantially the same risk, provided repeated and compelling circumstances requiring the department to review the effectiveness of relevant control measures,” the Comcare document said.

The Guardian previously revealed a series of incidents across the centres since Secure Journey took over, including escapes, staff injuries and sick detainees missing medical appointments due to a lack of staff to escort them.

Lyndal Ryan, national president of the United Workers Union, which represents workers in the centres, said the notices from Comcare show “the continuing dangerous situations facing workers and detainees inside detention centres, and Secure Journeys’ inability or unwillingness to address those issues”.
The union has continually raised concerns about understaffing in the centres, and Ryan said Comcare has made it clear that the department has the responsibility to pull Secure Journeys into line.
“The list of eight fires at Villawood over a four-month period are signs of the instability and chaos our members are witnessing almost every day,” she said.
A spokesperson for MTC’s local subsidiary, Secure Journeys, said:
“In response to your questions, I can confirm that Secure Journeys’ commitment to maintaining safe and secure operations, as well as both staff and detainee welfare remains our top priority.”
The Australian Border Force was contacted for comment.

The district engineering offices of the Department of Public Works and Highways that received the highest allocations in the proposed 2027 national budget include those that cover the legislative districts of top officials of the House of Representatives, a House deputy minority leader said on Friday.

ACT Teachers party-list Rep. Sandro Marcos, Nueva Ecija Rep. Mikaela Suansing, and Speaker Faustino "Bojie" Dy III of Isabela.
He also mentioned the DPWH's second engineering district in Bulacan.

Sandro Marcos, one of the sons of President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., is the House Majority Leader, while Suansing is the chairperson of the House Committee on Appropriations that shepherded the budget bill through the House of Representatives.
The House on Wednesday gave second reading approval to the P7.2-trillion General Appropriations Bill. It is scheduled to approve the same on third and final reading on Monday.
GMA News has reached out to Dy, Marcos, and Suansing for comment and will post their side when it is available.

Tinio didn't refer to the Bulacan lawmakers, but those with jurisdiction in the area of the DPWH's second engineering district are Representatives Linabelle Ruth Villarica of the fourth district, Salvador Pleyto of the sixth district, and Arturo Robes of San Jose Del Monte City.
GMA News has also sought their comment on the budget data Tinio raised and presented.

"Overall, kung ira-rank natin ‘yung mga district engineering offices, ang may pinakamalaki overall ay Ilocos Norte 1st. Meron siyang total of P4.79 billion na DPWH projects," Tinio said in an online interview on Friday.

"Ang pangalawa, Nueva Ecija 1st district engineering office, P3.91 billion. Pangatlo, Bulacan. Bulacan second district engineering office, may tatlong legislative districts na saklaw ‘yan, P3.5 billion. Sumunod d’yan, Isabela. So may dalawang districts na saklaw itong DEO na ito, P3.1 billion," he added.
"Well, obviously, I'm talking about the majority leader, the chair of Committee on Appropriations, and the Speaker, 'di ba?" Tinio said.
As for the allocation for each legislative district, Tinio said, "Supposedly ang baseline per district is P500 million. Tapos puwedeng bumaba, tumaas o bumaba batay sa so-called formula."
But the deputy minority leader also disclosed that even party-lists have allocations.

"Yung party-list, as I've said, meron ding alokayson sa DPWH infrastructure projects, anywhere from P120 to 160 million. Pero again, puwedeng madagdagan o mabawasan 'yan depende pa rin sa lapit sa kusina," Tinio said.
When asked if the Makabayan Bloc in the House of Representatives also has allocations, Tinio replied, "Decision namin na walang alokasyon dito sa DPWH or infrastructure projects."

"Nagdesisyon kami na ‘yong medical assistance, yes. Dahil ‘yan ang kailangan ng mamamayan, lumalapit ang mga constituents at ang mamamayan sa amin. So rather than tanggihan at ituro sa iba, na doon lang kayo, eh di direkta na namin hinahawakan. So ganoon ‘yon. Pero nananatili ang posisyon natin na dapat walang ganoon," Tinio said. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream execution puts US in dubious company
articles.summary: Only Iran and Afghanistan routinely carry out sentences in public, with Saudi Arabia appearing to have ended practice

blocks.text: If the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, goes ahead with plans to livestream the execution of a soldier radicalised to extremist Islam who killed 13 people at a military base in Texas, his country will join a motley assembly of lesser powers and rogue actors who have conducted public executions in recent years.

Only two countries currently systematically carry out capital sentences in public: Iran and Afghanistan. In 2025, the Taliban authorities carried out six such killings and the regime in Tehran 11, according to Amnesty International.

In April last year, the Taliban executed four men accused of murder in three different cities. All were shot dead in crowded public sports stadiums. Such events were common when the hardline Islamist militia movement was in power in the late 1990s. Then as now, the Taliban claimed a due court process had been followed.

In July, two young men accused of killing police officers were hanged by Iranian authorities in the central square of Isfahan, Iran. Human rights monitors have reported about 30 public executions in Ithe country in the last five years, with an intensification in recent months after massive popular unrest earlier this year and the war with the US and Israel. Historically, many hangings have been carried out using a crane as a makeshift gallows.

blocks.caption: Protesters gathered last year in Paris and other cities around the world to demand an end to executions in Iran. Photograph: Siavosh Hosseini/LightRocket/Getty Images

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia appears to have ended the practice after decades of beheading convicted criminals in a square in the capital, Riyadh, and sometimes publicly in provincial cities.

Legal experts and historians argue that public executions perform different functions. If the rule of law is shaky or there is doubt about the efficacy of the criminal justice system, they offer authorities seeking to win support a way of convincing the community that criminals will be punished. Such public spectacles can also be a way of cowing a population through terror.
Armed militant groups have frequently resorted to public executions – often in an effort to assert their authority.

Islamic State, which ruled a swath of Iraq and Syria between 2014 and 2019, conducted thousands of executions for alleged offences ranging from homosexuality to theft. Many of the executions took place in public or were videoed. A large number were deliberately choreographed to provide a spectacle for broadcast to terrorise enemies and potential dissidents as well as to radicalise IS supporters and attract new ones.

In October 2025, as Hamas sought to reassert its control over the population of Gaza, it carried out a public execution of six men apparently accused of collaborating with Israel. In 2017, the group had executed three men accused of the same crime, partly livestreaming the event on Facebook.

blocks.caption: The planned public execution of Nidal Hasan would be the first in the US in many decades. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: The execution of Maj Nidal Hasan, a former army psychiatrist, at Fort Hood in Texas would be the first public execution in the US in many decades.

In the US, the practice of public executions was largely stopped in the 1930s, though in 2001, some survivors and victims’ relatives were allowed to watch the execution by lethal injection of Timothy McVeigh, convicted of the 1995 bombing of a government office in Oklahoma City.

Hasan’s execution has been scheduled for 3 December. Hegseth, who has the authority to decide the conduct of the killing, has said that “of course” it would take place at the same time and in the same place as Hasan’s attack 17 years ago and would use firearms, as Hasan did.
Hasan can launch appeals within the civilian federal court system that could delay the execution for many years.

In 2025, Amnesty International recorded 2,707 executions, the highest total globally since 1981, and an increase of two-thirds on the previous year. The sharp rise was mainly due to more than 2,100 executions by Iran, its highest number of executions in decades.
Amnesty said authorities had placed the death penalty “at the centre of flawed public security and ‘tough on crime’ narratives to assert control, project state power and score political points”.

“This trend was strongest in countries where the authorities have tightened their grip on power by restricting civic space, silencing dissent and displaying disregard for protections established under international human rights law and standards,” the campaign group reported.

articles.title: PCG drives away Chinese maritime militia vessel, 22 ‘sampans’
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said that it successfully drove away a Chinese maritime militia vessel and 22 smaller boats on Friday, Oct. 9, reportedly fishing and dumping…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said that it successfully drove away a Chinese maritime militia vessel and 22 smaller boats on Friday, Oct. 9, reportedly fishing and dumping waste within the territorial waters of Kota Island (Loaita Island) in the West Philippine Sea.

The PCG said that its personnel stationed at Kota Island spotted Chinese Maritime Militia Vessel (CMMV) 9622 and small boats, also known as “sampans,” approximately 0.55 nautical miles (NM) northwest of Kota Island, with the nearest sampan observed 250 meters from the shoreline.
Their position is well within the 12 NM territorial sea of the islands, it said.
It added that they were observed conducting unauthorized fishing activities and dumping waste at sea.
The CMMV 9622 was the same vessel that was spotted last Sept. 28, with 24 small boats deployed about 300 yards off the island, according to the PCG.

At around 3:30 p.m., after the sighting, the PCG deployed a team aboard two rubber boats from its Special Operations Group, Maritime Law Enforcement Group, Coast Guard District Kalayaan Island Group, medical personnel, and Philippine Marines.
During the operation, it said that the Chinese mothership encircled their boats, while ordering them to leave over the radio.
After approximately two hours, some of the Chinese sampans withdrew from the area. One sampan temporarily refused to leave, which resulted in minor contact. It then departed after some time.
No injuries or damage were sustained in the incident, the PCG said.
All Chinese vessels had pushed back approximately 3.5 NM from Kota Island by 5:30 p.m., before eventually departing northwest.

“The presence of a Chinese maritime militia vessel coordinating a fleet of sampans as close as 250 meters from the shoreline is a blatant violation of the territorial sea of Kota Island and an affront to Philippine sovereignty,” the PCG said.
Kota Island, also known as Loaita Island, is one of the features in the Kalayaan Island Group in the Spratly Islands. It is part of the municipality of Kalayaan in Palawan province.
The PCG said that under international law, no foreign vessel may conduct fishing activities within the Philippines’ territorial waters.
“Such conduct is likewise a clear violation of Philippine laws, including the Philippine Fisheries Code and the Philippine Maritime Zones Act,” it said.

Likewise, the presence of a Chinese maritime militia vessel and its fleet of sampans about 250 meters from Kota Island is a “blatant violation of the territorial sea” and “affront to Philippine sovereignty”.
It further dismissed the claims of the Chinese vessel’s command personnel, asserting that the area belongs to China.
“The claim made by the Chinese vessel’s master that the area belongs to China has no basis whatsoever under international law,” the PCG stressed.
The PCG added that it is continuously monitoring the area and is sustaining vigilance against any further foreign intrusion within the Kalayaan Island Group. /cb

articles.title: Alexander Cabrera is last witness of prosecution in VP Sara impeachment trial
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel on Friday confirmed that financial forensic analyst Atty. Alexander Cabrera is the last witness that they will present in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara…

blocks.text: Published October 9, 2026 9:44pm

The House prosecution panel on Friday confirmed that financial forensic analyst Atty. Alexander Cabrera is the last witness that they will present in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

House prosecutor Akbayan party-list Rep. Chel Diokno said this on the 37th day of the trial when asked by Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero if the prosecution will still present the witness from the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) after the testimony of Cabrera.
“Atty. Alexander B. Cabrera is our last witness, Your Honor, for our case-in-chief,” Diokno answered.

Impeachment court spokesperson Regie Tongol explained that if the prosecution will already be resting for Article 2, which alleges that Duterte should be impeached for amassing unexplained wealth, then it means that Article 3 would be tackled next.

“Pero alam ko na alam niyo na rin na nakatanggap ang impeachment court ng manifestation that formally manifest to the impeachment court na ido-drop ang Article 3. Hintayin po natin ‘yung ating Presiding Officer to take that up on Monday,” Tongol said in a press conference.

(But I know that you are also aware that the impeachment court has received a manifestation that formally manifests to the impeachment court that Article 3 will be dropped. Let’s wait for our Presiding Officer to take that up on Monday.)

The prosecution announced earlier today that it already filed a manifestation with the Senate impeachment court that it will drop Article III or the bribery charges in the trial of the Vice President.
The trial on Friday ended with the direct examination of Cabrera. The defense will proceed with the cross-examination of the witness on Monday next week. –NB, GMA News

items: A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot and wounded a 28-year-old Dominican man who was in a car with a five-year-old child Thursday.
The shooting drew outrage from New Yorkers, including Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who called for the release of the wounded man and the end of all ICE enforcement in the city.

In a news conference this morning, U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said Mamdani’s comments were political theatre and an incitement to violence. A senior ICE official said agents opened fire because they believed their lives were in danger.
