articles.title: Ethiopia warns Eritrea it will defend itself after troops cross border
articles.summary: Truckloads of Eritrean soldiers have been seen driving into Ethiopia, which has reportedly responded with drone strikes.

blocks.text: Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of an "all-out invasion" of its northern Tigray region and warned it will defend itself, days after residents told the BBC Eritrean troops had crossed into the country.

In a letter to the UN Security Council, Ethiopia's foreign minister called it a "blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia's inherent right to self-defence", following reported strikes on Eritrean troops in Tigray.
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel responded by saying it was facing "an unprovoked war of aggression" from its neighbour.
Fighting broke out between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), two weeks ago.
Both blame each other for violating a 2022 deal that ended its civil war. Ethiopia says Eritrea backs the TPLF, which it denies.
During the two-year civil war, Eritrea was a key ally of the Ethiopian government, having fought alongside them against the TPLF.

But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated - largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports - leading to the severing of diplomatic ties last week.
Accusing Eritrea of violating its sovereignty, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said Eritrean forces had advanced up to 60km (37 miles) into Tigray.
Ethiopian drone strikes reportedly targeted Eritrean forces in the Tigrayan town of Adigrat on Wednesday and Thursday, amid fears of a wider regional war.
US-based conflict monitor Acled said "Eritrean troops and ammunition" in Adigrat were hit by "multiple drone strikes" overnight.
One resident told AFP news agency "there were many, many drone strikes", and that some Eritrean lorries had been destroyed.
Another witness said Eritrean forces appeared to be retreating north after the strikes, AFP reported.

Dated 8 October, Ethiopia's letter to UN Security Council members read: "In this time of difficulty, when Ethiopia is left with no other option but to defend itself, we count on your understanding, support, and solidarity."
But while Ethiopia accuses its neighbour of supporting the TPLF, Eritrea has blamed the conflict on Ethiopia's leaders, and accused them looking for a reason to seize Eritrean territory.
On Friday, Eritrea's information minister called the accusations levelled against Asmara as "duplicity in their most extreme forms".
In a post on X, he said Ethiopia was "openly working to bring about regime change in Eritrea by providing shelter and support to certain mercenaries who claim to be opposition".
Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, but ties were only normalised in 2018, when Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power.
This latest unrest follows months of tension and the launch of new alliance of armed groups in Ethiopia - including the TPLF - in September.
Last week, TPLF forces withdrew from Tigray's main city of Mekelle, which is 115km (71 miles) south of Adigrat and is now under army control.

articles.title: EU ‘pulling out all stops’ with minerals projects as it tries to avert China trade war
articles.summary:
Commissioner Stéphane Séjourné says bloc will support 46 strategic projects including lithium and rare earths plants

The EU is “pulling out all the stops” to fend off an imminent potential…

blocks.text: The EU is “pulling out all the stops” to fend off an imminent potential trade crisis with China, the industry commissioner, Stéphane Séjourné, has said, as the bloc announced its backing for a string of critical materials projects.
Séjourné said on Friday that the EU would support 46 new strategic projects to accelerate supplies of critical raw materials by 2030 across the bloc.

“We could face a crisis in the coming months,” he said. “We may face trade tensions that could also trigger a crisis in a number of sectors. We need to be prepared for that. And we’re getting ready right now.”
The new projects include plants for supplies of lithium, gallium and rare earths needed for the auto, defence and renewable energy industries, with a funding cost of €21bn (£17.8bn).

They were unveiled just as the EU works to avert a trade war with China, with the trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, continuing talks on Friday in Beijing aimed at reducing China’s “unsustainable” £1bn-a-day trade surplus with the bloc.

“We’re pulling out all the stops to move as quickly as possible. The primary objective is the targets set by law, and beyond that, there’s a geopolitical challenge that could catch up with us very quickly,” said Séjourné.
“Mines are opening, factories are being built, financing agreements are being signed, and a European value chain is emerging,” Séjourné added.

Amid some scepticism over the EU’s ability to meet its 2030 targets to reduce dependencies on China, Séjourné cited three “emblematic” projects which have previously been identified as strategic, earmarking them for accelerated permits.

These included a rare earths plant near Pau in south-western France. The Carester plant, which is expected to be up and running in late 2026, produces dysprosium and terbium, “two raw materials for which we are almost entirely dependent on China”, used in magnets for electric vehicles and offshore wind turbines.
“This single project could account for about 15% of global production of these oxides. That is no small feat,” Séjourné said.
He also name-checked a gallium plant in Greece which is already up and running.
The third, Keliber, a lithium extraction and processing plant in Finland, is also operational after €150m support from the European Investment Bank.

The 46 projects are the second batch of initiatives to receive flagship status since the Critical Raw Materials Act of 2024, which legally mandates the European Commission to reduce the bloc’s dependency on foreign countries.
after newsletter promotion

The EU hopes to follow in the footsteps of Japan, which has reduced dependency on China for rare earths to 60% from 90% since 2011, when Beijing prohibited exports of about 20 entities to Japan, claiming they were being used for military purposes.
Although the flagship status does not bring the projects direct funds, it enables accelerated permitting, and help in mobilising funds.
However, there has been criticism in industry within the EU that the scheme is not strong enough to deliver targets to mine 10%, process 40% and recycle 25% of the bloc’s needs by 2030.
The French lithium refiner Viridian Lithium, which received EU strategic status in 2025, went into judicial liquidation in March this year.

Earlier this year, a group of 23 of the 60 projects designated strategic in 2025 wrote to the European Commission calling for more action to “urgently unlock projects, particularly those working towards final investment decision which face acute liquidity and market pressure and ​immediate jeopardy”.
Séjourné said member states had unlocked €1bn for six of the projects, with the European Investment Bank providing another €660m for eight projects.

articles.summary: Manases Carpio-owned Cale88 listed only two employees in its general info sheet despite reporting P150 million in sales in 2024

Inday Sara Duterte's Facebook page
Manases Carpio-owned Cale88 listed only two employees in its general info sheet despite reporting P150 million in sales in 2024

items: Senator-judges scrutinized Cale88 Foods Corporation's financial records during Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial, noting discrepancies between reported sales and employee count.
Senator Risa Hontiveros also raised issues regarding foreign remittances to Cale88 from Ukrainian company Arkmen LLC, which is under investigation for alleged fraud and money laundering.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Senator-judges on Friday, October 9, scrutinized the financial records and workforce of Cale88 Foods Corporation, a company linked to Vice President Sara Duterte‘s husband, Manases Carpio.

On Day 37 of Duterte’s impeachment trial, Senator-judge Joel Villanueva raised concerns over Cale88’s 2024 general information sheet, which listed only two employees despite the company reporting P150.6 million in sales and P6.13 million in losses.
“This is alarming, Your Honor. You’re looking at a company with P150 million sales and P6.13 million in losses but only [has] two employees,” Villanueva said.

Citing the company’s financial records, Bureau of Internal Revenue chief of staff Anne Loraine Garcia-Marquez said Cale88 reported P150,595,605 in sales classified as exempt from income tax and P169,564 in sales subject to regular income tax in 2024.
The company also reported a loss of around P6.13 million in the same year, Garcia-Marquez said.
Villanueva questioned how the company managed its operations with very few employees and who funded its continued operations.

Marquez said she had no personal knowledge of Cale88’s operations, adding that it would seem “impossible” for a banana chip manufacturer to operate with only two employees unless machinery handled much of the work.

Meanwhile, Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros flagged Ukrainian company Arkmen LLC, one of the foreign-based entities that sent inward remittances to Cale88, citing alleged involvement in a fraud and money laundering investigation in Ukraine.

Hontiveros said her office checked the background of the foreign-based companies that remitted to Cale88 and found that Kyiv authorities investigated Arkmen LLC over alleged fraud and money laundering involving 1.225 million euros in May 2025.
Authorities reportedly ordered a search of its premises in March, while its assets were frozen in April.
“The last remittance of Arkmen LLC to Cale88 was in May 2025 after the start of the criminal proceedings,” Hontiveros said.
Hontiveros asked Marquez whether legitimate transactions involving international remittances from Arkmen LLC to Cale88 should have been reported as sales and subjected to tax.
“If these were sales, they should have been reported in the annual income tax return,” Marquez said.

Hontiveros had previously claimed that some Chinese companies that sent funds to Cale88 were Chinese state-owned enterprises that could be “advancing the interests of the Chinese Communist Party.” – Rappler.com

Confessed drug war perpetrators are also expressing interest in sharing their stories, according to the Truth Commission.

In a "24 Oras" report from Mariz Umali on Friday, the Truth Commission held its fourth session earlier in the day. The Commission aims to document and seek out what happened during former president Rodrigo Duterte’s war on drugs.

“We are getting calls and interest even from former perpetrators, so maybe against the backdrop of what has already been documented, but former perpetrators are also now expressing interest in telling their stories," Commissioner Al Fuertes said.
While the Truth Commission stressed that it is not a prosecutorial body that could directly file a case, they are listening to the victims and survivors, which could be key to reopening their cases.

“The challenge is, and this is what the Commission intends to do, is to really pressure the government to take the lead in pursuing justice for the victims because the victims, they need all the help they can get,” Commissioner Carlos Conde said.
It has been six years since Lorna Pepaño lost her son. Her neighbor had told her that her son Christian was gunned down.
“Nakita ko na po yung anak ko, nakabulagta. May malay pa naman siya, sabi niya, ‘hindi po ako yun’... pero tinuluyan pa rin siya,” Pepaño said.
(I saw my son lying there. He was still conscious; he said, ‘it was not me’... but they still killed him.)
Pepaño said it was a case of mistaken identity.

Now, she hoped that she could find justice for her son who, by her account, was a good and prayerful man. She also expressed hope that there would be no more killings like the one that happened to her son and other victims. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Is China seeking to restrict Taiwan's cultural presence?
articles.summary: From coffee competitions to literature awards, Beijing appears to be working to limit Taiwan's international cultural and political impact on its own terms.

image.caption: Taiwan Travelogue follows a young Japanese writer visiting Japanese-colonized Taiwan in May 1938 on an official government-sponsored lecture tourImage: Pete Speller/Avalon/IMAGO

blocks.text: When Taiwaneseauthor Yang Shuang-zi's Taiwan Travelogue won the 2026 international Booker Prize, it marked a historic breakthrough on the global stage. But behind the triumph lay a sharp geopolitical reality.
On stage, English translator Lin King voiced the anxiety looming over Taiwan.

"In 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, I made the explicit decision that rather than translating Sinophone works indiscriminately, I would only translate writing from Taiwan for the foreseeable future. I will continue to do so until the day comes that my homeland's sovereignty is no longer a provocation or a punchline — until no English speaker feels comfortable saying to me, 'I really should come visit you in Taiwan while it still exists.'" King said this in her acceptance speech.
Literature and politics

Taiwan Travelogue follows a young Japanese writer visiting Japanese-colonized Taiwan in May 1938 on an official government-sponsored lecture tour. As she and her Taiwanese interpreter explore local street food together, a subtle intimacy unfolds between them. It is written in a narrative that centers Taiwan's history rather than Beijing's preferred Great China framework.

"Literature and politics are directly connected. Politics determines the allocation of resources, and the allocation of resources determines which works get pulled out, held up high, and defined as 'good literature.' The idea that politics can just be kept out of it doesn't exist," Yang told DW.

A few days after the Booker Prize was announced, China's Taiwan Affairs Office reacted that, "Writers from both sides of the Taiwan Strait should firmly uphold a national standpoint, respect historical facts, and squarely face the immense suffering inflicted upon the Chinese people ... by Japan's war of aggression and fascism."
"From China's perspective, they do not want to see Taiwan's voice gain prominence." Yang said.

Her book demonstrates that Taiwanese culture is shaped by multiple historical strands — including Indigenous, Japanese colonial, and local Han influences, rather than being merely a "branch of Chinese culture."

During Yang's German book tour this October, an event in Literaturhaus München sparked controversy when her interpreter significantly shortened certain statements concerning Taiwan, China and historical politics. The interpreter later admitted oversights and shortcomings in the interpretation but denied deliberately deleting content due to political stance or the political situation in Taiwan.
Taiwan and China

Beijing claims Taiwan as a Chinese province and has long threatened to use force to bring the island under its control. Taiwan's democratically elected president has rejected Beijing's assertion that its laws apply to Taiwan.
Since 1949, Taiwan has functioned with de facto independence, maintaining its own government, military, and legal systems while facing ongoing military pressure from Beijing.

blocks.caption: Taiwan's democratically elected President Lai Ching-te has rejected Beijing's assertion that its laws apply to TaiwanImage: Taiwan Presidential Office/AP Photo/Picture alliance

blocks.text: China's international overreach?
In the past, China's monitoring of Taiwanese international engagement has reached far further than words over a literature prize.

"The target of suppression and harassment primarily include outspoken individuals, exiled activists, diaspora community organizers, alongside their family members and close affiliates back home. From the PRC's (People's Republic of China) eyes, these groups are a threat to regime security, as they are able to amplify the dissenting voices and alternative stories of China to the West," said Dr. Yan-ho Lai, a senior fellow of Georgetown Center for Asian Law.

In April this year, Taiwanese barista Lin Shao-hsing, also known as Bala, won the 2026 World Latte Art Championship, but soon after, all mentions of Taiwan as they relate to Bala's win were removed from the official World Coffee Championships website.

It now credits Bala's win to "Chinese Taipei," a term which is often used in international competitions, like the Olympics, to refer to Taiwan. The term, however, is almost never used in Taiwan. The vast majority of people in Taiwan identify as "Taiwanese," while only 2.5% identify as Chinese, according to a 2026 poll by National Chengchi University's Election Study Center.

In 2024, China allegedly planned a car collision during Taiwan's vice president Hsiao Bi-khim's visit in Prague. Czech intelligence officials told local media that the incident was part of a much larger and escalatory plan by Chinese diplomats and intelligence officers working out of the embassy in Prague.

In early October this year, the FBI says authorities arrested a California woman for allegedly spying on the son of Taiwan's president at the direction of Chinese officials. According to the US Department of Justice, the woman traveled to Seattle in 2025 under instructions from Beijing to monitor the president's son and his family, capturing photos, video footage, and license plate information.
During a press conference on October 6, China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it "consistently opposes the hype surrounding so-called 'Chinese spies' and the smearing and vilification of China."

"It reflects the ambiguity and limitation of international law, that PRC using soft power to restrict the visibility of Taiwan may not directly fall into international law arena as Taiwan is not recognized by international bodies as a sovereign state party." added Dr. Lai.
This article was edited by Kate Martyr

articles.title: Art for freedom: Maria Kalesnikava in Bonn
articles.summary: The Belarusian musician and civil rights activist Maria Kalesnikava held the keynote speech on the importance of art at the 2026 Beethovenfest in Bonn. She also visited DW.

image.caption: Maria Kalesnikava continues to fight for freedom Image: Sebastian Gollnow/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Maria Kalesnikava knows all too well how authoritarian regimes repress art: The Belarusian flautist and activist spent five years in detention as a political prisoner, three of which were in solitary confinement.

Speaking at this year's Beethovenfest, she said: "A person's external freedom can be taken away, sometimes almost entirely. Their freedom of movement, contacts with other people, and access to information can be limited." She pointed out that it is, however, much harder to control what has already become part of one's memory, imagination and inner experience. "And it is precisely in this that I find the explanation for why culture is so important for a free society and why authoritarian systems so often view it with distrust" she concluded during the keynote speech.

blocks.caption: German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul welcomed Maria Kolesnikova at the Federal Foreign Office in December 2025Image: Amrei Schulz/AA/photothek.de/picture alliance

blocks.text: A key figure of the Belarusian opposition, the artist and political activist was arrested by the regime of Alexander Lukashenko in the summer of 2020, after the regime had violently suppressed the peaceful revolution for democracy and freedom. Across the country, mass protests and a democratic civil rights movement took place after the controversial presidential election on August 9, 2020.

Kalesnikava recalled how, during her imprisonment, she had carried her world and her experiences, with her all along. This enabled her to remain free, and not to feel like a victim. To Kalesnikava, this is precisely the power of art and also the reason why all dictators — whether Stalin, Hitler or Putin and Lukashenko — hate independent arts and culture, even if it's not overtly political.
During a panel discussion in Bonn, Kalesnikava stressed this point directly:

"The question often arises: what are we defending in Ukraine? Why do we need so much money and new weapons? For me, it is completely clear: the war Russia started is not just against Ukraine. It's a war against European values and European culture. It is a war against our civilization." Kalesnikava realized this immediately when she heard about the Russian war against Ukraine in February 2022, while she was imprisoned.
Music saved her

Kalesnikava was released and has been living in freedom again for ten months now — a miracle that she didn't think was possible and an achievement of international diplomacy. The fact that she emerged and returned to her life full of resilience is thanks in part to Beethoven and Bach, as Kalesnikava, who studied the flute and earned a degree in early and new music in Minsk and Stuttgart, recalled. "I spent a lot of time in complete silence. But this silence was almost never empty, because music constantly played in my head," Kalesnikava said in Bonn. "We musicians know this state very well — sometimes a melody or a musical phrase gets so stuck in your head that it's simply impossible to get rid of it. In normal life, this can even be annoying. In prison, I realized for the first time that this could bring great happiness."

blocks.caption: Maria Kolesnikova appeared on the Russian-language DW program "DW Novosti," on October 2, 2026Image: DW

blocks.text: During her visit to Bonn, the Belarusian activist also visited DW and appeared as a guest on the DW Russian language show "DW Novosti." Kalesnikava currently lives in Berlin following an invitation by the German government, where she is also recovering from the horrors she experienced. She sees it as her responsibility to remind the world about what is happening to more than 800 political prisoners in Belarus, as well as the importance and fragility of free artistic expression. On October 2, 2026, she held her keynote speech at the Beethovenfest in Bonn as part of a conference titled "Cultural Events as Political Spaces?," organized with the support of the German Federal Cultural Foundation.
The concert hall as a space for freedom

More than 200 representatives from concert institutions and music festivals from across Germany came to the newly renovated Beethovenhalle in Bonn for the final weekend of this year's Beethovenfest. Together, they debated innovative forms and formats for music, as well as issues that stretch far beyond the music industry and urge on to think outside the box.

blocks.caption: Steven Walter, artistic director of the Beethovenfest, spoke about the importance of music and freedom at the conference in BonnImage: Michael Staab/Beethovenfest

blocks.text: "Arts and culture are not responsible for taking on specific opinions from political parties, or for making explicitly political statements," Steven Walter, artistic director of the Beethovenfest and host of the conference, told DW. "What art always creates, however, is spaces for encounter, and places where people can tolerate ambivalence. And that is such an important part of our society, that we're able to handle making collective experiences." To Walter, this is precisely where arts and culture come in, as artists create spaces for independent thought, subjective interpretations, as well as doubts. "Perhaps it's true that there is something like a DNA of freedom in the nature of art," Walter explained in an interview with DW.
The most successful Beethovenfest in years

The festive closing of the 2026 Beethovenfest took place on 3 October, which is also German Unity Day. The BBC Philharmonic Orchestra, under the baton of conductor Anja Bihlmaier, performed Johannes Brahms' "A German Requiem," an iconic piece that evokes reconciliation and trust.

blocks.caption: At the closing concert of the Beethovenfest, Anja Bihlmaier conducted Brahms's Requiem with the BBC Philharmonic Orchestra and the Audi Youth Choir AcademyImage: Nekame Klasohm

blocks.text: After four weeks of Beethovenfest 2026, the festival recorded the highest number of visitors in a decade. Around 35,000 people came to experience, celebrate and discuss art together at more than 100 concerts and events.

articles.title: CHR chair faces graft complaint over alleged corruption in allowance
articles.summary: The NBI claims CHR Chairperson Richard Palpal-latoc allegedly still received allowances for a trip already funded by a foreign sponsor

HOR Quad Comm
The NBI claims CHR Chairperson Richard Palpal-latoc allegedly still received allowances for a trip already funded by a foreign sponsor

items: CHR Chairperson Richard Palpal-latoc and three others face a graft complaint filed by the NBI over alleged corruption related to a foreign-funded training program.
The complaint alleges violations of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, claiming Palpal-latoc improperly claimed allowance even though this was already covered by the sponsor.
The NBI's investigation revealed issues with documentation and approvals related to the disbursement voucher, implicating all four individuals in misconduct.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Commission on Human Rights (CHR) Chairperson Richard Palpal-latoc and three other individuals are facing a graft complaint before the Office of the Ombudsman over alleged corruption involving a month-long training.

The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) filed the complaint on Friday, October 9, for alleged violation of Section 3(e) of Republic Act No. 3019 or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act. Other respondents are as follows:

items: Onesimo Cuyco
Maria Teresa Dolor
Russel Mani

blocks.text: “Respectfully transmitting for Preliminary Investigation are the results of the investigation conducted by this Bureau’s Public Corruption Division as represented by xxxx,” said the NBI’s transmission document to the Ombudsman.
Rappler has already reached out to CHR for a statement. We will update this story once they respond.

According to the NBI, Palpal-latoc attended the 54th International Institute for Human Rights Summer School in 2025. It was a month-long training with the airfare, accommodation, meals, and subsistence fully funded by the Friedrich Naumann Foundation for Freedom (FNF).
The CHR chairperson, however, allegedly still claimed daily subsistence allowance and representation for the period of the training.

The NBI argued that Executive Order No. 77, series of 2019 prohibits claims for public officials if the travel is covered by the sponsor. It added that Section 16(b) “specifically disallows representation expenses for officials attending trainings or travelling on donor-funded trips.”
In addition, the disbursement voucher also allegedly concealed the funding arrangement and did not contain a disclosure of the foreign donor.

“Despite missing mandatory documents, the mismatched program documentation, the prohibited claims, and the undisclosed sponsorship, the voucher passed through every control point. Mani certified the supporting documents as complete. Dolor certified that funds were available. Cuyco approved the voucher for payment,” said the NBI.

“Taken together, these acts establish liability of Palpal-latoc, Cuyco, Dolor, and Mani for violation of Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019 and for Gross Misconduct: Public officers acting in their official functions: the Chairperson as claimant, and the certifying and approving officers in processing the voucher. Manifest partiality, evident bad faith, or gross inexcusable negligence: a claim for expenses already paid by a sponsor, a concealed donor, and certifications issued over facially defective documents,” the NBI added.

blocks.caption: Marcos names ex-Malacañang deputy executive secretary as new CHR chair

blocks.text: In 2022, Marcos appointed Palpal-latoc, a former Malacañang deputy executive secretary for legal affairs, as CHR chairperson.

Palpal-latoc has experience in anti-corruption prosecution. He served assistant prosecutor at the Quezon City prosecutor’s office. He had also served in various positions in the Office of the Ombudsman and in the Department of Social Welfare field office in Calabarzon, including as graft investigation and prosecution officer under the Ombudsman. – Rappler.com

articles.title: What is your seafood eating? Investigation traces problems in global feed supply
articles.summary: Much of the fish meal and fish oil that support farmed salmon and imported seafood consumed in Canada come from global supply chains linked to pollution, labour abuses, overfishing, and food…

image.caption: Small fish like these Peruvian anchoveta are harvested from the wild to produce fish oil and fish meal that feeds aquaculture operations around the world. An investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project traces those global supply chains that are linked to pollution, labour abuses, overfishing, and food

blocks.text: The following story is part of a larger investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization in Washington, D.C.
In 2020, a team of government investigators in Goa, India, arrived at a factory named United Marine Products to find out how it was disposing of its toxic wastewater.

For years, local residents had complained that the factory was making their air unbreathable and their drinking water deadly. This factory produces fish meal, a protein-rich powder used to feed farmed fish, which is made by pulverizing and cooking wild-caught fish.

Soon enough, the inspectors discovered that the plant operators had employed a new and illegal way to dispose of the facility's wastewater, drilling bore holes into the ground in a field behind the plant. The authorities later concluded these holes likely contaminated groundwater and sickened villagers and livestock.

The United Marine Products plant in Councolim, Goa, India. In 2020, investigators determined the plant had drilled holes into the ground behind the plant to illegally dispose of wastewater from fish meal processing. (Changing Markets Foundation)
The plant owner denied wrongdoing.
Seafood consumers in Canada might think they have no connection to these sorts of far-away problems.

But this factory in India supplied Skretting, a major feed producer used by dozens of fish farms in Canada — so its product may feed the salmon from British Columbia and New Brunswick or trout from Quebec you see on store shelves.

A five-year investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization in Washington, D.C., uncovered a variety of similar hidden costs involved in producing this feed, including the loss of artisanal fishing jobs, chronic chemical exposure, avoidable worker deaths, and violent protests spurred by the horrid stench from fish meal factories.

These social and environmental impacts exact a price primarily paid by the poorer countries where the feed ingredient is harvested and processed, far from where the resulting luxury types of seafood are eaten.

A worker unloads a crate of anchovies from the holding area of a boat at the port of El Callao, Peru. The world’s largest producer of fishmeal, Peru faces growing concern about overfishing and pollution from its fishmeal industry. (Rodrigo Abd/The Associated Press)

Whether domestically raised or imported, the most popular types of farmed seafood consumed in Canada – salmon, shrimp, trout, sea bass, sea bream – are fed fish meal, which is made from the very kinds of wild fish that aquaculture claims to be saving, thereby accelerating ocean depletion, say fisheries scientists.

“Any accounting of the true impact of aquaculture has to start not with the farm, but with the feed,” said Daniel Pauly, project director of the Sea Around Us initiative at the University of B.C. in Vancouver.
“And that kind of accounting offers a very different picture than the industry offers.”
Canada’s reliance on global fish meal

Since 2022, more than half of the seafood eaten globally has come from fish farms rather than wild catch, according to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization. Aquaculture is a $444-billion industry and the fastest-growing segment of global food production. Most of these fish farms are powered by fish meal and fish oil, made from wild fish pulled from the ocean.

Unlike growing bivalves such as oysters, clams, and mussels, which do not typically require external feed, the toughest challenge to raising carnivorous seafood, such as salmon and trout, is feeding them.
A worker drives a tractor past mounds of fish meal made from menhaden fish to be used as animal feed supplements in Reedville, Va., in 2015. (Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty Images)

Canada has more than 200 fish farms, most of which rely on fish meal or fish oil that, when made domestically, comes primarily from Pacific anchoveta, chub mackerel, herring, haddock, pollock, sardines, and frigate tuna.

Canada prohibits boats targeting fish for the sole purpose of making fish meal or fish oil, so domestic fish meal is typically made using skin, bones and other byproducts of processing that would otherwise be thrown away. That’s widely viewed as a more sustainable way to produce feed protein than using whole human-edible fish.

However, at least two-thirds of the fish meal used in Canada, primarily by aquaculture farms – roughly 53,000 tonnes in 2023 – is sourced from abroad, which ties Canadian consumers to these hidden and overseas social costs. Canada also imports more than $4 billion in seafood annually, of which a third is primarily farmed salmon and shrimp, which rely heavily on fish meal and fish oil.
Food for Feed investigation

The Outlaw Ocean Project’s five-year investigation mapped roughly the entire global fish meal industry, including more than 1,400 fish meal factories across 64 countries, tracing supply chains from fishing vessels to processing plants, feed mills, fish farms and seafood retailers.
The reporting effort involved dozens of journalists from as many countries who visited factories and farms and boarded fish meal ships at sea.
In Gambia and Mauritania, the investigation documented how the industry drives food insecurity as fish that once sustained local communities are diverted into fish meal factories for export.

Workers sort catch aboard the China-flagged Lu Lao Yuan Yu 010 in Gambian waters in 2019. When Outlaw Ocean reporters boarded vessels, they documented widespread complaints about poor living and working conditions. (Fábio Nascimento/The Outlaw Ocean Project)

In India and Peru, the industry was tied to at least 80 protests, some violent, in the form of labour strikes and demonstrations sparked by the water pollution or the stench from factories cooking thousands of tonnes of decomposing fish. Canada is the largest importer of fish oil from Peru.
In China’s Xinjiang region, the reporting detailed the use of forced labour on fish farms.

The investigation mapped more than 1,000 fish farms in Xinjiang and Tibet — two regions subjected to severe state repression — that produce an estimated half-billion dollars’ worth of farmed seafood annually, some of which is exported to the United States and Canada.
A worker tosses fishmeal pellets into pens at a fish farm in Thailand in 2021. Over half of the seafood eaten worldwide comes from fish farms. (Mako Kurokawa)
‘Overexploited’ or worse

The investigation assessed more than 2,400 ships tied to fish meal production in at least 30 countries. It found that most of these ships do not fully comply with the Global Charter for Fisheries Transparency, a guide created by ocean-focused civil society groups detailing accountability standards for industrial fishing fleets.

For example, less than 30 per cent of the fleet had publicly available location information and less than 25 per cent had a unique vessel identification number (or ship licence plate). Such opacity makes the fleet difficult to police.

items: A third of global fishing goes unreported, UBC researchers find
Somalis say foreign ships are stealing their fish, and it's fuelling a piracy resurgence

blocks.text: At least half of the species landed by the assessed fish meal vessels were classified by scientific studies as “overexploited” or worse — including flat and round sardinella in Senegal, oil sardines in India, and anchoveta in Chile.

Most of the vessels in the global fish meal fleet are purse seiners or trawlers, which deploy vast nets to capture dense schools of fish, which can indiscriminately sweep in bycatch and non-target species.
At least 165 of the ships in the fleet were bottom trawlers, a destructive gear type that scrapes the ocean floor with weighted nets.
Fish meal reliance declining, industry says

In response to questions from The Outlaw Ocean Project about the sustainability of fish meal, the IFFO, which is the international fish meal association, emphasized that its “role is not to advise which markets should use fish meal and fish oil.”
Véronique Jamin, a spokesperson from the organization, said that fish farming is “the most efficient animal protein system” and is becoming more efficient over time.

Sacks of fish meal stored at a factory in Lima on December 3, 2009. While the aquaculture industry says it has decreased its reliance on fish meal overall, some companies have increased demand as they grow. (Ernesto Benavides/AFP/Getty Images)

In response to a question about overfishing by the fish meal industry, Jamin said, “Because small pelagics are fast-renewing stocks, their sustainable harvest threshold is much higher than for slow-growing species like cod, tuna, or deep-sea fish.”

The feed and aquaculture industries have emphasized that they are decreasing their reliance on fish meal and fish oil by adding other ingredients to the mix, such as insects, algae, and krill. Between 2000 and 2020, the share of fish meal in global aquaculture feed fell from 23 per cent to eight per cent, according to the IFFO.

Producers of salmon, which typically requires larger amounts of fish meal and oil to thrive, say they have made progress, too. Members of the Canadian Aquaculture Industry Alliance, which includes large producers like Cermaq and Mowi, reduced the proportion of these ingredients in salmon feed to less than 20 per cent, according to a November 2025 press release.

“These results show salmon farming companies have adopted science-based methods that have improved the standard of salmon farm sustainability overall in Canada,” said Timothy Kennedy, president of the Canadian Aquaculture Industry Alliance, in the release.
A salmon farm near Campbell River, B.C., is shown during a routine health inspection in 2018. (Jonathan Hayward/The Canadian Press)
However, as aquaculture overall grows so too has demand for fish meal.

For example, to meet demand, five of the world’s largest salmon companies increased their absolute use of fish meal or fish oil made from whole wild fish by as much as 39 percent between 2020 and 2024, according to a report from the Farm Animal Investment Risk and Return Initiative.

Two of the salmon companies that increased their absolute use of fish meal have a presence in Canada: Mowi, which announced in June 2025 that it was selling its Canadian farms to Cooke; and Grieg Seafood, whose Canadian farms have since been acquired by Cermaq. (Mowi, Cermaq, Cooke, and Grieg Seafood did not respond to a request for comment.)
Skretting opens investigation
As of 2025, there were at least seven factories processing fish meal and fish oil in Canada, and these plants are not without problems.

Between 2021 and 2024, at least two of the plants were tied to pollution or unsustainable fishing practices, according to Bait to Plate, an online tool created by The Outlaw Ocean Project that tracks the fishing and seafood industries. Neither company responded to the project’s request for comment.

However, the far greater burden of food insecurity, collapsed fish stocks, social unrest, and air and water pollution is borne by the poorer countries that produce the fish meal or farmed seafood that Canada imports.

For example, Canada imports over a third of its shrimp from India, where the investigation found explosions, fires, and worker asphyxiations at factories producing fish meal that supplies the country’s shrimp farms.
Freshly caught live shrimp are seen on a shrimp farm in India, April 11, 2025. (Sahiba Chawdhary/Reuters)

As recently as 2022, United Marine Products, the Goan fish meal plant that was found to be illegally dumping wastewater, supplied fish meal to Skretting Canada, which produces feed for many of Canada’s fish farms.

At another factory called Bismi Aquatic Products in 2021, a migrant worker died while he was cleaning a wastewater tank and passed out from the fumes. Major shrimp brands like IFC and AZ Gems, which source much of their shrimp from India, are sold across Canada at major supermarket chains like Metro Canada, Loblaws, and Costco Canada.

Skretting has a “zero-tolerance policy” for breaches of its policies that clearly state business partners abide by all applicable laws and regulations that govern their business activities, said the company’s Sustainability and Communications Director, Jorge Diaz, and has opened an investigation to verify the information found in this reporting.

In response to questions from Outlaw Ocean, Metro spokesperson Stephanie Bonk wrote: “All Metro suppliers are required to respect working conditions across the supply chain as outlined in our Supplier Code of Conduct for responsible procurement.”
IFC, AZ Gems, and Loblaws did not respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 37: Bribery article dropped, financial records examined
articles.summary: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte concluded its 37th day with the prosecution wrapping up the presentation of its last two witnesses, as well as the dropping of the bribery article.

blocks.text: Published October 9, 2026 8:59pm

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte concluded its 37th day with the prosecution wrapping up the presentation of its last two witnesses, as well as the dropping of the bribery article.
The session on Friday resumed with the defense’s cross-examination of the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) Office of the Commissioner's chief of staff Atty. Anne Loraine Garcia-Marquez.

Defense counsel Kristine Ferrer presented to the court the letter of authority issued by the BIR to Duterte and her husband, Atty. Manases Carpio. While private prosecutor Erwin Matib raised that the information was supposed to be confidential, Ferrer said that her clients gave permission.

There was also a brief disagreement on when the BIR could assess and file tax records in a fraud case, which Garcia-Marquez clarified: upon the discovery of fraud, the BIR has 10 years to assess the case.
Outside of the impeachment court, House prosecutor Keith Flores confirmed that they were dropping the bribery article against Duterte, citing time constraints.

During the interjections of the senator-judges, a few raised concerns about the Duterte couple’s financial records. Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros said that a Ukrainian company remitted money to Cale88 Foods Corporation, one of the businesses linked to Carpio. Meanwhile, Senator-judge Joel Villanueva raised concern over Cale88’s P150 million in sales in 2024 while only having two workers.

One of the biggest revelations of the day, however, included the testimony of the prosecution’s last witness: forensic financial expert Alexander Cabrera. While the defense questioned why Cabrera was allowed access to confidential documents, the prosecution maintained that lawyers were allowed to make use of experts.

Cabrera then delivered a report alleging that Duterte and Carpio had P817.87 million in unexplained wealth. He had pieced together, through the various tax and financial records provided by the prosecution, that the vice president had grossly underdeclared her and her husband’s income.
The defense has yet to cross-examine Cabrera and will question him on Monday. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: A local’s playbook to Makati-maxxing
articles.summary: So many cities in the world, but no one quite like her (Makati)

blocks.text: Makati has been gaining popularity (not that it has ever been out of its game), but social media, especially TikTok, has given the city a brand-new personality. Trends like “Salcedo girlie” and “United States of Makati” show just how many interesting things the city has to offer. All of a sudden, the routines locals have had for years have been given names and tied to certain aesthetics.

But when you have lived here for most of your life, what feels like a spectacle to others can simply be the norm. The places people intentionally visit might just be where you usually buy late dinner or somewhere your family has been taking you since childhood.

So what is it actually like to live here, move through here, and call this city home? If you think this is a list of the newest or coolest places in the city, well… it’s not. Instead, it’s a field guide to the spots that have stood the test of time and captured the hearts of many Makati residents.
When Makati feels like a neighborhood
On Sundays, one of Makati’s busiest streets becomes one of its most inclusive and democratic public spaces.

blocks.caption: CAR-FREE SUNDAYS. Makati opens Ayala Avenue to runners, cyclists, families, and visitors.

blocks.text: You will see all kinds of people here — runners, families, athletes, and sometimes even a celebrity. For a few hours, Ayala Avenue kind of becomes an equilibrium. You’ll see people from all walks of life sharing the same road, stripped of whatever separates us during the week.
You come to realize that, after all, we are just people longing for an open space in the heart of the city.
Power Plant or “Rockwell” to locals, is actually less of a mall and more like one big living room.

blocks.caption: THE ICONIC ROCKWELL CENTER SKYLINE. A prime example of life in a curated community, where everything you need is within walking distance.

blocks.text: There’s a running joke that if you go here on a Sunday, you’ll bump into everyone you’ve ever known: old classmates, former coworkers, and even ex-situationships (lol).
Rockwell’s tight-knit community is exactly its appeal, which is why it has earned its place as a third space for many locals.

blocks.caption: POWERPLANT MALL. For many locals, this place can be familiar ground where errands easily become mini reunions.

blocks.text: For when you want to gather family and friends
The OGs! For lunch with family — or any group large enough to make choosing a restaurant complicated — there are these two.

Both are reliable classics that serve homestyle Filipino food for multigenerational tastes. It also helps that they have warm, stand-alone settings that feel more like grandma’s house than usual commercial spaces.

blocks.caption: A FAMILY FAVORITE. Romulo Café pairs homestyle Filipino food with a setting made for large family gatherings.
A MAKATI INSTITUTION. Milky Way has served classic Filipino dishes and generations of Makati families for decades.

blocks.text: They have also been around long enough to witness many milestones in the lives of Makati residents. A baptism, an engagement party, a birthday celebration — eventually, another generation grows up and returns with a family of their own.
A MICHELIN Guide-selected Spanish restaurant in the heart of Salcedo Village, Pablo Bistro is one of those places that is easy to keep in mind if you live or work in Makati.

blocks.caption: WHERE REGULARS RETURN. Pablo is a true neighborhood favorite for its Spanish comfort food and warm atmosphere.

blocks.text: It is open from 7 am to 12 mn, so it works for almost any kind of plan. That flexibility makes it an easy meeting place for all kinds of groups. Whenever everyone becomes available, there is a good chance it is still open.

Also selected by the MICHELIN Guide, Papillon is for girls’ night or date night when you want something a little more elevated. Its dramatic Asian interiors give you a reason to turn up the ante a bit.
It can get busy as it often hosts private events, so it’s worth reserving ahead.

blocks.caption: FOR SPECIAL NIGHTS. Papillon offers a refined take on Southeast Asian cuisine.

blocks.text: Where Makati feels a little fancy

Sometimes, you want to feel a little fancy, and for that, there is the Pen lobby. This place carries an older image of Makati in all its grandeur, reflecting the dreams and ambition Makati has always represented.
There is always the piano, and from Thursday to Sunday, an orchestra. It’s where you can have your usual coffee or tea when you want something a little more upscale than a café.

blocks.caption: THE ICONIC PEN LOBBY. Have lunch, sip coffee, and savor live music beneath Napoleon Abueva’s Sunburst.

blocks.text: For when you want to go solo
Commune lives up to its name. Apart from serving Philippine coffee, it has become a meeting place for the different communities that pass through Poblacion.

blocks.caption: A MAKATI HOME FOR CREATIVES. Commune is a place for laid-back moments within Poblacion.

blocks.text: Its second floor also serves as a haven for creatives. You can catch a workshop, an improv show, or a small performance. It’s a place that has actually built a community for various creative groups.

This well-loved place understands the city like no other. It’s a café by day, then come evening, its not-so-secret bar opens. After more than a decade in the Legazpi Village neighborhood, it remains the kind of place both locals and visitors make a point of visiting.

blocks.caption: A MODERN CLASSIC. After more than a decade, The Curator still sets the standard for handcrafted drinks.

blocks.text: Makati before the aesthetic

Long before Japanese food went ubiquitous, locals flocked to Chino Roces for reliable favorites at Little Tokyo, while nearby Makati Cinema Square (officially Makati Central Square) retains its unpretentious charm — a retro hub where you can find old-school eateries, bowling alleys, art galleries, and eccentric bars. The ukay-ukay stalls here also draw a younger generation of thrift shoppers.

blocks.caption: THE ORIGINAL JAPAN TOWN. Little Tokyo has remained a favorite for Japanese food and a taste of old Makati.
STILL STANDING STRONG. Makati Cinema Square has outlasted trends by remaining stubbornly itself — eccentric and unapologetically old-school.

blocks.text: To see Makati as a local is to know the city in all its contradictions. It is glass towers and narrow side streets, MICHELIN-recognized restaurants and Jolly Jeep meals, and so much more.

People may come for the version of Makati they have seen online, but when you’ve lived here most of your life, you come to recognize it in all its versions. Still, Makati has never belonged only to those who live here.

Every day, it welcomes people who come to work, eat, explore, or simply find their place in the city. And maybe this is why “Makati-maxxing” has captured the attention of many. The city leaves enough room for everyone to make some part of it their own. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Poland: Lifeline for Ukrainian refugees confronts donor fatigue and online abuse as anti-Ukrainian sentiment grows
articles.summary: A Ukrainian woman who fled the war in her country built a lifeline for refugees in Poland. Now her organization faces donor fatigue, funding cuts and rising hostility as support for Ukrainians in…

image.caption: Nastya Podorozhnya was a 24-year-old Ukrainian graduate living in Poland when Russia invaded her native country in 2022. She decided to use her knowledge of Poland to help Ukrainian refugees arriving in the countryImage: Adam Easton/DW

blocks.text: Hours after Vladimir Putin announced his "special military operation" in Ukraine on February 24, 2022, Russian troops began attacking Kyiv's Antonov Airport close to the home of Nastya Podorozhnya's family.
Nastya was 24 at the time and living in Krakow in neighboring Poland, having recently graduated from the city's Jagiellonian University.

Alarmed by the news from Ukraine and fearful of what was coming, Nastya rushed back to Ukraine two days before the invasion to be with her family and help her sister and her three children cross the border to safety in Poland.
Helping compatriots fleeing Ukraine

Nastya realized she could use her experience of living in Poland — how to get a doctor's appointment or simply buy a tram ticket — to help the flood of mostly women and children arriving in the country.

blocks.caption: After Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, refugees flooded across the border into Poland. In the months after the invasion, there was an outpouring of support from Polish peopleImage: Krzysztof Kaniewski/ZUMA Wire/IMAGO

blocks.text: Poles were offering help and food at the border, but some people sought to take advantage of the vulnerable arrivals.

"I spoke to activists engaged in anti-human trafficking and they said what was happening at the border in the first weeks after the invasion was like Christmas, Easter and birthdays rolled into one for traffickers because people were so easily trusting the volunteers," Nastya told DW in a two-bedroom apartment in central Krakow her organization uses to provide shelter to vulnerable women refugees escaping domestic abuse or trafficking.
Hotline still fields 100 calls a months
Named Martynka, after Nastya's youngest niece, the organization also runs a hotline. It has received more than 5,000 requests for help since March 2022 and now gets about a hundred every month.
Her small team provides psychological and moral support in four languages as well as legal assistance and counselling.

blocks.caption: Podorozhnya's organization, Martynka, runs a shelter in Krakow for vulnerable women and children refugees escaping domestic abuse or traffickingImage: Adam Easton/DW

blocks.text: "One of the very young women who lived with us for a long time was drugged by her boyfriend who she met as a teenager when she escaped the full-scale invasion and after years of relationship she found out that he has been drugging her and selling sex with her to other people" she said.
Nastya said she was motivated to help partly because of a traumatic experience of her own. While studying in Krakow, a Ukrainian man tried to rape her outside of her dormitory.

After a long and difficult legal process, during which police detained the suspect before releasing him, he was eventually found guilty of violating Nastya's bodily autonomy and given a restraining order.

"This terrible, traumatic experience not only gave me horrible PTSD, which later on sort of helped me be empathetic and understand survivors with PTSD, but also it put me through the system of justice and how survivors are being treated," she added.
Aid cuts and donor fatigue
Since 2022, around 100 women and children have found shelter in the apartment. Her team's work relies largely on donations from international organizations.

blocks.caption: Nastya Podorozhnya holds a box that was handmade by one of the women who stayed in the shelter Image: Adam Easton/DW

blocks.text: But cuts to USAID have led to increased competition for grants, while donor fatigue has forced the team to cut its one-to-one therapy sessions.

"Ukraine is not in the headlines anymore," says Nastya. "The international attention has moved elsewhere. For all of summer 2026 we have been running a very challenging fundraising campaign. It is so hard to convince people to donate to a Ukrainian organization right now. There is something called exhaustion, donor exhaustion, fundraising exhaustion."
The UNHCR's acting representative for Poland, Czechia and Slovakia, Jun Shirato, confirmed the difficult situation in the aid sector.

Speaking to DW in Warsaw, she said that funding cuts last year have forced UNHCR to scale back its staff in Poland by two thirds from 120 at its peak in the months after the invasion to 40 now. The UNHCR has now closed three of its regional offices opened in Krakow, Lublin and Rzeszow after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Its sole remaining office in Poland is in Warsaw.
Changing attitudes to Ukrainians
Nastya's fundraising efforts increasingly meet with online abuse, too.
Attitudes toward Ukrainians in Poland have changed. In the months after the invasion, many Poles opened their homes to refugees, including Nastya's sister and her daughters.

blocks.caption: Historical disputes between Poland and Ukraine — in particular surrounding the role of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army in the Volhynia massacre during World War II — are fueling hostility toward Ukrainians in PolandImage: Marek Antoni Iwańczuk/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: The situation is now very different. Earlier this year, new rules restricting access to child benefits and free healthcare for refugees who don't work were introduced.
In the first half of this year, reports of hate crimes committed against Ukrainians in Poland rose by a third according to Polish Police statistics.
Historical disputes fuel tension

At the same time, historical disputes between Poland and Ukraine, have resurfaced, fueling further hostility toward the Ukrainian community, which accounts for more than three quarters of all foreigners living in Poland.

In May, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's decision to name a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which took part in the murder of tens of thousands of Poles during the Second World War, triggered outrage in Poland.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped Zelenskyy of Poland's highest state honor, the Order of the White Eagle.

While Poles focus on the UPA's massacre of Polish citizens, many Ukrainians view the UPA and nationalist leaders like Stepan Bandera as heroes because they fought against the Soviet occupation after the war.

blocks.caption: A pro-Ukrainian demonstration under the slogan 'Don't Be Indifferent' opposing xenophobic attacks on Ukrainians was organized by the Committee for the Defense of Democracy in 22 cities across Poland this summerImage: Klaudia Radecka/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: "This week we are supporting a family of Ukrainians whose car was completely destroyed. No windows left in the car and with spray paint someone wrote 'Bandera people go back where you came from,'" said Nastya, adding, "I think it is so devastating and I've recorded a video about it. We have hundreds of comments there, of people wishing me death, wishing me to go back where I came from. It is very tough emotionally."
Animosity stoked by Russian bots
Nastya said the hostility is also driven by Russia using online bots to stoke tensions between Poles and Ukrainians.
"They do not want us to be together, or to remember who our common enemy is. They don't want Ukrainian refugees to integrate or feel welcome," she said.
Despite the strain, Nastya remains optimistic that she and her team can continue their work.

"For some reason I am — and this is the weirdest thing. I love my job so much. I want to do this beautiful thing. I would easily send my mother, my sister, my best friend to Martynka for support. I know there are few organizations that could provide such wonderful help."

articles.title: Canadian economy lost 68,000 jobs in September
articles.summary: The decline marks a second straight month of job losses. Economists polled ahead of the release predicted employers added 9,200 positions in September.

image.caption: Employment-seekers line up for a chance to interview at the CNE job fair, held at the Enercare Centre, in Toronto, on July 29, 2026. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Business·Breaking
The decline marks a second straight month of job losses. Economists polled ahead of the release predicted employers added 9,200 positions in September.
Decline comes after economy shed 42,000 jobs the month before
Canada lost 68,000 jobs in September, according to Statistics Canada, marking a second month of losses in a row, while the unemployment rate rose to 6.5 per cent.
The decline was concentrated in youth aged 15 to 24, who accounted for 48,000 job losses, according to the data agency.
Statistics Canada says job losses were split between full- and part-time work and were concentrated in the public sector.

By sector, educational services, health care and social assistance, and manufacturing led the declines. More workers in "other services," which includes things like repair and maintenance, offset the losses.
A Reuters poll of economists ahead of the release predicted employers added 9,200 positions in September.
The decline follows 42,000 job losses in August, which came as a surprise to economists and snapped a hot streak for the labour market.

Before the two monthly declines, Statistics Canada data showed employment trending upward, with 181,000 jobs added between April and July. Employment is still up compared to a year ago by 95,000 positions.
The jobs data will be the Bank of Canada's last look at the labour market before its next interest rate decision on Oct. 28.
With files from the Canadian Press

articles.title: Financial analyst flags P11.35-M checks paid to Sara Duterte's dentist
articles.summary: Financial forensic analyst Alexander Cabrera, a witness presented by the prosecution, on Friday revealed that P11.35 million worth of checks was supposedly paid to the dentist of Vice President Sara…

blocks.text: Published October 9, 2026 8:35pm

Financial forensic analyst Alexander Cabrera, a witness presented by the prosecution, on Friday revealed that P11.35 million worth of checks was supposedly paid to the dentist of Vice President Sara Duterte.

On Day 37 of the impeachment trial, House prosecutor Rep. Chel Diokno presented parts of Cabrera’s summary report, which highlighted certain banking behaviors of the Vice President and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio “that may warrant further review and investigation.”

In the report, the witness noted several check payments with the payee's name being blacked out under a BDO checking account. He said he was able to list the names of the payees because they were still visible.
One of the names listed was Lourdes Lebosada, who supposedly received check payments amounting to P11.35 million.
Cabrera said that Lebosada, whom he identified as a dentist of the Vice President, was a partner of Carpio in Cale88 Foods Corporation.
“Si Ms. Lourdes Lebosada po ay ito po ang partner ni Atty. Mans Carpio sa kanyang business na CALE88. 47.5 percent po ‘yung kanilang ownership sa CALE88,” the witness said.
(Ms. Lourdes Lebosada is Atty. Mans Carpio’s partner in his business, CALE88. She holds a 47.5 percent ownership of CALE88.)
“Ang total po ng tseke na binayad po kay Ms. Lourdes Lebosada ay P11.35 million na sa palagay ko po ay hindi po ‘yan bayad sa pasta,” he added.
(The total amount of the checks paid to Ms. Lourdes Lebosada is P11.35 million—which, in my opinion, is not payment for dental fillings.)
Defense counsel Kristine Ferrer reacted to the statement of Cabrera, but Diokno himself immediately volunteered to have it stricken off the record.
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero then issued a reminder to the witness.
“The witness is reminded to kindly avoid unresponsive additions to the answer he will give to questions propounded by counsel,” Escudero told Cabrera.
The witness apologized for his remarks.
Diokno likewise asked Cabrera for a basis that Lebosada is the dentist of the Vice President.
“Meron po kaming nakitang Facebook post ng Lebosada Clinic kung saan magkasama si Dr. Lebosada at si VP Sara,” he answered.
(We saw a Facebook post from Lebosada Clinic showing Dr. Lebosada and VP Sara together.)
The photo of Lebosada and Duterte was flashed on the screen during the trial. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: India's 'cockroaches' vs Election Commission: What you need to know ahead of CJP's October 10 protests
articles.summary: New Delhi has been turned into a fortress with train and metro cancelations, barricades and heavy police presence ahead of Saturday's planned protests against the chief of India's electoral body.

image.caption: Parts of central New Delhi have been barricaded amid a strong presence of security personnel ahead of the October 10 protestsImage: Arvind Yadav/Hindustan Times/IMAGO

blocks.text: India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has called for a nationwide march on New Delhi on Saturday, after its ultimatum demanding the resignation of the country's election chief was ignored.

In the days leading up to the planned gathering, authorities have been clamping down on protesters gathering at Jantar Mantar, the 18th-century observatory that serves as Delhi's designated protest site.
These include the general public, student activists and leaders of opposition, including the Indian National Congress' Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke urged people to turn out in huge numbers, while adding that the Delhi police were already detaining protesters: "The more people you detain, the more people will show up!"
The stakes remain high: the credibility of the body that runs the world's largest elections is on the line.
What is the controversy about?

Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar is currently in the hot seat after the Indian Express newspaper published an investigation that revealed that fellow Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months to decisions concerning voter registrations, deletions and restorations, as well as control of electoral-roll data.

blocks.caption: Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar flanked by Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi at a 2025 press conference Image: Jitender Gupta/ANI

blocks.text: In one of the objections, Sandhu complained that the Election Commission of India (ECI) acted against the written advice of the two commissioners and claimed its action was "unauthorized and illegal."

Kumar became the chief election commissioner (CEC) in 2025 after being chosen by a selection panel led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Rahul Gandhi, who was also a member of the panel, had opposed Kumar's appointment.

Now, Kumar, along with Sandhu and Joshi, is responsible for overseeing the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), a nationwide re-verification of the electoral rolls requiring voters to prove their eligibility to remain on them.

The ECI says the process is meant to remove redundancies in India's electoral rolls, including deceased individuals, those who have permanently moved abroad and duplicate entries — as well as avoiding the "inclusion of the names of foreign illegal immigrants."
But critics say it has gone far beyond that remit.
The Indian Express report says more than 130 million names were removed from electoral rolls across the country. For scale, Germany has about 60 million eligible voters in total.

blocks.caption: Opposition leaders, including Priyanka Gandhi Vadra (pictured here holding a copy of India's constitution) have been demanding Kumar's resignationImage: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

blocks.text: Who are the 'cockroaches' and what do they want?

A play on the name of Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the youth-led movement emerged in May after the chief justice of India, Surya Kant, referred to unemployed young people as "cockroaches" in an offhand remark during an unrelated court hearing.

The move backfired, with young people embracing the tag and turning it into an avenue for disillusionment over what they see as failings in the country's education system and its massive youth unemployment problem.
The CJP has amassed nearly 25 million Instagram followers, more than double that of the BJP's 9.9 million. Modi, however, remains far ahead at 106 million.
A campaign protesting multiple competitive exam leaks launched the CJP into nationwide relevance, securing the resignation of the then-Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
Education minister concedes to 'Cockroach' demands, resigns
Now, the CJP is demanding:

items: Kumar's resignation and initiation of criminal proceedings against him
An immediate hold on upcoming elections, and freezing the SIR
The repeal of the 2023 law on the appointment of the Election Commissioners of India

blocks.text: Is CJP really leading the protests?
The CJP is not alone in its call for protests.

For days ahead of the planned October 10 march to Jantar Mantar, student activists, civil society members — including former high-ranking government officials — and leaders of opposition have been taking to the streets of Delhi calling for accountability and Kumar's resignation.

The CJP was joined by representatives of several student associations, including the left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA) and its breakout star Neha Bora, who has been leading protests in the capital all week.

Meanwhile, dramatic scenes emerged from New Delhi as leaders from the opposition INDIA alliance, including the Gandhis, were detained repeatedly by authorities as they took to the streets calling for Kumar's resignation.

blocks.caption: Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi has been a part of the protests all week, and detained on multiple occasions by local policeImage: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

blocks.text: Bharatiya Kisan Union spokesperson and farmer rights activist Rakesh Tikait also extended his support to the march and vowed to join on October 10. Tikait was part of the leadership behind the 2020-2021 farmers' agitation, which forced the Indian government to repeal three laws intended to liberalize the agricultural sector.
The other side

Amid heavy police presence and barricading near the ECI offices in lush central Delhi, the electoral body has rejected any suggestion of a split and Kumar's overreach, maintaining that all decisions, including on the SIR, were unanimous.

It also addressed allegations that opposition parties were not allowed to meet with its officials on Tuesday, saying that till "4.00 pm today, no political party, through its representatives, had sought an appointment for a meeting with the Election Commission."

A day earlier, a delegation of retired senior bureaucrats had also attempted to approach the office of the ECI to submit a charge sheet and impeachment notice against Kumar on behalf of the public, but were unable to reach the premises.
Delhi police said no permission has been given for the October 10 protests, calling it illegal.
"I request everyone to refrain from participating in this protest," Delhi's Deputy Commissioner of Police Shrishti Pandey told news agency ANI.

Some BJP politicians had previously referred to the CJP as a "cross-border influence operation" aimed at destabilizing India, with federal minister Kiren Rijiju accusing them of seeking social media followers ⁠from archenemy Pakistan and the "anti-India gang."
What to watch for on October 10
New Delhi has been turned into a fortress, with the government deploying close to 43,000 security personnel ahead of the protests, local media reported.
Several independent journalists and others associated with the last round of CJP protests have claimed that authorities have been using intimidation tactics to keep them from joining the march.
Among those arrested is CJP national spokesperson Deepak Baliyan, who was taken into police custody on Thursday, but released hours later.
In the last round of CJP protests, the police had used tear gas, sticks and pellet-firing shotguns to subdue the demonstrators.
