articles.title: Thieves steal 30,000 wine bottles worth €5m in Italy, reports say
articles.summary: The heist at the Florence-based winery is believed to be one of the largest thefts of its kind in Italy.

blocks.text: Thieves have stolen 30,000 bottles of wine collectively worth about €5m (£4.2m) from a prestigious Italian winery, Italian media reports.

Marchesi Antinori, one of Italy's biggest family-owned wineries, said the theft at its storage facility in Tuscany took place on Saturday as the company was preparing to ship a consignment to customers abroad.

At least seven masked men are believed to have deactivated the alarms, disabled the cameras and used company forklifts to load two large trucks of the company's prized Tignanello, Solaia and Guado al Tasso Tuscan reds.
Renzo Cotarella, the chief executive, told Corriere della Sera this was the largest theft of its kind in Italy.
"A theft of this scale and value has certainly never occurred in Italy," he said.
He added that he was hopeful the authorities would be able to trace the stolen wine.

"Two trucks full of merchandise can't just disappear into thin air. The Tuscan roads are full of cameras; perhaps with a bit of luck we'll be able to recover at least some of the bottles stolen from us."
He told the Financial Times: "These wines have a great value and I don't know how they can sell all this wine around the world without being seen."
The company believes the selection of bottles, which usually sell for between €150 and €500 each, suggests the thieves were wine connoisseurs and had inside knowledge.
The theft was only discovered on Monday morning as staff arrived on site. No arrests have been made.
Marchesi Antinori was founded in 1385 and exports to 170 countries. It had a revenue of €263m (£223m) last year.
There has been a spate of wine thefts in Italy this year, including two in the northern Piedmont region where hundreds of thousands of euros worth of bottles were reportedly taken.

articles.title: Who is Alexander Cabrera, the financial forensic analyst witness?
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel on Friday presented Alexander Cabrera, the financial forensic analyst who is expected to tie together the tax and financial records of Vice President Sara Duterte and her…

blocks.text: Published October 9, 2026 5:08pm

The House prosecution panel on Friday presented Alexander Cabrera, the financial forensic analyst who is expected to tie together the tax and financial records of Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio.

Cabrera faced the court on the 37th Day of Duterte’s impeachment trial. Before he was presented however, Defense counsel Sheila Sison raised an issue with the witness, questioning why Cabrera was allowed access to confidential documents.
House prosecutor Rep. Chel Diokno argued that the documents were already declared to be public, adding that it was standard practice for lawyers to consult experts for their cases.

Impeachment presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero also said that it was standard for experts to be given legally-acquired materials for their insights, saying that the defense was free to raise questions during their cross-examination.
Diokno then proceeded to establish Cabrera’s credibility as an expert.

Cabrera said that he graduated high school from Our Lady of Peace in Antipolo, Rizal. He then acquired his degree in Bachelor of Science in Business Administration and Accountancy from the Philippine School of Business Administration.

He went on to become a certified public accountant in 1988 and began work as a staff auditor at the accounting firm, Isla Lipana & Co, which is internationally known as the PwC Philippines. The firm is a member of the PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) network.

Since then, he rose through the ranks to become a senior associate in the tax department, and then became a senior manager before becoming a managing partner. He eventually became the vice chair of the firm before assuming the post of chair.
He retired from the firm in 2025 as the Chair Emeritus.
Part of his work was detecting fraud in financial records, saying that in his nearly 40 years, he has analyzed thousands of mergers and acquisitions.

Forensic audit was part of Cabrera’s job, saying that he had also spent thousands of hours on cases. During Diokno’s questioning, Cabrera said that he considered tax structuring and tax planning as his specialties.

Cabrera has also served as a resource person for legislative hearings in multiple hearings in Congress, saying that he offered his expertise in taxation. He has also worked in Congressional technical working groups. He estimated that he offered his expertise to Congress almost 100 times.
He also has a column in The Philippine Star called the “As easy as ABC”, where he talks about business and other national matters. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: BIR witness confirms issuance of LOA to Mans Carpio's CALE88
articles.summary: The Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) has issued a letter of authority (LOA) for Cale88 Foods Corporation, one of the listed business interests of lawyer Manases Carpio, husband of Vice President Sara…

blocks.text: Published October 9, 2026 5:07pm

The Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) has issued a letter of authority (LOA) for Cale88 Foods Corporation, one of the listed business interests of lawyer Manases Carpio, husband of Vice President Sara Duterte.

This was confirmed by BIR Office of the Commissioner chief of staff Atty. Anne Loraine Garcia-Marquez on the 37th day of the impeachment trial, where the Vice President’s alleged unexplained wealth was being scrutinized.

During his interjection, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian pointed out the discrepancy between the declared sales of CALE88 to BIR amounting to P208 million, and its remittances worth P700 million as found by the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC).
The witness explained that inflows may be loans or any kind of donations, but emphasized that the company should still declare such funds in the financial statements.

“This should have been declared in the audited financial statement dahil…nandito lahat ng cash flow statement wherein dapat lahat ng galaw ng cash ng isang company ay nakalagay. So any inflow na na-receive ng company should've been declared in the audited financial statement,” Garcia-Marquez explained.

(This should have been declared in the audited financial statements because… the cash flow statement is in here, reflecting all of the company’s cash movements. So, any inflow received by the company should have been declared in the audited financial statement.)
“As to those na outside or hindi na-declare sa audited financial statement, maraming pong possibilities but hindi ko masasabi, Your Honor,” she added.
(As for those that are outside or not declared in the audited financial statements, there are many possibilities, which I cannot say for sure, Your Honor.)
Gatchalian then asked Garcia-Marquez if such a scenario would make CALE88 a candidate for the issuance of a LOA from the BIR.
“In fact, Your Honor, meron na pong letter of authority,” the witness answered.
Gatchalian clarified, “Ah, so meron na nga siyang letter of authority, so iniimbestigahan na itong company na ito?”
(So it already has a letter of authority, meaning this company is already being investigated?)
The BIR official answered in the affirmative.
The Senate President asked about possible penalties if a company is found not declaring sales.

“Under declaration po ng sales, magko-compute po tayo dito ng deficiency taxes. Meron po kasing civil and merong criminal cases. So sa civil, dito pumapasok ‘yung mga deficiency taxes na dapat bayaran. At kapag napatunayan na may tax evasion man, then dito papasok ang sa criminal case,” Garcia-Marquez said.

(Regarding the declaration of sales, we will compute the deficiency taxes here. We have civil and criminal cases. Civil cases cover the deficiency taxes that must be paid, while criminal cases come into play if tax evasion is proven.)
During Thursday’s trial, the BIR official said the agency found no records of the transfer of shares of stock of Cale88 to Pikimong Pikimong Corporation.

Cale88 is one of the business interests listed under the joint Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN) of Duterte and her husband in multiple years, including the years when the Vice President already assumed office. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Bosnia and Herzegovina will soon have a new Grand Mufti
articles.summary: The new leader of the Islamic Community in Bosnia and Herzegovina will be elected on October 10. The reis-ul-ulema's role is not only important for Muslims in the country itself, but could inspire…

image.caption: The headquarters of the Islamic Community of Bosnia and Herzegovina are in SarajevoImage: Samir Huseinović/DW

blocks.text: The reis-ul-ulema or Grand Mufti of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the head of the country's Islamic community, represents the interests of Muslims before the state, expresses himself on political, moral and social issues and defends the independence of the Islamic Community in Bosnia and Herzegovina against attempts at foreign influence.
Having served two seven-year terms, the current Grand Mufti, Husein Kavazovic, is no longer permitted to run.

Three candidates are competing to become his successor: Salem Dedovic, the Mufti of Mostar, Nedzad Grabus, the Mufti of Sarajevo, and Mensur Malkic, the head of the Directorate for Religious Affairs of the Islamic Community in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Grand Mufti's envoy.

While Malkic's focus lies in strengthening the Islamic Community in religious and institutional terms, Dedovic has stated that he sees the office in a more political light and would like it to become more engaged in social debates. Grabus, who has the most international experience as the former Grand Mufti of Slovenia, says he would like to strengthen the community in times of globalization and secularization.

"No other Islamic personality in Europe holds a position like the Reis-ul-ulema in Sarajevo," said Imam Benjamin Idriz, the head of the Islamic Community in the Bavarian city of Penzberg and the chair of the Munich Forum for Islam. "That's why the importance of this election extends far beyond the country, to Muslims and non-Muslims alike, across Europe."

blocks.caption: Grand Mufti Husein Kavazovic has reached the end of his two termsImage: Samir Jordamovic/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: The President of the Islamic Community of Bosniaks in Germany (IGBD), Zenahir Mrakovic, said that the "election is important to us, because historically, theologically and institutionally, we share close ties with the Islamic Community of Bosnia and Herzegovina."
"Bosniak" is the name Bosnian Muslims use for themselves. With around 100 communities across the country, the IGBD is one of Germany's smaller Muslim associations.

Muslims have lived in Bosnia and Herzegovina for centuries. Islam was introduced to the population when to Ottoman Empire spread through southeastern Europe. The organizational structure of the Islamic Communities was established after the Berlin Congress in 1878, which, among other things, placed Bosnia and Herzegovina under Austro-Hungarian rule.

Following the example of Christian churches, the Austro-Hungarian rulers soon officially recognized Islam as a religious community and in 1882, they founded the Council of Ulema and appointed the first Reis-ul-ulema as president.
Unique self-organization of the Muslim faith

This kind of Islamic self-organization could become a model for Muslims across Europe. The Islamic Community of Bosnia and Herzegovina is independent from the state and is financed with donations, membership fees and zakat, a form of charity given by Muslims.

The Islamic Community has its own sort of parliament, the Sabor, and a Constitutional Court that ensures the community's actions are in line with the constitution of the country in which it operates. The Riyaset is the community's highest executive body, responsible for implementing decisions. Its headquarters are in Sarajevo.

In the 150 years since its founding, the Islamic Community of Bosnia and Herzegovina has survived numerous political upheavals and repeatedly adapted to new circumstances. After the Ottoman Empire came the Habsburg monarchy and Austro-Hungarian rule, then the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Yugoslavia under Josip Broz Tito. Following Tito's death, the Bosnian War for independence ended in 1995 with the Dayton Accords.

Today, Bosnia and Herzegovina is a secular state with a democratic constitutional order. Time and again, the Islamic Community has clearly distanced itself from radical tendencies. It has a history of cooperation and coexistence with Jewish and Christian communities.
This has also left an impression on the roughly 400,000 Bosnian Muslims living in Germany.

"In the process of institutionalizing Islam in Germany, the experience of the Bosniaks' Islamic Community should be taken more strongly into account," said Esnaf Begic, a former imam and a lecturer at the Institute for Islamic Theology at Osnabrück University. "We are autochthonous European Muslims and to a certain extent, we share more similarities with Germans than with Muslims from Afghanistan, Iran or Saudi Arabia."

Mrakovic, head of the IGBD, agrees that Bosnia's experience with organizing religious life in a democratic and pluralistic society could also be useful to other Muslim communities. "It's not about telling other people how to live their Islamic faith but about learning from our own experiences: how we preserve our religious identity while remaining a natural part of European, democratic society.

blocks.caption: Islamic feminism is more widespread in Bosnia and HerzegovinaImage: Samir Huseinović/DW

blocks.text: An office in challenging times

The new head of Bosnian Muslims will be assuming his role in challenging times. Statehood in Bosnia and Herzegovina remains fragile, and foreign actors are vying for more influence. "Attempts to exert more influence aren't only coming from Ankara or Riyah, but also from Washington, Berlin or Brussels. They, too are, trying to act upon the Reis-ul-ulema in their own interest," Begic said.

In Europe, anti-Muslim racism and Islamophobia have reached levels that are becoming increasingly frightening for Muslims. Right-wing populists are on the rise, and extremist parties are attracting more and more supporters bent on denying Muslims the right to participate in society.
Given the circumstances, the new Reis-ul-ulema will be expected to employ the full democratic and historical legitimacy of his office to actively engage in debates about Islam in Europe.

This is what Idriz, the imam from Penzberg, hopes for, too. He believes the new Reis-ul-ulema could inspire more confidence not only in Bosniaks, but in all European Muslims, while signaling to majority societies that Islam is a part of Europe, and that it affirms and embraces values such as the rule of law, gender equality and freedom of expression. "In the future, the Reis-ul-ulema should lay an even stronger emphasis on this," Idriz said.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Finland, the world's happiest nation, faces a glum winter
articles.summary: Finns have many reasons to feel content, but the country's pile of debt is not one of them. Russia's war in Ukraine has added to the fiscal burden. Can the Nordic nation absorb another shock?

image.caption: Finland's policymakers will spend the winter deciding where the ax should fallImage: Ardan Fuessmann/IMAGO

blocks.text: There's an uneasy mood in Finland, the country that's ranked the world's happiest for nine consecutive years. A colder-than-usual winter is on the way and so is the toughest austerity budget in years.
With an election due in April, the argument is no longer how much to cut, but which services, benefits and pensions will face the biggest cuts.

Finland's debt and deficit levels are in their worst state since the 1990s, when a banking crash and the collapse of the Soviet Union — a key export partner — pushed the Nordic nation into its own Great Depression.
Finland's debt ratio climbed sharply since the COVID-19 pandemic

Last month, Finland's national statistical institution confirmed that the national debt had reached 90.3% of gross domestic product (GDP) in the second quarter. Before the pandemic, that figure was around 65%.

Trouble to the east is, again, part of the reason. Finland ramped up defense spending after joining NATO a year after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Helsinki, which used to rely on Moscow for about a third of its energy, also faced much higher costs as it transitioned to other suppliers.

The Finnish government has spent more than it earns since the 2008/9 global financial crisis, partly due to an aging population and sluggish economic growth. Last month, the State Treasury projected the fiscal deficit would reach 4.2% of GDP in 2026.
EU scrutiny over growing deficit

Brussels has piled pressure on Helsinki to bring down the borrowing gap, as European Union rules require member states to stay below 3% of GDP. In January, the European Council opened an excessive deficit procedure and gave Finland until the end of 2028 to reach the desired target.

Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's government, which took office in June 2023, said it would aim to save about €9 billion ($10.1 billion) during this parliamentary term. But whoever wins the next election will have to cut much deeper, economists warn.
"The amounts currently estimated range from €8 to €11 billion," Jarkko Kivisto, an advisor to the Bank of Finland's monetary policy and research department, told DW.
Earlier this year, all but one political party agreed to support a debt brake, where the next government commits to tightening the country's deficit to about 2% of GDP by 2031.
Finland: Europe's race for critical raw materials
National Coalition rules out tax hikes

To date, Orpo's center-right National Coalition is the only party to promise a further €9 billion in cuts if he wins a second term. As well as further savings from health, social care and welfare, Orpo also plans to target workplace pensions, without reducing current payouts.
While the Social Democrats plan to split the reforms between spending cuts and tax hikes, Orpo plans to achieve his target without raising taxes — meaning public services will bear the brunt.
Kivisto, however, cautioned: "The deficit is so large that it would need a package that includes tax increases and expenditure cuts."

While Finland's at-risk-of-poverty rate is lower than the EU average, unemployment is higher than anywhere else in the bloc. In August, Finland's jobless total stood at 10.3%, just above Spain's 10%, according to Eurostat, the bloc's statistics agency. Youth unemployment reached 23.3%, against an EU average of 15.4%.
With household spending already falling, Lauri Holappa, director of the Finnish Centre for New Economic Analysis, warned that a new round of austerity would be a hard blow for the domestic economy.

"More than a quarter of the population works in the public sector, so if those workers face the threat of being sacked, the savings rate will rise and private spending will drop again," Holappa told DW.

Successive pressures ranging from the COVID-19 pandemic, higher interest rates and the global financial impact of two current wars have hurt efforts to cut the growing gap between income and borrowing. The 2027 budget proposal still counts on a spending gap of €12.4 billion.

blocks.caption: Finland has hiked up defense spending, and recently received its first delivery of F-35 fighter jetsImage: Jeremy Lock/REUTERS

blocks.text: Finland rearms after Russia's full-scale invasion
Before the Ukraine war, Finland had already committed to buying 64 F-35A fighter jets from the United States, in a deal worth about €8.4 billion.

During more than four years of Russia's war in Ukraine, the Nordic nation raised military spending from $4.5 billion to over $8 billion per year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
In April, the government said it would further increase defense spending to 3.2% of GDP, close to NATO's 3.5% target.
A night in Finland's largest underground defense bunker

With oil prices remaining close to $100 a barrel due to the Iran war, the government has so far resisted pressure to increase fuel subsidies. That's despite the Bank of Finland recording a 50% rise in the cost of imported energy in the early months of the Iran war.

While Finland’s shift to renewables, along with the opening of the Olkiluoto 3 nuclear power plant in 2023, has helped avoid a worse energy crisis, the central bank warned this summer that sustained high oil and gas prices would mean "lower economic growth and higher inflation" next year.

On another positive note, parts of Finland's export sector are booming, thanks to strong metal and shipbuilding orders, which Holappa described as strong as "the boom years of Nokia," when the once market-leading phone maker carried Finnish economic growth.
"There is a possibility that the export sector can steer us out of this recession," he told DW, as long as demand from the rest of Europe remains strong.

blocks.caption: Despite the country's financial woes, Finns are consistently ranked as the world’s happiest peopleImage: Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: Markets give Helsinki time to reform

Despite the multiple roadblocks to bringing down the deficit, market reaction to Finland's debt woes has, so far, been muted. Rating agencies have kept the country's outlook stable, apart from S&P, which turned negative in April without cutting the rating.

On October 6, the premium the Finnish government pays over Germany to borrow for 10 years was 38 basis points. That compares to 128 for France and 107 for Italy. In other words, investors still treat Finnish debt as among the safest in Europe.
That is, as long as the next shock is not another extended oil-price spike, a fresh escalation from Russia, or a Europe-wide debt crisis centered on France.

Next March, Finland could still be named the planet's happiest nation for the 10th year in a row. How long the smiles last, once the bill for decades of borrowing arrives a month later, is anyone's guess.

articles.title: How good is this year's flu shot? Here's what to know about flu season
articles.summary: Health officials say flu season has arrived early this year, but how worried should Canadians be? As we head into Thanksgiving weekend, the CBC looks at where the flu is hitting hardest and how you…

image.caption: As we head into cold and flu season, some experts are expecting less severe illness due to a milder strain of flu dominating so far, but the early start to the flu season has others stressing early prevention methods. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Walking down the street this week, it may seem like everyone is sneezing and hacking up a lung. But as health officials announce the start of an earlier than usual flu season, how worried should Canadians be? And as we head into Thanksgiving weekend, should we be scrambling to update flu and COVID-19 shots?

Some experts say that while this year's flu season may have arrived on our doorstep sooner than usual, it's not necessarily a cause for alarm — but other experts are stressing the importance of prevention in heavy-hit regions such as Toronto and Calgary, where authorities reported one person had already died from the virus.

The strain making up roughly 98 per cent of cases in Canada so far tends to be a milder one, according to Brian Ward, professor emeritus at the Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre in Montreal.

"So far at least, this looks like an H1N1 dominated year, and the years where H1N1 dominates, you can have very large outbreaks, but the number or the proportion of people … who get very sick, is relatively small compared to years that are dominated by H3N2," he told CBC News.
"I'm not convinced yet that we're actually seeing the beginning of a real outbreak. What we're seeing is sort of isolated, small outbreaks."
But where the flu is striking, doctors say it's striking hard. There are currently more than 400 confirmed flu cases in Alberta, where vaccines aren't yet widely available.

items: Doctors say flu season is ahead of schedule this year as cases pop up across Ontario
1 dead, more than 400 confirmed flu cases ahead of vaccine availability in Alberta

blocks.text: Some regions have started rolling out flu and COVID-19 shots to high-risk populations, with most regions set to offer shots to the general public by mid-October.
Here's what we know.
Is everyone getting sick right now?
According to the latest national numbers, which include data on influenza trends up to Sept. 26, there have been 2,102 detections of influenza across the country since the end of August.

It's an early start to the season. Between Sept. 20 and Sept. 26, 3.7 per cent of influenza tests came back positive, much higher than the average 0.5 per cent rate seen this time of year in 2023-2025.

items: Nova Scotia opens COVID-19, flu vaccine bookings ahead of respiratory illness season
Flu and COVID-19 vaccinations underway in B.C. as respiratory illness season arrives early
Vaccine-preventable illnesses on the horizon again as Canadian kids head back to school

blocks.text: But much of this national increase is driven by an uptick of cases in B.C. and Yukon, and in large cities such as Toronto and Calgary. The person who died in Alberta lived in the Calgary area and was in the 70-79 years age range, authorities say.
"The rest of the country is really very quiet," Ward said.
B.C. warns of early start to flu season, launches fall immunization campaign
He noted that in B.C., outbreaks in long-term care homes are driving the increase in cases, warning that families getting together this holiday weekend could result in further spread.
"That may be the seed that moves the virus … into the schools and universities and marketplaces and so on. But overall, we're still below the 5 per cent [epidemic] threshold."
Official figures don't catch every case of flu, as not everyone seeks out a test when they fall ill.

In hard-hit Toronto, family doctor Joseph Param told CBC News the increase of flu patients he's seeing at his practice is mainly among young adults who are more likely to travel on public transit and may still go to work when feeling under the weather, perhaps because they're used to flu season starting later.
You're not imagining it — flu season has started early this year
"Over the last couple of weeks, patients who are very healthy who see me rarely have been coming in with severe symptoms," he said.
"So it is important that the general population is aware that we are seeing … early cases now and so that we start taking precautions earlier than expected."
Doctors advise Canadians to stay home if they feel ill and to get vaccinated as soon as shots become available in their area, particularly with the long weekend coming up.
How effective is the flu shot this year?
The protection of flu shots varies from year to year depending on the most dominant strain of influenza in your area.

This year, it's a "good" match, Ward said. Although H3N2 viruses dominated for much of 2025, that subtype hasn't cropped up much in 2026, and this year's vaccine is well-positioned to protect against H1N1.
He said "influenza viruses march to their own drummers" and can mutate even within one flu season.

It's not just flu season in Canada — historically, we see more respiratory illnesses in general cropping up during the fall and going into winter, including colds and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), the latter of which is most dangerous in young children.
Around 98 per cent of lab-confirmed cases of influenza in Canada since the end of August have been of the H1N1 strain, according to government data. (New Africa/Shutterstock)

Rates of COVID-19 are currently trending lower right now than last year, with 3.8 per cent of tests coming back positive in the last week of September compared with 10.3 per cent at the same time in 2025.

The National Advisory Committee on Immunizations (NACI) said in September that it continues to "strongly recommend" the latest COVID-19 booster shots for those at a higher risk of developing severe COVID-19, including health-care workers, adults over the age of 65, those with immunocompromised systems and people in long-term care homes.
When can I get my flu and COVID-19 shots?

Several provinces such as Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia are already advising residents that appointments for flu vaccines and COVID-19 booster shots are available now for residents over the age of six months.
New Brunswick, Saskatchewan and Manitoba are currently allowing residents to book their flu and COVID-19 vaccines, with immunization efforts officially kicking off on Oct. 13.
Those living in Newfoundland and Labrador can receive flu and COVID-19 shots starting Oct. 19.
In Ontario, flu and COVID-19 immunizations have been available since last week for high-risk groups, but don't open to the general public until Oct. 26.

In Quebec, you can start making appointments as of Oct. 13, but the flu and COVID-19 vaccination campaign itself doesn't begin until Oct. 20. It is only free to eligible residents deemed high-risk, meaning non-eligible residents must pay for the shots.

items: Updated COVID-19, flu vaccines available in N.B. on Oct. 13
Alberta now providing free RSV antibodies to newborns after calls from pediatricians to expand access

blocks.text: Flu and COVID-19 shots can be booked now in Alberta, with the first appointments starting Oct. 19. While flu shots are free to everyone, Albertans who aren't considered high-risk for COVID-19 will have to pay.
In B.C., those registered in their Get Vaccinated system will receive a notification reminding them to get their flu shots. Flu and COVID-19 shots are available starting Oct. 13.

COVID-19 and flu shots will be available at specific clinics in the Northwest Territories this fall, but a timeline hasn't been released yet. Those in Yukon have been able to book appointments for flu and COVID-19 shots since the end of September. No details have been released for Nunavut's rollout as of Oct. 8.
Before heading out to the pharmacy, it's important to check the requirements in your area to be sure that you're eligible. Most regions offer RSV vaccines to eligible patients as well.

In the future, we could see more variety in our flu vaccines: an mRNA influenza vaccine made by Moderna was approved by the FDA in the U.S. in the summer, making this the first flu season it'll face. It's still under review by Health Canada.

articles.title: 11 things we learned about Terry Fox from Run Terry Run
articles.summary: Run Terry Run, a new documentary directed by Sean Menard, offers a deeper look at Terry Fox beyond his status as one of Canada’s most celebrated heroes. The film draws from 96 reels of previously…

blocks.text: New Terry Fox documentary shares gripping, unseen footage from Marathon of Hope

Terry Fox is one of Canada's most recognizable heroes, with generations of Canadians having seen archival footage of his iconic 1980 run, as he crossed the country to raise awareness and money for cancer research.

But Run Terry Run, a new documentary that premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival last month, makes the case that there is still much to learn about the young man behind the Marathon of Hope.
Directed by Sean Menard, the film draws on 96 reels of previously unseen footage, bringing Fox's voice, humour, frustrations and determination to the screen.

items: Run Terry Run, the upcoming Terry Fox documentary, has a new trailer
IN PHOTOS | TIFF movies and moments

blocks.text: Menard, who previously made the self-funded MuchMusic documentary 299 Queen Street West, was inspired to search for first-hand documentation of Fox's marathon due to the limited amount of high-quality footage available. Aided by the Terry Fox Foundation, he discovered the footage in a Toronto storage unit a few blocks from his own home. He subsequently restored the reels of film to 4K quality and used it to make his film.
Here are some of the things we learned from the documentary.
1. Terry Fox didn't reach his destination — but he ran thousands of kilometres for his cause
Fox's goal was to run from St. John's to Victoria, a total distance of about 8,000 kilometres. He planned to cover about 42 kilometres — the distance of a marathon — each day.

In Ontario, however, he made several detours to speak at rallies, meet supporters and promote cancer research. Those stops meant he did not travel as far west as he might have on a more direct route — perhaps reaching Manitoba or Saskatchewan — but they did help turn the Marathon of Hope into a national movement.
He was forced to stop near Thunder Bay, Ont., on Sept. 1, 1980, after learning that the cancer had spread to his lungs. By then, he had run 5,373 kilometres in 143 days.
2. Terry Fox and his best friend fought, so Fox's younger brother joined the journey

Terry Fox and his best friend, Doug Alward, began the Marathon of Hope in St. John's on April 12, 1980, but the physical demands of the run and the strain of living together in a van had created tension.
Terry's younger brother, Darrell Fox, then 17, joined them in New Brunswick in May. He helped ease the friction between the two friends by acting as a mediator.
3. He was frustrated by some media coverage

Fox cared deeply about how journalists portrayed him and the Marathon of Hope. He became frustrated when stories failed to capture the purpose of his run, particularly when they focused on disagreements with Alward or Darrell.

Before Terry became a national figure, Toronto Star journalist Leslie Scrivener documented his journey in a weekly column called Running with Terry. Her reports helped build public support for the run, which grew from a cause many people initially doubted into a national movement.
4. He did not want sponsorship money for himself
Terry was determined that money raised throughout his run would go to cancer research. He did not want to accept sponsorship money or personal financial support.
But organizations began helping in other ways. The Canadian Cancer Society hired a publicist named Bill Vigars, Ford donated a van and Adidas provided running shoes.
The public campaign also inspired music. Country singer Nancy Ryan recorded Run, Terry, Run, written by Vern Kennedy, with proceeds donated to the Canadian Cancer Society.
Terry Fox, centre, poses with best friend Doug Alward, left, and younger brother Darrell Fox, right, in front of the Van of Hope in White River, Ont., in August 1980. (Submitted by Darrell Fox)
5. He thought a car accident contributed to his cancer
When Terry was 18, he was involved in a car accident that he believed caused or contributed to the cancer in his right knee.
Doctors, however, told him there was no connection between the accident and his osteosarcoma — a rare and aggressive form of bone cancer.
The pain he experienced after the crash was an early symptom of the disease, which was diagnosed in 1977 and ultimately led to the amputation of his right leg.
6. He drew inspiration from other children with cancer
Terry's experience recovering in hospital, including watching other young patients die from cancer, helped shape his decision to run across Canada.

The film shows how Terry wanted the Marathon of Hope to give people affected by cancer a sense that something could be done. His goal was to raise money for research so future patients would have better treatment options.
7. He disliked going to the doctor and avoided it
Terry Fox was determined and disciplined, but he did not enjoy medical appointments. The documentary reveals a young man who resisted seeing doctors and did not want to be defined by his illness.
This scene from Run Terry Run captures Terry Fox reattaching his prosthetic leg at a roadside rest stop in northern Ontario after swimming with friends in the summer of 1980. (Elevation Pictures)
8. He had a complicated relationship with his prosthetic leg

As Terry lost weight during the run, his prosthetic leg became increasingly difficult and painful to wear. Because it no longer fit properly, it caused friction against his stump, and he needed to have it replaced. In one particularly difficult moment, Terry becomes angry after someone notices blood running down his leg.
The documentary footage captures the growing strain between Terry's changing physical condition and his determination to keep running.
9. Quebec was a difficult part of the journey
Terry was frustrated by his experience in Quebec, where the language barrier made communication more difficult.

Many drivers were unaware of the Marathon of Hope and repeatedly forced him off the road. Concerned for his safety, Alward and Darrell urged Terry to wear a safety vest, but he refused because he wanted people to see his Marathon of Hope shirt.
Ontario brought a different challenge. By then, public attention had become overwhelming. Terry was no longer simply a young man running along the highway — he had become a national celebrity.

Terry Fox, left, walks with 10-year-old Greg Scott in Terrace Bay, Ont., on Aug. 27, 1980. Both lost a leg to bone cancer. Scott came from Welland, Ont., to meet Fox on his marathon run. (Boris Spremo/Toronto Star via Getty Images)
10. He could still let loose despite the seriousness of his mission
The footage also shows Terry's playful side. He jokes with Darrell and Alward, pulls pranks and enjoys moments of levity.

The film includes a particularly touching moment in which Terry is able to relax and connect with a young boy who also had a leg amputation. It is a reminder that Terry Fox was still a 21-year-old who could laugh, play and be silly.
Why Terry Fox's brother feels new doc does the icon justice
11. Darrell Fox did not know his brother had gone to the hospital

On Sept. 1, 1980, in Thunder Bay, Ont., Terry was having trouble breathing and told Alward to drive him to the nearest hospital. Darrell, who was travelling in a support vehicle behind them, initially thought it was a regular stop. He didn't realize this would be the end of the Marathon of Hope.

For 93 days, Darrell had known where his brother was at almost every moment. Suddenly his brother was nowhere to be seen. When Darrell arrived at the hospital, he learned that the cancer had spread to Fox's lungs.

At the hospital, Darrell says the roles were suddenly reversed. "It was Terry that was trying to comfort me," he told CBC News. "He had already accepted it and was thinking of the positive somehow — that this will only give more meaning to what [he's] just accomplished.
"I think that defines who Terry Fox is, always thinking of others and not himself," he added.

Terry Fox, pictured at a speaking event for 2,000 supporters in Gravenhurst, Ont., on Aug. 11, 1980, helped bring cancer into the public conversation at a time when it was rarely discussed openly. (Elevation Pictures)
Terry Fox's legacy

Terry died nine months later, in June 1981 at age 22, but the fundraising campaign he started continues worldwide. Annual Terry Fox runs, which take place in Canadian communities and at schools each fall, have raised more than $1 billion for cancer research.

Honoured with the Order of Canada at 22, Terry Fox remains an inspiration. His brother Darrell hopes audiences leave the new documentary with the sense that his brother's example is not impossible to follow.
"Terry was just an average guy," he said. "But look what he did. Look what he accomplished."
Run Terry Run opens in theatres on Oct. 9.

articles.title: The WNBA set an attendance record. What new heights can the league reach?
articles.summary: Experts say the WNBA could play more games in larger venues as it surges in popularity, thanks to the rise of star players, new teams and a wave of interest in women's sports more broadly.

image.caption: Golden State Valkyries guard Tiffany Hayes celebrates during Game 2 of the WNBA semifinals against the Las Vegas Aces on Wednesday. (Jeff Chiu/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Sports
Experts say the WNBA could play more games in larger venues as it surges in popularity, thanks to the rise of star players, new teams and a wave of interest in women's sports more broadly.
Experts say league could play more games in larger venues as it surges in popularity
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 09, 2026 4:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 2 hours ago

The latest season of the WNBA set a new attendance record and experts say the rise of star players, new teams and a wave of interest in women's sports more broadly are fuelling the league's growing popularity.

Some 3.79 million fans attended WNBA games in 2026, according to a Sports Business Journal analysis this week. That's a 20 per cent increase from the previous year, driven by the 25 games that were relocated to larger arenas to meet higher demand.
Average capacity was at 90 per cent or higher for eight of the league's 15 teams over the past season, the analysis also showed. Overall, the league average was 83 per cent.

items: Valkyries, Dream each 1 win away from WNBA Finals
Gabby Williams powers Valkyries past defending champion Aces in Game 1 of WNBA semifinals

blocks.text: "If you look at the numbers, nobody's really surprised," said Cheri Bradish, an associate professor and director of the Future of Sport Lab at Toronto Metropolitan University.
"We know that the WNBA has [more than] 25 years behind it, and so the growth of the league is very much following the hockey-stick curve that folks expected."
2020 'Wubble' season

Ann Pegoraro, the Lang chair in sport management at the University of Guelph, says a "pivotal moment" in the league's ascent was the 2020 season, when the WNBA — like the NBA — played without crowds in a COVID-19 pandemic isolation zone called the "Wubble."
"People were in their homes and had a chance to watch, and they saw how good the women's game is," Pegoraro told CBC News.
Around the same time, women's college basketball surged in popularity, propelled by stars such as Caitlin Clark, who brought a huge following with her to the WNBA.
That has translated into greater sponsorship revenue, expansion teams and now attendance records, Pegoraro said.
Local group looking to bring WNBA team to Vancouver
Larger arenas draw record crowds
The Toronto Tempo is one of those expansion teams, and became the first WNBA team in Canada this year.

While the Tempo finished 11-33 and didn't make the playoffs, the team drew 20,996 fans to the Bell Centre in Montreal for a July game against the Dallas Wings — the biggest crowd for a regular-season game in WNBA history.
Pegoraro said there has been some hesitancy in the past to play games in larger venues amid fears that empty seats would fuel detractors who have argued no one cares about women's sports.
But "every time a team plays in a larger venue, they dispel that myth quite quickly," she said, pointing to the Tempo game in Montreal as a recent example.
The Professional Women's Hockey League (PWHL) set attendance records in 2024, when Montreal took on Toronto at the Bell Centre.
According to Pegoraro, women's leagues need to strike a "fine balance" between keeping interest up and ensuring that fans have access to games.
"I think we're going to start to see them move into the larger arenas on a more regular basis," she said of the WNBA.
Already, at least one WNBA team has announced plans to permanently move into a bigger arena.
Atlanta Dream forward Angel Reese sets up for a foul shot against the New York Liberty in Game 2 of the WNBA semifinals on Wednesday. (Daniel Varnado/The Associated Press)

The Atlanta Dream, who are looking to sweep their semifinals series against the New York Liberty on Thursday, said this week that they'll play all their 2027 home games at State Farm Arena, the 16,888-seat home of the NBA's Atlanta Hawks.
The Dream said it has seen more than 400 per cent growth in season ticket members over the past five years.

"State Farm Arena gives us the opportunity to welcome thousands of additional fans while creating an even bigger stage for women's basketball in Atlanta," said Morgan Shaw Parker, the team's president, in a written statement.
New commissioner
As the WNBA's popularity has grown, it has also became a focus in heated debates around social issues, from women's rights to racism and the inclusion of transgender women in sports.

This season, Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham's comments about trans athletes drew protests and widespread media attention. The WNBA, whose fanbase includes many members of the 2SLGTBQ+ community, does not have any openly transgender players.
Two ex-NBA players announced plans to join the 2027 WNBA draft in what critics said was a "bad-faith" stunt that denigrated the league.

Both Pegoraro and Bradish say that negative attention won't stop WNBA players from speaking out — nor will it significantly distract the league "from the growth and development of the game," Bradish told CBC News.
How the WNBA got sucked into America’s culture war
She noted that the WNBA will soon choose a commissioner to succeed Cathy Engelbert, who is stepping down at the end of the year.
"Then from there, how do they strategically grow?" said Bradish. She said playing in larger venues and possibly adding new expansion teams will be part of that discussion.

Pegoraro said the league could also consider expanding its playoff model to give fans more games to watch. Currently, the WNBA playoffs feature four best-of-three first-round matchups, two best-of-five semifinals and a best-of-seven final.
"Two games and [teams] are done, is not enough in playoffs," she said of the first round. "They need to give these women more games in the playoffs to play."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jillian Kestler-D'Amours is a senior writer at CBC based in Montreal. You can reach her at jillian.kestler-d.amours@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Canada can't launch rockets on its own. A handful of companies want to change that
articles.summary: Canada has long relied on its allies to get technologies like satellites into space. But as the cross-border relationship with the U.S. changes, a handful of companies — including the newest player,…

blocks.text: Business

Canada has long relied on its allies to get technologies like satellites into space. But as the cross-border relationship with the U.S. changes, a handful of companies — including the newest player, Canada Rocket Company — are trying to change that and capitalize on a growing market.
The newest Canadian rocket builder is targeting 2032 for the first launch of its medium-lift vessel
The high-stakes race to get Canadian rockets into orbit
As the only G7 nation without its own launch capabilities, Canada is eager to have a Canadian-made rocket.

A handful of Canadian companies are racing to give the country its own way to space as quickly as possible — at the same time that some SpaceX customers worry the industry giant could soon give fewer rides into orbit.
But the rocket companies are working to complete an expensive task under a tight deadline and ever-changing government priorities, making the journey to space anything but simple.

Because Canada has no ability to launch rockets itself, customers in this country — both private companies and governments — are dependent on outside forces to put their satellites in orbit. They're often American ones — namely SpaceX, which launched all 12 Canadian satellites sent up in 2025, according to Canadian industry publication SpaceQ.

And those pieces of technology are critical, says Marc Boucher, founder of the Canadian space publication SpaceQ. They power telecommunications, as well as military uses like threat detection, and for earth observation like wildfire tracking.
If Canada doesn't control its own launches, Boucher says the fear is that foreign entities could refuse to launch Canadian tech.
'Canada cannot permit itself to fall behind' in space: MacKinnon touts Space Launch Act
A sovereign solution

The Canadian government named space as a key sovereign capability in its February Defence Industrial Strategy and introduced legislation in April that would allow the government to authorize launches from Canadian soil if passed.

Funding has flowed in recent months, too, including $8.3 million each for three Canadian companies working on rockets, as part of a multi-year contest aimed at achieving light-lift rocket capabilities by 2028.

NordSpace — a company launched in 2022, focused on building satellites and robotic space technologies as well as the launch pad and rocket to get them off the ground — was one of them. Its first suborbital rocket test launch attempt in 2025 was unsuccessful, but the company says it plans to try again soon, possibly within weeks.
NordSpace's suborbital rocket on the launchpad in 2025. The company's first attempt to launch the vessel in summer 2025 was unsuccessful, but it's preparing to try again soon. (Peter Cowan/CBC)
Reaction Dynamics was another. That company has been working on a unique engine design since 2017.
Both NordSpace and Reaction Dynamics are working to get rockets to orbit by 2028, in line with the government's target.

items: NordSpace scrubs latest attempt to launch rocket in N.L., will try again later

blocks.text: Canada Rocket Company — the newest player — rounds out the three.

CEO Hugh Kolias founded Canada Rocket Company late last year with the goal of building a medium-lift rocket — a middle-size category that can carry potentially dozens of satellites into low Earth orbit at once — powered by nine methalox-fuelled engines.

Hugh Kolias, founder of Canada Rocket Company, is pictured in the company's Etobicoke headquarters on Sept. 23. With newfound attention from the Canadian government on space sovereignty and the help of private funding, Kolias says he is confident his team can make it to space by 2032. (Laura MacNaughton/CBC)
The company has hired dozens of engineers — many of them from top rocket firms like SpaceX and Blue Origin — and is building a $30-million test facility in London, Ont., to help meet that goal.
It will take time and lots of testing to build such a vessel, and the target for a first launch isn't until 2032.
Kolias says his firm has attracted $22 million in private investment on top of the government cash.
He and Boucher both say funding has long been an obstacle in Canada that's made the already expensive and difficult task of building rockets extra challenging.
"We have the skillsets … because Canada produces a lot of good engineers. But where we've been lacking is funding," Boucher said.
But with private and public funds flowing, Kolias is optimistic that tide has turned — even if some other CEOs and experts are more cautiously hopeful.

Executives of Canada Rocket Company and other attendees toss the first shovels of dirt at the groundbreaking of the firm's test facility under construction in London, Ont. (Submitted by Canada Rocket Company)
Fly away, Falcon 9

At the same time, SpaceX plans to eventually scale back its Falcon 9 rocket as it transitions to a bigger vessel called Starship, according to Elon Musk — a worry for customers who rely on the company to get their satellites to space, but a potential opportunity for emerging rocket makers.
SpaceX's reusable, medium-lift Falcon 9 transports the company's own Starlink satellites to space, as well as those of other companies at a cost.

The company has reportedly started turning away satellite customers looking to launch on the Falcon 9 past 2028 as it shifts to the new rocket. That's especially concerning for smaller players who rely on SpaceX's rideshare program, which allows multiple companies to send up one or two satellites each on a shared rocket.

A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket lifts off from Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Fla., on Sept. 24, 2025. The Falcon 9 has become the workhorse of the launch industry, and its eventual phaseout has some customers worried about how they'll get to space. (John Raoux/The Associated Press)
Canadian satellite communications company Kepler has launched the majority of its 33 satellites on the Falcon 9.

CEO Mina Mitry, who is an adviser to Canada Rocket Company, says he expects SpaceX competitors — including Rocket Lab, which he's already secured a future ride with — will be able to take up some of that demand. But smaller players could feel the pinch of less rideshare access.
"If you're looking to launch one, two, three satellites on an experimental basis, your barrier to entry now has grown significantly," Mitry said. "That's a huge problem for the industry."
The Falcon wind-down only makes having a Canadian rocket maker more important, Mitry adds.

And with its medium-lift rocket aimed at the same market as the Falcon 9, Kolias is hoping Canada Rocket Company can capture some of the market SpaceX leaves behind once it moves on to the bigger Starship vessel.
A long way from liftoff
At NordSpace, CEO Rahul Goel is more cautiously optimistic.

Goel had dreamed of building rockets since childhood, but says he spent the first decade of his career building another company and making his own millions to invest in NordSpace "because nobody would write a cheque."

He says the attention on his industry and the funding his company has received is positive. But he worries it could go away again soon, and is rushing to establish launch capabilities in case that happens.

Rahul Goel, founder and CEO of NordSpace, says he is proud to be launching an all-Canadian made and built rocket from Canadian soil, particularly at a time when there's been an increase in nationalism. (Anand Ram/CBC News)
"I've seen how quickly the tides can turn and I know how quickly the tides can turn back," Goel said.

Boucher of SpaceQ estimates it could take upwards of $50 million to get a rocket that's reliably launching from Canada. He says more private and public money for each of the companies will likely be needed to reach orbit — especially on the tight 2028 timeline.

"This is not a short-term thing. This is a long-term play," Boucher said. "It took SpaceX … years before they got their first successful launch. It's going to take several years before we get to the point where we see regular launches from Canada."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Abby Hughes is a writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Orillia, Ont., she studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. She covers news from the worlds of business, entertainment, health, science and education, and her favourite stories focus on the real people in those areas — the customers, fans, patients, citizens and students. You can reach her with story ideas at abby.hughes@cbc.ca.

image.caption: Chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee Jorgen Watne Frydnes speaking at the Peace Prize ceremony last year [FILE December 2025]Image: Stian Lysberg Solum/NTB/REUTERS

blocks.text: What you need to know

items: Navanethem "Navi" Pillay has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
The Peace Prize committee is the only one that regularly recognizes achievements from the previous year
It has been awarded 106 times to 143 laureates between 1901 and 2025
The prize carries a cash award of 12 million Swedish kronor (around $1.2 million; €1 million)
This week, Nobel laureates have already been named in medicine, physics, chemistry, and literature.

blocks.text: Below is all the news and views, previews and reviews surrounding the award of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize.
October 9, 2026
Nobel Peace Prize awarded to Navi Pillay
South African human rights lawyer Navanethem "Navi" Pillay has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize.

Born in 1941 in Durban, Pillay grew up under apartheid and became one of South Africa's first women of Indian descent to practice law. She defended anti-apartheid activists and fought against discriminatory prison conditions.

After apartheid, she became a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, where she helped establish landmark legal precedents recognizing rape as an act of genocide. She later served as a judge at the International Criminal Court and as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 to 2014.
More recently, she chaired a UN commission investigating human rights violations in Israel and the Palestinian territories.

articles.title: Winner of 2026 Nobel peace prize to be announced - Europe Live
articles.summary:
The winner will be announced in a ceremony that starts at 10am UK time (11am CEST)

The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize will be announced this morning, with all sorts of speculation about who…

blocks.text: Key events

items: nowOne hour to go
25m agoMorning opening: Who will win the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize?

blocks.text: One hour to go
It’s one hour to go until we learn who is the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize winner.
10am UK, 11am CEST.

blocks.caption: The room where a press conference will be given to announce the winner of the Nobel Peace Prize 2026 at the Nobel Institute in Oslo, Norway. Photograph: Javad Parsa/NTB/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Last year’s peace prize was won by Venezuelan politician María Corina Machado for her dogged struggle to rescue the South American country from its fate as “a brutal, authoritarian state”.
She later presented her award to Donald Trump, meeting him in the White House, nearly a fortnight after he ordered the abduction of Venezuela’s president, Nicolás Maduro.
In his 1895 will, Swedish chemist and inventor Alfred Nobel wrote:

“All of my remaining realisable assets are to be disbursed as follows: the capital, converted to safe securities by my executors, is to constitute a fund, the interest on which is to be distributed annually as prizes to those who, during the preceding year, have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind. The interest is to be divided into five equal parts and distributed as follows: one part to the person who made the most important discovery or invention in the field of physics; one part to the person who made the most important chemical discovery or improvement; one part to the person who made the most important discovery within the domain of physiology or medicine; one part to the person who, in the field of literature, produced the most outstanding work in an ideal direction; and one part to the person who has done the most or best to advance fellowship among nations, the abolition or reduction of standing armies, and the establishment and promotion of peace congresses. The prizes for physics and chemistry are to be awarded by the Swedish Academy of Sciences; that for physiological or medical achievements by the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm; that for literature by the Academy in Stockholm; and that for champions of peace by a committee of five persons to be selected by the Norwegian Storting. It is my express wish that when awarding the prizes, no consideration be given to nationality, but that the prize be awarded to the worthiest person, whether or not they are Scandinavian.”
And here we are, 125 years later!
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor, which is about €1.1m or £910,000.
Morning opening: Who will win the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize?

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize will be announced this morning, with all sorts of speculation about who could be this year’s worthy winner.
(Despite his hopes, Donald Trump is very unlikely to win it, again.)
Mykola Kuleba and Save Ukraine who work on rescuing Ukrainian children abducted by Russia during the war have long been among the favourites, alongside Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms.

But in the last few hours, Yulia Navalnaya, the wife of late Alexei Navalny, has gone straight to the very top of the list on some popular prediction websites. Could she be the one – just days after Vladimir Putin’s birthday in Russia?
Well: no one really knows, except a handful of members of the Norwegian Nobel Committee.
Its chair Jørgen Watne Frydnes will appear in front of cameras at 10am UK time (11am CEST) this morning to give us the name of the winner.
We will bring it live to you here.
It’s Friday, 9 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: Meet India's feisty Gen Z protester who is taking on Modi
articles.summary: Neha Bora has emerged as one of the most recognisable faces from India's recent Gen Z-led protests.

blocks.text: When India's Gen Z-led protesters return to Delhi this weekend for demonstrations seeking the resignation of the country's top election official, one of the prominent faces at the forefront will be that of a 29-year-old PhD student.

Neha Bora is a theatre artist and activist who has been with the All India Students' Association (Aisa), a Left-wing organisation known for campus politics, for the past decade and been its president for the past two years.
But Neha's - who uses "they" and "them" as personal pronouns - visibility is no longer limited to campuses.

Viral videos over the past few days show them being dragged through the street by a group of female police officials, climbing on top of police barricades, raising their fist and shouting slogans, and being detained.
Photos of them smiling while being carried away by policewomen have also gone viral.
In a recent BBC Bangla interview, Neha played down the attention they've been receiving.

"I know it happened in front of the camera so it seems like it's something different," they said. "But I have seen all student activists with the Left doing the same things that I have been doing. It's just that there is a camera on me, so people think something different is happening."

The attention on Neha comes at a time when several high-profile protests are being held on India's streets in what is being seen as one of the biggest challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's 12 years in power.

There's the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - a Gen Z-led online satirical movement - that held weeks-long protests in Delhi in the summer over education reforms. It ended in July only after education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation.

Separately, some of India's opposition parties, especially the Congress, have also taken to the streets over electoral reforms. For the past few days, videos of Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra being shoved and jostled and detained have gone viral and made headlines in India.

Saturday's protest in Delhi has been called by the CJP, which is seeking the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating electoral rolls to favour Modi's BJP. Both the Election Commission and the BJP have rejected the accusation.
Although not a member of the CJP, Neha has said their group would also participate.
Born in the northern state of Uttarakhand, Neha lived in different cities as a child as their army officer father moved for his postings.
After graduating from Delhi University, they did a master's degree from Ambedkar University in the capital and are now a PhD student at the prestigious Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU).
Neha first came into the spotlight in the summer during the CJP's protest over education reforms.

Neha and Aisa were at the protest from the start, but not many knew them at that point. That changed after 28 June, when educationist and scientist Sonam Wangchuk began a hunger strike in CJP's support and Neha and a few others from Aisa also joined him.
"It was an obvious choice for us. We've been protesting against paper leaks and education reforms for a long time," Neha later said in an interview.
While most of the attention was focused on Wangchuk, whose reputation and presence galvanised the movement, Neha's outspokenness and combative speeches began to get them noticed.
After Wangchuk and others were moved to hospital, Neha continued fasting despite having lost 8kg.
Even after being moved to hospital, they said in a video: "The fight continues. Once I've recovered, we'll meet you again on the streets to continue our fight for our right."
After the protests ended in July, Neha has established themselves as a Gen Z leader who's courted by the CJP and media, besides appearing alongside Rahul Gandhi at press conferences.

But Neha's involvement with Aisa and leftist politics and statements criticising PM Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and other BJP leaders have also led to "lots of disagreements with my family as my parents are staunch supporters of BJP".

And last month, at least three police complaints were lodged, external in Uttar Pradesh state by BJP against Neha for making "objectionable remarks" against the chief minister - they came two days after Aisa's police complaint that Neha had received death threats, external.

Neha, who has been travelling to many Indian cities to participate in protests in support of students, also made headlines when a man allegedly threw ink, external at them during a protest march in Jharkhand state. A photo Neha shared on Instagram showed their face streaked with ink stains. Police said they had detained the man.
The noisy protests and repeated detentions have earned Neha a reputation for being a street fighter.
"The streets have always dictated the course of politics in this country and they will continue to do so, more so in the coming few years," they told BBC Bangla.
"If we look at the social changes of the recent past, those social changes did not come from people sitting in parliament; they came from the streets," they said.
Now as the authorities gear up for 10 October's protest at Jantar Mantar against CEC Kumar, Neha and Aisa have said they would be back in the streets with the CJP to "protect democracy".

articles.title: Why Elon Musk is taking on India's richest man over Starlink
articles.summary: Musk has taken pot-shots at Reliance owner Mukesh Ambani as Starlink struggles to launch in India.

blocks.text: Elon Musk has questioned whether billionaire Mukesh Ambani is the "real boss of India" as his satellite internet company Starlink struggles to secure final approval to launch in the country.

The remark came a day after Musk accused unnamed powerful business interests of trying to block Starlink's entry into India. He then singled out Ambani, whose Reliance conglomerate owns Jio, India's biggest mobile network operator.
India has rejected Musk's allegations, saying its satellite communications rules are fair and non-discriminatory.
Ambani and Reliance Group have not responded to Musk's remarks. The BBC has reached out to them for comment
The row comes as competition grows in India's satellite internet market, with Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel also preparing to launch services.
The rivalry is complicated by the fact that Starlink has also partnered with Ambani's Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel.

In March 2025, both companies signed agreements with SpaceX to distribute Starlink equipment and services in India, subject to government approval. The companies also said they could explore sharing network infrastructure. The BBC has also reached out to Bharti Airtel for comment.
Musk first made the allegations on Wednesday, accusing "certain oligarchs" of maintaining a "monopolistic chokehold" on Indian consumers.
"You can guess who they are," he wrote on X, external, adding that blocking Starlink was "a crime against the people of India".

On Thursday, India's Ministry of Communications responded, saying that three operators - Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio Satellite Communications - were at broadly the same stage of the approval process, with all three awaiting security clearances and spectrum allocation before they can launch commercial services.
"The suggestion that the framework or its application is unfair or discriminatory is baseless and misconceived," the ministry said, without naming Musk directly.
Musk continued to question the delay, saying Starlink was already licensed in more than 165 countries.

"Starlink is licensed in over 165 countries and has spent five years complying with every single law and requirement of the government of India, so why still no license? Is Ambani the real boss of India?" he wrote on X on Thursday.

Starlink, owned by Musk's SpaceX, uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas where mobile networks and broadband cables are difficult or expensive to install.
The company has been trying to enter India since 2021 and has secured key licences. But it still needs final security clearances and spectrum allocation before it can begin commercial services.

Wednesday's row unfolded as senior executives from Starlink, Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel gathered at the India Mobile Congress in Delhi, where all three companies discussed their plans for satellite internet services.

Speaking at the event, Akash Ambani, chairman of Reliance Jio Infocomm and Mukesh Ambani's son, said the company was developing its own satellite communications technology and working towards regulatory approvals.
Asked by a reporter about Musk's allegations, Akash declined to comment and only said, "We want to be heads down and deliver value to our Indian consumers."
Bharti Airtel chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal said his company's satellite venture was also awaiting government approvals.

SpaceX executive Lauren Dreyer, who oversees Starlink's business operations, said the company had spent years working with Indian regulators and had built security controls into its network to meet the country's requirements.

Security has been a key concern surrounding Starlink's entry into India. In 2024, Indian authorities said they had recovered Starlink equipment during a drug-smuggling investigation in the remote Andaman and Nicobar Islands and an army operation in the northeastern state of Manipur.
Musk said at that time that Starlink's service had never been active in India, arguing that the equipment recovered by authorities could not have been using its satellite network.
Questions also remain over how affordable the service would be for Indian consumers, particularly those in rural areas.
India is one of the world's largest internet markets but access remains uneven, particularly in remote areas where mobile networks and broadband cables are difficult or expensive to build.

Musk has argued that Starlink could help bridge this gap. "Starlink in India would enable high-speed, affordable internet connectivity for those who can't afford current prices or who don't have a connection at all!" he wrote on X on Wednesday.
The company has yet to announce prices for India, but some experts say its plans elsewhere suggest the service could be beyond the reach of many Indian households.
In the US, Starlink's residential plans start at $55 a month, although prices and equipment costs vary by plan and location.

image.caption: Kuala Lumpur's skyline has been shrouded in haze for weeksImage: Wong Fok Loy/SOPA Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Malaysian authorities closed schools in the capital, Kuala Lumpur, and other parts of the country on Friday due to haze caused by forest fires in nearby Indonesia.

"I have instructed all state education departments and district education offices to continue monitoring the haze situation and take immediate action if conditions require it," Education Minister Fadhlina Sidek said in a statement.
The minister announced which schools would be fully closed and which would continue operating partially in five states and two federal territories.
"Going forward, we will ensure that any decision to close schools is communicated in advance so that parents have enough time to prepare," Fadhlina added.

blocks.caption: Indonesia has been struggling to contain a series of forest fires Image: Elly Priatno/DW

blocks.text: Deteriorating air quality
Air quality measurements in Kuala Lumpur remain at "unhealthy" levels, with Swiss air-quality monitor IQAir ranking the Malaysian capital among the most polluted cities in the world.
Malaysia's King Sultan Ibrahim weighed in on the issue on Thursday, saying schools should be closed whenever air-quality readings reach 150 or higher on the Air Pollutant Index (API).
API readings above 200 are considered very unhealthy, while levels above 300 are deemed hazardous. Readings exceeding 500 constitute the threshold for declaring a local emergency.
Kuala Lumpur recorded an API reading of 170 on Friday.

The city lies about 1,200 kilometers (745 miles) from Indonesia, where a wave of forest fires has affected millions of people since August. According to IQAir, Kuala Lumpur is currently the world's second most polluted city, behind only neighboring Singapore.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Thursday that Indonesian President Prabowo ​Subianto had ⁠agreed to take measures to tackle the haze, but did not provide more details.

articles.title: Adidas accuses Australian label White Fox of ‘trading off its reputation’ with use of four-stripe branding
articles.summary:
Global sportswear brand is suing online retailer in the federal court for selling clothes featuring ‘deceptively similar’ design

  • Get our

blocks.text: Global sportswear brand Adidas claims Australian label White Fox is trying to trade off its reputation by infringing its distinctive three-stripe trademark.
Adidas is suing the online fast-fashion retailer in the Federal Court for selling clothes with a four-stripe design, which it argues is deceptively similar to its classic design.
White Fox rejected repeated requests to stop selling and promoting clothing bearing the four parallel stripes, its rival claims.
During the first mention of the dispute on Friday, Adidas’s barrister Patrick Flynn SC argued the Sydney-based company had been using the stripes as a trademark for months.
He pointed to a picture of a White Fox-endorsed influencer wearing the company’s four-stripe shorts with genuine Adidas shoes as a promotion that would confuse consumers.
“There’s an intention to trade off our reputation,” Flynn said.
Adidas has held the trademark for a three-stripe design in Australia for more than 50 years and successfully sued another retailer for infringement over shoes bearing four stripes in 2013.
It meant the action filed against White Fox in September was “not uncharted territory”, Flynn noted.
“This is a pretty simple matter,” he said.
White Fox’s barrister Ed Heerey KC said the Australian company would argue the four stripes emblazoned on the label’s clothing were simply decorative rather than a trademark.

blocks.caption: (L-R) Adidas track pants alongside White Fox track pants. Composite: Federal Court of Australia

blocks.text: He highlighted similar items bearing the four stripes from other brands such as fast-fashion labels Princess Polly, Glassons, and Shein.
“Obviously Adidas has a reputation,” Heerey said.
“Their own slogan is that it’s the brand with three stripes. Emphasis on the three.”
The boutique will interrogate whether the use of four stripes was deceptively similar to Adidas’s trademark and whether any consumers would actually be misled.
after newsletter promotion
He noted the 2013 judgment in favour of Adidas found it was common for branding to be placed on the side of shoes, but there was no such common practice for clothing.
Adidas is seeking orders that will prevent White Fox making clothing with four stripes and force it to hand over profits it made on the products.
Justice Ian Jackman – brother of one of Australia’s most famous exports Hugh Jackman – set the dispute down for a hearing in early 2027.
It marks the first high-profile litigation of this kind against White Fox Boutique, which has become a major player in the retail industry since it was launched in Sydney in 2013.
Co-founders Georgia and Daniel Contos, who own the company with Daniel’s mother Melina Maceri, focused on social media and influencer marketing to build their brand.
The online retailer later expanded to the US and UK and generated $542m in revenue in the year to June 2025.
Meanwhile Adidas, which generated a record $39.9bn in 2025, has vigilantly defended its three-stripe trademark across the globe with varying success.
The sportswear giant recently lost its trademark infringement cases against luxury brand Thom Browne in the US, UK, and Germany.
The upcoming battle in the federal court could prove to be a battleground for Adidas in a world of fast fashion and prolific imitation.
